x: An architecture in which a generative language model is conditioned on documents fetched by a retrieval system at inference time, combining parametric memory (model weights) with non-parametric memory (an external index). Introduced by Lewis et al. (2020) as a way to give seq2seq models explicit, updatable access to knowledge and provenance for their outputs. Instead of forcing the model to memorize everything, give it an open-book exam: look up the relevant passages first, then write the answer with those passages in front of it.

A learned mapping from discrete items (words, symbols, documents) to dense, continuous vectors in a relatively low-dimensional space, such that geometric proximity in the space reflects semantic or functional similarity. Popularized for words by Mikolov et al. (2013), whose word2vec models showed that such vectors capture syntactic and semantic regularities as directions in the space. Turn things into points on a map where 'nearby' means 'similar in meaning or behavior', so a computer can measure similarity with distance instead of exact string matching.

A database system designed to store, index, and query high-dimensional vectors (typically embeddings), supporting fast similarity search — usually approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search — rather than exact-match lookups. It is the standard retrieval infrastructure behind semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. A search engine for meaning: instead of finding rows that match keywords, it finds the stored vectors closest to a query vector, at millisecond latency over millions of items.

A graph-structured knowledge representation in which nodes denote entities and edges denote typed relations between them, typically augmented with schema (ontology), identity resolution, and context. Hogan et al. (2021) survey the data models, query languages, deductive and inductive techniques used to build and exploit such graphs. A machine-readable map of 'things' and how they relate — companies, instruments, events, concepts — so software can traverse relationships instead of just matching text.

In computer and information science, an explicit specification of a conceptualization: a set of representational primitives — classes, attributes, and relations — with definitions of their meaning and constraints on their logically consistent use, used to model a domain of knowledge (Gruber). Ontologies sit at the 'semantic' level, above logical and physical data models, and enable interoperability and automated reasoning. A formal contract about what kinds of things exist in a domain and how they may relate, so that different systems and people use the same words to mean the same things.

A controlled vocabulary organized as a hierarchy of broader/narrower (parent/child) concepts, used to classify content consistently. ANSI/NISO Z39.19 defines conventions for constructing, formatting, and managing such vocabularies — including lists, synonym rings, taxonomies, and thesauri — as knowledge organization systems. A family tree of categories: every item gets a place, and the place tells you what more general and more specific categories it belongs to.

a: preferred term canonical name authorized heading
x: The single designated representation of a concept within a controlled vocabulary, to which all synonymous or variant terms (aliases) point. ANSI/NISO Z39.19 calls this the 'preferred term': the term selected to represent a concept in displays and indexing, with non-preferred variants linked to it by equivalence relationships. One concept, one official name — every other way of saying it is a pointer back to that name, so nothing is counted or filed twice.

a: synonym resolution name normalization equivalence mapping
x: The process of mapping non-preferred or variant terms (aliases, abbreviations, synonyms, misspellings) to the canonical concept they denote, using the equivalence relationships of a controlled vocabulary. In ANSI/NISO Z39.19 terms, this applies the USE/UF (used-for) cross-references that link non-preferred terms to preferred terms. Whatever name someone uses — 'MACD', 'moving average convergence divergence', 'MACD indicator' — the system figures out they all mean the same concept.

a: named entity disambiguation NED entity disambiguation
x: The NLP task of detecting entity mentions in text and resolving each mention to the specific entity it refers to in a knowledge base. Neural entity linking systems typically combine candidate generation, mention-context encoding, and entity ranking to disambiguate mentions such as 'Apple' (company vs. fruit) or 'Mercury' (element vs. planet). Figure out which real-world thing a name in the text actually points to, and attach that thing's knowledge-base ID so downstream systems know exactly what is being discussed.

Information about the entities, activities, and agents involved in producing a piece of data or content, which can be used to assess its quality, reliability, or trustworthiness. The W3C PROV family of specifications defines an interoperable model (PROV-DM), ontology (PROV-O), and serializations for representing and exchanging such provenance. A chain of custody for information: where did this claim come from, who produced it, and what processing steps touched it along the way.

The property of a knowledge system that every asserted claim can be traced back, through its provenance records, to the specific source document and location that supports it. It operationalizes the attribution and derivation relations of provenance models such as W3C PROV at the granularity of individual claims. No orphan claims: for every statement the system makes, you can click through to the exact document, page, or section it rests on and verify it yourself.

A governance label recording the degree of verification a knowledge artifact has undergone — for example this library's ladder of candidate, provisional, reviewed, trusted, and disputed. It reflects the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's premise that trustworthiness of AI outputs must be actively managed through defined processes, not assumed. A badge that says how thoroughly a claim has been checked and by whom, so consumers know how much they can lean on it.

The generation by a language model of content that is fluent and plausible but factually incorrect or unsupported by any source — including fabricated facts, citations, and data. NIST and industry glossaries increasingly prefer the term 'confabulation'; hallucination remains the widely used name. The model is a confident storyteller optimizing for plausible text, not a database: when it does not know, it often makes something up that sounds right rather than saying so.

Connecting a generative model's output to verifiable sources of information so that its claims are tethered to specific data rather than invented. Grounding reduces hallucination, anchors responses to designated data sources, and provides auditability through links to the supporting sources. Make the model show its work: every claim must hang on a document you can open and check, not just on what the model happens to remember.

Model output constrained to follow a declared machine-readable format — typically JSON conforming to a schema — rather than free-form prose, so downstream systems can parse, validate, and route it deterministically. JSON Schema is the standard declarative language for describing the required structure and constraints. Instead of an essay you must re-read, make the model fill in a form with fixed fields, so software can consume the answer directly.

The automated checking of a data instance (e.g., a JSON document) against a formal schema that declares its required structure, types, and constraints, using a validator implementing the schema specification. In the JSON ecosystem, a JSON Schema validator verifies that a document conforms to the declared keywords before the data is accepted. A bouncer with a checklist: data gets in only if every required field is present, correctly typed, and within the declared limits.

a: function calling tool calling API calling
x: The ability of a language model to invoke external tools — calculators, search engines, databases, trading or market-data APIs — by emitting structured calls whose results are fed back into the model's context. Schick et al.'s Toolformer (2023) showed a model can learn in a self-supervised way which APIs to call, when, and with what arguments. Let the model operate the instruments instead of playing every instrument itself: it decides what it needs, calls the tool, and reads the result.

The modular information stores that give a language agent persistence and context beyond a single prompt: working memory (the active context window) plus long-term episodic, semantic, and procedural memory. The CoALA framework (Sumers et al., 2023) organizes language agents around these memory modules, an action space over them, and a decision cycle that reads and writes them. The agent's notebooks: a scratchpad for right now, a diary of what happened, a reference book of facts, and a habits manual for how to do things.

The long-term memory of an agent's own past experiences: records of specific episodes — observations, actions taken, and outcomes — from earlier decision cycles or sessions. In the CoALA framework, episodic memory stores sequences of past events the agent can retrieve to inform current decisions, paralleling the cognitive-science distinction introduced by Tulving. The agent's diary: 'last Tuesday the user asked X, I did Y, and the result was Z' — specific events, retrievable later.

An agent's store of decontextualized facts and knowledge about the world and about the user — as distinct from records of specific episodes. In the CoALA framework, semantic memory holds world knowledge (including facts distilled from experience) that the agent retrieves to ground reasoning. The agent's reference book: facts like 'ES has a $50 multiplier' or 'this user is risk-averse', without any memory of when or where they were learned.

An agent's store of 'how-to' knowledge: the rules, routines, and skills that govern how it acts — in language agents, implemented as a mixture of the model's trained weights, system prompts, code, and tool-use procedures. In the CoALA framework this contrasts with declarative stores (episodic and semantic memory) that record what, not how. The agent's habits and training manual: not facts or events, but the procedures it follows — like 'always verify contract specs before sizing a trade'.

A vulnerability class in which crafted inputs alter a language model's behavior or output in unintended ways — ranked LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Direct injection comes through the user's own prompt; indirect injection arrives embedded in external content (web pages, documents, tool results) that the model processes. Because the model reads instructions and data through the same channel, anyone who can slip text into that channel can try to reprogram it — like a SQL injection, but in natural language.

An integrity attack in which pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors, or biases into a model — OWASP LLM04 in the Top 10 for LLM Applications. Because tampered training data compromises the model's ability to make accurate predictions, poisoning is classified as an integrity attack, and backdoors may remain dormant until a trigger activates them. Corrupt the textbook, not the exam: if the training data teaches the model a hidden wrong rule, every future answer can carry the contamination — and you may never see it until a trigger fires.

The systematic measurement of a model's or AI system's performance, behavior, and risks against defined criteria, datasets, and contexts of use. In the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation sits in the MEASURE function: risks and trustworthiness characteristics are identified, measured, and tracked with appropriate metrics and testing throughout the lifecycle. Report cards with a rubric: you decide in advance what 'good' means, test against data the model did not train on, and record the results so regressions are visible.

a: gold standard dataset reference dataset ground-truth dataset
x: A curated, high-quality dataset of examples with authoritative labels or answers, used as the reference against which a system's outputs are judged. The term derives from the 'gold standard' in measurement and diagnostics: the best available benchmark under reasonable conditions, against which new methods are compared to gauge their validity. The answer key: a carefully vetted set of questions with known-good answers, so 'did the system get it right?' is a checkable comparison instead of an opinion.

a: adversarial testing red teaming attack simulation
x: Deliberately probing an AI system with inputs designed to make it fail — evasion attacks, poisoned data, prompt injections, extraction attempts — in order to find vulnerabilities before an adversary does. NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2) classifies such attacks by ML method, lifecycle stage, and attacker goals, capabilities, and knowledge, and pairs them with mitigations. Hire the burglar to test the locks: instead of asking 'does it work?', ask 'how can it be made to break?'

a: HITL review human oversight human verification step
x: A workflow design in which human judgment is inserted into an AI system's pipeline — labeling data, reviewing outputs, approving consequential actions — rather than letting the system run end-to-end autonomously. Surveys of human-in-the-loop machine learning organize these roles into data processing, interventional model training, and system-level HITL design. The AI drafts; a person signs off. Anything the system gets wrong still has to pass a human checkpoint before it counts.

The property that a model's stated confidence matches its true correctness likelihood: among predictions made with 80% confidence, about 80% should be correct. Guo et al. (2017) showed modern deep networks are typically poorly calibrated (overconfident) and that simple post-processing such as temperature scaling can substantially fix it. A well-calibrated model's 'I'm 90% sure' is right nine times out of ten — its confidence number means what it says.

a: reject option selective prediction selective classification
x: The design choice that lets a model decline to answer on inputs where it is likely to be wrong, trading coverage for accuracy. In selective classification (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017), the system pairs a predictor with a selection function that rejects low-confidence instances so that a user-chosen risk level is met with high probability. A system allowed to say 'I don't know' can be far more trustworthy on the answers it does give — you choose how much silence to buy for how much accuracy.

a: pre-trade risk control agent risk control
x: A deterministic control that bounds what an automated trading agent may do, enforced outside the model: order-size and price limits, credit/capital thresholds, duplicate-order rejection, restricted-instrument lists, and kill switches. The regulatory archetype is SEC Rule 15c3-5, which requires broker-dealers with market access to maintain automated, systematically applied financial and regulatory risk management controls that prevent the entry of erroneous or excessive orders. The agent proposes; hard code disposes. Whatever the model decides, orders must pass through non-negotiable software checks before they can reach the market.

A trading agent whose tool permissions are restricted to data retrieval and computation — market data, knowledge bases, analytics — with no capability to submit, modify, or cancel orders. It operationalizes the least-privilege principle: the system's action space is limited to the minimum necessary for its function, so even malfunction or prompt injection cannot move money. An analyst with a terminal and no trading button: it can look everything up and tell you what it thinks, but it physically cannot place a trade.

A trading agent with the technical capability to submit, modify, or cancel orders on a market — the category of automation that pre-trade risk controls exist to govern. Under SEC Rule 15c3-5, any broker-dealer providing such market access must maintain automated financial and regulatory risk management controls — credit/capital thresholds, erroneous-order prevention, restricted-security checks — under its direct and exclusive control. The moment an agent can touch the order book, it stops being software and starts being market access — with the same regulatory obligations and blow-up potential as any automated trading system.

A control point in an agentic workflow where a designated human must explicitly authorize a proposed action before the system executes it. OWASP lists requiring human approval for high-risk actions — human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations — as a core mitigation against unauthorized actions by LLM-integrated applications. The agent can prepare the trade, fill in the ticket, and explain the reasoning — but a person has to click 'confirm' before anything happens.

A tamper-evident, time-ordered record of significant system events — actions taken, by whom or what, when, and with what inputs and outcomes — maintained for security, accountability, and forensics. NIST SP 800-92 provides guidance on establishing log management infrastructures and processes, covering log generation, protection, storage, analysis, and disposal across an organization. The black-box recorder of the system: when something goes wrong (or right), you can reconstruct exactly what happened, in order, and prove it wasn't rewritten afterward.

An analysis whose results can be independently regenerated from the same data, code, and documented procedure. The U.S. National Academies (2019) distinguish reproducibility — obtaining consistent results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, and code — from replicability, obtaining consistent results across studies aimed at the same question with new data. Someone else (or you, six months later) should be able to rerun the pipeline from the recorded inputs and get the same numbers — otherwise the result is a story, not a finding.

The decay of a deployed model's predictive performance over time as the world departs from the conditions captured in its training data. It is the observable symptom of underlying data drift or concept drift: the model stays the same, but the mapping it learned fits reality less and less. The model is a snapshot of how the world worked at training time; as the world moves on, the snapshot yellows — predictions get stale even though nothing in the model changed.

a: covariate shift input drift feature drift
x: A change over time in the distribution of a model's input data, P(X), while the relationship between inputs and labels may remain unchanged. In the concept-drift literature it is distinguished from 'real' concept drift: the world looks different, but the rule mapping features to outcomes has not (yet) changed. The questions arriving at the model change, even if the correct answers to each question would still be computed the same way — like an exam suddenly full of topics the course barely covered.

An unforeseeable change over time in the underlying relationship between inputs and outputs — formally, a change in P(y|X) — so that the mapping a model learned no longer holds even for identical inputs. The concept-drift literature (e.g., Lu et al., IEEE TKDE) organizes the field into drift detection, drift understanding, and drift adaptation. The rules of the game changed: the same setup that used to mean 'buy' now means nothing — the model's knowledge itself is outdated, not just its inputs.

A single-candlestick formation in which the open and close are equal or virtually equal, producing a very small or nonexistent real body. In technical analysis it is read as a sign of indecision between buyers and sellers; as with all candlestick patterns, it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictive law. Buyers and sellers fought to a draw during the period: price traveled up and down but ended essentially where it started, so neither side is in control.

A doji variant with long upper and lower shadows and open and close at or near the same price, typically near the middle of the period's range. It is interpreted in technical analysis as strong two-sided pressure ending in a standoff, often read as a sign that the prior trend is losing conviction. Price was pushed far up and far down during the period, but neither side could hold its gains; the market ended exactly where it began after a wide-ranging battle.

A doji variant in which the open, high, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long lower shadow and little or no upper shadow (a T shape). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod selling that was fully absorbed by buyers, and treat it as a possible bullish reversal sign when it appears after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor. Sellers drove price sharply lower during the period, but buyers pushed it all the way back to the opening level, showing demand underneath the market.

A doji variant in which the open, low, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long upper shadow and little or no lower shadow (an inverted T). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod buying that was fully rejected by sellers, and treat it as a possible bearish reversal sign when it appears after an advance; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor. Buyers drove price sharply higher during the period, but sellers forced it all the way back down to the opening level, showing supply sitting above the market.

A single candlestick with a small real body vertically centered between upper and lower shadows that are both noticeably longer than the body. Like the doji, it is read as indecision between buyers and sellers and is treated in technical analysis as a possible sign of trend exhaustion when it follows an extended move; it is a hypothesis requiring confirmation, not a predictive law. Both bulls and bears pushed price around during the period, but neither could keep it anywhere; the close near the open shows the tug-of-war ended in a draw.

A long-bodied candlestick with no (or almost no) shadows, so that the open and close coincide with the period's extreme prices: a white/green marubozu opens at the low and closes at the high, and a black/red marubozu opens at the high and closes at the low. It is read as one-sided dominance throughout the period and is usually interpreted as a continuation signal. One side controlled the entire session from the first trade to the last: buyers never let price dip below the open (bullish marubozu) or sellers never let it rise above the open (bearish marubozu).

A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the period's range, a long lower shadow (conventionally at least twice the body length), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal because sellers drove price down but buyers recovered nearly all of the loss; it is a hypothesis that requires confirmation. Sellers smashed price down during the period, but buyers hammered it back up to close near the open, showing the decline was rejected.

A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the range, a long lower shadow (conventionally two or more times the body), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after an uptrend. It has the same shape as a hammer; technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal warning because the deep intraperiod selloff revealed latent selling pressure, though the reading requires bearish confirmation. Price was dumped hard during the session and only partly recovered; the fact that sellers could push it that low at all, after a long rise, is taken as a crack in the uptrend.

A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal: buyers mounted an intraperiod rally that sellers could not fully erase, hinting that demand is emerging; confirmation by a higher close next period is normally required. In a falling market, buyers finally staged a real push upward during the session; even though it was sold back toward the open, the attempt shows bulls are waking up.

A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal signal: buyers drove price sharply higher intraperiod but sellers forced it back near the open, showing the rally was rejected; it is a hypothesis that needs confirmation. The market shot up during the session but fell back to earth before the close, leaving a long tail that shows buyers could not hold the highs.

A two-candlestick pattern in which a small black (down) body is followed by a larger white (up) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major bottom reversal signal because buyers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor. After a falling session, buyers arrived with enough force to open lower and close above where the previous session opened, swallowing the sellers' progress whole.

A two-candlestick pattern in which a small white (up) body is followed by a larger black (down) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major top reversal signal because sellers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor. After a rising session, sellers hit the market hard enough to open higher and close below where the previous session opened, erasing the buyers' progress in one move.

A two-candlestick pattern in a downtrend: a long black candle is followed by a white candle that opens below the prior low (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway up into the prior black body. Technical analysts read it as a potential bottom reversal signal, a weaker cousin of the bullish engulfing pattern. Sellers gapped the market down at the open, but buyers drove price back up through more than half of the previous session's losses, piercing deep into their territory.

A two-candlestick pattern in an uptrend: a long white candle is followed by a black candle that opens above the prior high (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway down into the prior white body. Technical analysts read it as a potential top reversal signal, the bearish mirror of the piercing line and a weaker cousin of the bearish engulfing pattern. Buyers gapped the market up at the open, but sellers dragged price back down through more than half of the previous session's gains, casting a dark cloud over the rally.

A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps below the first body, and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major bottom reversal signal marking a shift from selling to indecision to buying. Sellers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle, then buyers take over and recover most of the lost ground, like dawn after a dark night.

A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps above the first body, and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major top reversal signal marking a shift from buying to indecision to selling; it is the bearish mirror of the morning star. Buyers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle near the highs, then sellers seize control and erase much of the advance, like nightfall after a bright day.

A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a doji that gaps below it (the doji star), and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the morning star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger reversal signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in selling. After heavy selling, the market opens lower but goes absolutely nowhere (a doji), then buyers storm back and reclaim most of the decline; the dead-flat middle candle shows sellers are spent.

A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a doji that gaps above it (the doji star), and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the evening star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger bearish signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in buying. After heavy buying, the market gaps up but freezes dead flat (a doji), then sellers drive price deep back into the prior gains; the motionless middle candle shows buyers are exhausted.

A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long white candles with progressively higher closes, each closing at or near its high and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained buying marking a bottom after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor. Three sessions in a row of determined buying, each marching higher and finishing near its highs, suggests the market has been taken over by confident bulls rather than one-day short covering.

A three-candlestick top reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long black candles with progressively lower closes, each closing at or near its low and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained selling marking a top after an advance; it is the bearish mirror of three white soldiers. Three sessions in a row of relentless selling, each closing near its lows and stepping lower, suggests determined distribution rather than a single day of profit-taking.

A two-candlestick pattern in which a small real body is completely contained within the prior session's large real body (the reverse of an engulfing pattern); 'harami' is Japanese for 'pregnant'. Read generically, it marks a sudden loss of momentum in the prevailing trend and is treated in technical analysis as a potential reversal warning, directional (bullish or bearish) according to the trend it interrupts. After a big, confident candle, the market suddenly shrinks to a small candle that fits entirely inside the prior body, as if the trend caught its breath and participants hesitated.

A two-candlestick pattern appearing after a downtrend: an unusually large black body is followed by a small white body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bullish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as selling pressure drying up; confirmation from subsequent candles is normally required. After a big down day, the market can only manage a tiny up day hidden inside the prior body, suggesting sellers have run out of ammunition and buyers are quietly testing the water.

A two-candlestick pattern appearing after an uptrend: an unusually large white body is followed by a small black body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as buying pressure drying up; it is the bearish mirror of the bullish harami and requires confirmation. After a big up day, the market stalls into a tiny down day nested inside the prior body, suggesting the rally's energy is spent and sellers are probing.

A two-candlestick pattern in which a large real body is followed by a doji contained entirely within that body, forming a harami whose second candle is a doji. Technical analysts regard it as a more potent reversal warning than a plain harami because the doji shows the trend's momentum has stalled into outright indecision; it is bullish after declines and bearish after advances. A big confident candle is followed by a session that goes absolutely nowhere and hides inside the prior body, suggesting the driving force behind the trend has abruptly evaporated.

A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose highs match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price ceiling, typically appearing in an uptrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same high as a minor bearish reversal signal, which gains weight when the candles themselves form other reversal shapes. The market probed the exact same ceiling twice and failed both times, as if pinched by tweezers at that price, suggesting sellers are defending that level.

A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose lows match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price floor, typically appearing in a downtrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same low as a minor bullish reversal signal, the mirror of the tweezer top, which gains weight when combined with other reversal shapes. The market probed the exact same floor twice and held both times, as if supported by tweezers at that price, suggesting buyers are defending that level.

A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish harami: a long black body in a downtrend is followed by a small white body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami. First the trend's selling stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes higher, confirming that buyers, not sellers, won the standoff.

A three-candlestick bearish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bearish harami: a long white body in an uptrend is followed by a small black body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing below the second candle's close. The third candle's lower close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami. First the rally stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes lower, confirming that sellers, not buyers, won the standoff.

A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish engulfing: a black body in a downtrend is engulfed by a larger white body (the engulfing), and then a third white candle closes above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close confirms the engulfing signal. Buyers first swallow the prior down candle whole, then prove it was no fluke by closing higher again the very next session.

A three-candlestick bearish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bearish engulfing: a white body in an uptrend is engulfed by a larger black body (the engulfing), and then a third black candle closes below the second candle's close. The third candle's lower close confirms the engulfing signal; it is the mirror of three outside up. Sellers first swallow the prior up candle whole, then prove it was no fluke by closing lower again the very next session.

A five-candlestick bullish continuation pattern: a long white body is followed by three small bodies (normally black) that all remain within the first candle's range, and then a final long white body closing above the first candle's close. Technical analysts read it as a brief, contained pause within an ongoing advance; it is a continuation, not reversal, formation. The market surges, then drifts sideways-to-down for three small sessions without giving back the surge, then surges again, showing the pullback was only profit-taking inside a healthy uptrend.

A five-candlestick bearish continuation pattern: a long black body is followed by three small bodies (normally white) that all remain within the first candle's range, and then a final long black body closing below the first candle's close. It is the bearish mirror of rising three methods, read as a contained pause within an ongoing decline. The market drops, then drifts sideways-to-up for three small sessions without recovering the drop, then drops again, showing the bounce was only short covering inside a healthy downtrend.

A rare three-candlestick reversal pattern similar to a morning/evening doji star but stricter: the middle doji must gap away from both neighboring candles such that its shadows do not overlap theirs at either side. The bullish version (doji gapped below between a black and a white candle) and bearish version (doji gapped above between a white and a black candle) are read as major reversal signals. A lone doji sits isolated on the chart with empty space on both sides, like an abandoned baby; the market gapped away from the trend, froze, and then gapped back the opposite way.

A two-candlestick reversal pattern consisting of two opposite-colored marubozu-type candles: the first moves with the prevailing trend, and the second gaps open at or beyond the first candle's open and drives in the opposite direction, nullifying it. Technical analysts regard it as one of the strongest reversal formations, typically attributed to a sudden news-driven shift in sentiment. The market is moving firmly one way, then overnight something changes so completely that price gaps to the other side of the prior open and runs the opposite way all session, kicking the trend into reverse.

A bar whose entire high-low range is contained within the range of the preceding bar (the 'mother bar'): its high is at or below the prior high and its low is at or above the prior low. Price-action traders read it as volatility compression and indecision, traded as a breakout setup in either direction rather than as an inherently bullish or bearish signal. The market took a breath: the latest bar traded entirely inside the previous bar's range, coiling like a spring while buy and sell stop orders pile up on both sides of the mother bar.

A bar whose high exceeds the prior bar's high and whose low falls below the prior bar's low, so its full range engulfs the previous bar's range. Price-action traders read it as volatility expansion and a battle between buyers and sellers, with the close's location indicating which side won; it differs from the engulfing candlestick pattern, which compares only real bodies. The market explored beyond both edges of the previous session in one bar, a burst of expanded volatility where both sides were tested and the close reveals the winner.

A single-candlestick price-action pattern with a small real body and one very long shadow protruding in one direction, the name deriving from Martin Pring's 'Pinocchio bar' because the long wick 'lies' about market direction by showing a rejected probe. Traders read the long shadow as rejection of a price level and use it as a reversal or continuation trigger, typically in confluence with support and resistance. Price made a quick dash far in one direction and was slapped back before the close, leaving a long nose; the dash is treated as a lie that reveals where the market refuses to go.

a: Head and shoulders top H&S top
x: A classical technical-analysis reversal pattern consisting of three successive peaks in which the middle peak (the head) is the highest and the two outside peaks (the shoulders) are lower and roughly equal, with the intervening reaction lows connected by a neckline. The pattern is treated as complete — and the prior uptrend tentatively reversed — only when price breaks below the neckline. It is an analytical framework for reading supply/demand shifts, not a proven predictive law. Buyers make one final push to a new high (the head), but the next rally (the right shoulder) can no longer reach it — a sign that demand is exhausting. When price then breaks the neckline, sellers have taken control.

a: Head and shoulders bottom Inverse H&S Reverse head and shoulders
x: The bullish mirror of the head-and-shoulders top: three successive troughs after a downtrend in which the middle trough (the head) is the deepest and the two outside troughs (the shoulders) are shallower, with the intervening reaction highs forming a neckline. The pattern is treated as complete only when price breaks above the neckline, ideally with a clear volume expansion, marking a tentative bullish reversal. Like all chart patterns it is a heuristic framework, not a proven predictive law. Sellers drive price to a final capitulation low (the head), but the next decline (the right shoulder) cannot reach it — supply is drying up. A break above neckline resistance shows buyers have seized control.

A classical bearish reversal pattern in which price in an established uptrend forms two peaks at roughly the same level separated by a moderate trough, and the pattern completes only when price breaks below the intervening trough (support). It is interpreted as two failed attempts to overcome the same supply zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis about trend change, not a proven predictive law. The market tests the same high twice and fails both times, showing that sellers consistently overwhelm buyers at that level; breaking the low between the peaks confirms the sellers' victory.

A classical bullish reversal pattern in which price in an established downtrend forms two troughs at roughly the same level separated by a moderate rebound, and the pattern completes only when price breaks above the intervening reaction high (resistance). It is read as two successful defenses of the same demand zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Sellers push price down to the same low twice and cannot force it lower; when the subsequent rally clears the peak between the two lows, buyers have taken control.

A classical bearish reversal pattern in which price in an uptrend tests the same resistance level three times, forming three roughly equal, well-spaced highs, and completes only when price breaks below the pattern's support (the lowest of the intervening lows). It extends the double-top logic: three rejections of the same supply zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Three failed attempts to push through the same ceiling exhaust the buyers; once the floor between those attempts gives way, there are no buyers left to hold the level.

A classical bullish reversal pattern in which price in a downtrend tests the same support level three times, forming three roughly equal, well-spaced lows, and completes only when price breaks above the pattern's resistance (the highest of the intervening highs). It is the mirror of the triple top: three successful defenses of the same demand zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Three times sellers try to force price through the same floor and fail; when the ceiling between those floors finally breaks, the accumulated buying pressure is released.

A classical consolidation pattern bounded above by a horizontal resistance line drawn through two or more comparable highs and below by a rising trend line drawn through successively higher lows. It carries a bullish bias — interpreted as accumulation against a fixed supply level — and usually resolves as a continuation of the prior uptrend, though it occasionally forms as a bottom reversal. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Sellers defend a fixed ceiling while buyers keep stepping in at higher and higher prices; the rising floor shows buying pressure building until the ceiling finally gives way.

A classical consolidation pattern bounded below by a horizontal support line drawn through two or more comparable lows and above by a descending trend line drawn through successively lower highs. It carries a bearish bias — interpreted as distribution against a fixed demand level — and usually resolves as a continuation of the prior downtrend, though it occasionally forms as a top reversal. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Buyers defend a fixed floor while sellers accept lower and lower prices on each rally; the descending ceiling shows supply pressing down until the floor finally collapses.

A classical consolidation pattern in which at least two lower highs and two higher lows produce converging trend lines, forming a contracting trading range. It is directionally neutral until the breakout: most often it resolves as a continuation of the prevailing trend, but a meaningful minority mark reversals. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Buyers and sellers reach into each other with shrinking swings, like a coiling spring; the stored-up indecision is released in whichever direction price finally escapes the converging lines.

A technical-analysis pattern in which price makes higher highs and higher lows but both bounding trend lines slope upward and converge, compressing the advance. When it appears in an uptrend it is read as a bearish reversal warning (momentum fading into the apex); in a downtrend it is read as a bearish continuation (a corrective rally). It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Price is still rising, but each push up is smaller than the last — buyers are paying more for less progress, and the advance typically resolves downward through the lower line.

A technical-analysis pattern in which price makes lower highs and lower lows but both bounding trend lines slope downward and converge, compressing the decline. It is conventionally read as bullish: the converging lines show the sell-off losing momentum, with resolution expected through a break above the upper trend line — as a reversal after a downtrend or as a continuation pause within an uptrend. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Sellers keep pushing price down, but each new low is harder to achieve — selling pressure is exhausting, and the spring typically releases upward through the upper line.

A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp near-vertical advance (the flagpole) followed by a brief, tight counter-trend consolidation in a small parallel channel sloping downward (the flag), typically lasting five to twenty bars. It is read as a pause that refreshes the uptrend, with continuation expected on a breakout above the flag's upper line. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. After a sudden surge, early buyers take profits in an orderly drift lower while new buyers absorb the supply; when the profit-taking is done, the trend resumes, often with similar force.

A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp near-vertical decline (the flagpole) followed by a brief, tight counter-trend consolidation in a small parallel channel sloping upward (the flag), typically lasting five to twenty bars. It is read as a pause within a downtrend, with continuation expected on a breakdown below the flag's lower line. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. After a sudden plunge, bargain hunters produce a weak, grinding bounce that never recovers much ground; when that feeble buying is exhausted, the decline resumes.

A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp advance (the flagpole) followed by a brief consolidation bounded by converging trend lines forming a small symmetrical triangle (the pennant), typically lasting one to three weeks. It is read as a pause of market indecision within an uptrend, with continuation expected on a breakout above the pennant's upper line on increased volume. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. After a sudden rally the market catches its breath in ever-tighter swings; the triangle-shaped breather ends when buyers overwhelm sellers again and price shoots out of the apex.

A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp decline (the flagpole) followed by a brief consolidation bounded by converging trend lines forming a small symmetrical triangle (the pennant), typically lasting one to three weeks. It is read as a pause within a downtrend, with continuation expected on a breakdown below the pennant's lower line on increased volume. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. After a sudden drop, buyers and sellers reach a shrinking stand-off in a tiny triangle; when the stand-off resolves, the stored selling pressure usually drives the next leg down.

a: Trading range Consolidation zone Congestion area Box range
x: A classical consolidation pattern in which price oscillates between a horizontal resistance line (at least two comparable highs) and a horizontal support line (at least two comparable lows), forming a trading range. It is directionally neutral: usually a continuation pause within the prevailing trend, but it can also mark significant tops and bottoms, and only the breakout assigns direction. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Bulls buy every dip to the same floor and bears sell every rally to the same ceiling; the range persists until one side runs out of ammunition and price escapes the box.

a: Saucer bottom Saucer Bowl U-shaped bottom
x: A long-term bullish reversal pattern in which a decline gradually flattens into a shallow U- or bowl-shaped low and then curves back upward, best seen on weekly charts. It represents a slow transfer from distribution to accumulation — sentiment shifting from bearish to bullish at a steady pace — and is confirmed when price breaks above the reaction high at the start of the pattern. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Instead of a violent V-shaped reversal, selling pressure fades week by week and buying interest returns just as gradually, tracing a bowl — patient accumulation replacing capitulation.

a: Inverted saucer Inverse saucer Dome top
x: A long-term bearish reversal pattern, the mirror of the rounding bottom, in which an advance gradually flattens into an inverted-U or dome shape and then curves downward as sentiment shifts slowly from bullish to bearish. It is interpreted as a distribution process — informed holders selling gradually without disturbing the price — and is confirmed when price breaks down from the dome's base. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Buyers lose the power to push price higher but sellers exit slowly, so the chart rolls over in a gentle dome rather than a spike; once the artificial support of patient distribution ends, price falls away.

A bullish continuation pattern popularized by William O'Neil in 'How to Make Money in Stocks' (1988), consisting of a U-shaped consolidation (the cup) followed by a smaller downward-drifting pullback (the handle) on the right side, completed by a breakout above the handle's resistance. The cup resembles a rounding bottom within an existing uptrend. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. After a strong rally the stock digests its gains in a wide bowl; the small final dip (the handle) shakes out the last weak holders before the uptrend resumes through the old high.

a: Megaphone pattern Broadening top Broadening bottom Expanding triangle Inverted triangle
x: A classical technical-analysis pattern in which successively higher highs and lower lows produce two diverging trend lines, so the trading range widens over time — the opposite of a triangle. Occurring more often at tops (where it is conventionally assigned bearish implications), it is read as a market out of control, with public speculation replacing informed participation. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Each swing overshoots the last in both directions — buyers chase new highs and then panic to new lows — a signature of emotional, leaderless trading rather than orderly accumulation or distribution.

A rare classical reversal pattern at the end of an uptrend whose outline resembles a diamond — often tilted — formed by an initial broadening phase (higher peaks and lower valleys) followed by a contracting phase (lower peaks and higher valleys, like a symmetrical triangle). The conventional expectation is a downward breakout reversing the prior rise. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Volatility first explodes outward and then collapses inward, as if the market thrashed itself into exhaustion; the diamond's tip marks where the uptrend's energy runs out.

A rare classical reversal pattern at the end of a downtrend whose outline resembles a diamond, formed by an initial broadening phase (higher peaks and lower valleys) followed by a contracting phase (lower peaks and higher valleys). The conventional expectation is an upward breakout reversing the prior decline; in Bulkowski's sample, diamond bottoms with upward breakouts were the best-performing of the 36 patterns he ranked for downward breakouts. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Panic first whips price violently in both directions, then the swings die down into a point — the diamond marks the moment the selling storm blows itself out and buyers quietly take over.

a: Measured move up Measured move down Swing measurement AB=CD move
x: A classical price-projection framework in which a trend leg, a corrective retracement, and a second trend leg are expected to be roughly equal in price (and, in the idealized version, in time): the second leg 'measures' the first. It is used both as a continuation pattern (a measured move up/down) and as a target-setting rule. It is a technical-analysis heuristic; empirical samples show the second leg typically falls short of the ideal. Markets often move in two similar thrusts separated by a pause; once you know the size of the first thrust and where the pause ended, you can estimate how far the second thrust should carry.

a: Parabolic arc Parabolic curve Parabolic run Blow-off trajectory
x: A chart formation in which an uptrend accelerates so that successive rallies steepen and the price path curves upward like a parabola, often with stair-step consolidations ('bases') beneath a curving trend line. It is interpreted as crowd-driven euphoria whose slope is mathematically unsustainable, so the pattern is used as a bearish-reversal framework: the signal is price breaking back below the curved trend line. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. When each wave of buying has to be more frantic than the last just to keep the rally going, the move is feeding on itself; once the curve cracks, there is no orderly bid underneath.

a: Parabolic sell-off Waterfall decline Capitulation arc
x: The inverted analogue of the parabolic advance: a downtrend that accelerates so successive sell-offs steepen and the price path curves downward like a downward-opening parabola, typically driven by panic, forced liquidation, or cascading stops. It is interpreted as a capitulation dynamic whose slope is unsustainable, with a tentative bullish-reversal signal when price breaks back above the curved trend line overhead. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Each wave of selling panics more holders into selling, so the fall keeps steepening — until everyone who could be forced out is out, and the collapse exhausts itself.

a: Island top Island bottom Island cluster
x: A classical reversal pattern in which a cluster of one or more trading sessions is isolated from the surrounding price action by a gap on each side — typically an exhaustion gap into the cluster and a breakaway gap out of it in the opposite direction. The stranded 'island' marks an abrupt sentiment flip, with island tops (bearish) more common than island bottoms. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Price leaps one way, trades in a brief frenzy, then leaps back the other way, leaving the late entrants marooned on an island of prices the market immediately abandoned.

The total number of futures or option contracts, long or short, in a delivery month or market that have been entered into and not yet liquidated by an offsetting transaction, exercised, or fulfilled by delivery. Open interest counts how many contracts are still 'alive' at the end of the day — positions traders are still holding, not how many changed hands (that is volume).

The cash commodity, security, futures contract, index, rate, or other reference item on which a derivative contract is based and from which its value is derived; for options, it is what must be delivered or accepted if the option is exercised. A derivative is a bet or a hedge on something else — that 'something else' is the underlying. The contract never stands alone; its price moves because the underlying's price moves.

a: point multiplier point value dollar multiplier
x: The fixed dollar amount per unit of quoted price (or per index point) set by the exchange in the contract specification, which converts a quoted price into the total monetary value of one contract; for equity options the standardized multiplier is typically 100 shares per contract. Quotes come in points, but money moves in dollars — the multiplier is the exchange-fixed exchange rate between the two.

The actual quantity of the underlying asset represented by one futures or derivative contract, as standardized by the exchange in the contract specification. One 'contract' is a fixed bundle — contract size tells you how big the bundle is, so one futures contract on crude oil always means the same number of barrels.

a: minimum price fluctuation minimum tick minimum price increment
x: The smallest increment by which the price of a given contract is permitted to move up or down, as fixed by the rules of the exchange. Prices on an exchange ladder are not continuous — they move on rungs, and the tick size is the spacing between rungs.

a: minimum price fluctuation value dollar value of a tick
x: The monetary profit or loss on one contract resulting from a one-tick (minimum price fluctuation) move in the contract's price. Tick size tells you the smallest price step; tick value tells you how many dollars that step is worth in your account.

The price, specified in the option contract, at which the underlying security, futures contract, or commodity will be bought (call) or sold (put) if the option is exercised. The strike is the deal price locked in at contract creation: it is the yardstick that decides whether exercising the option is worth anything.

The date on which an option contract automatically expires and ceases to exist; it is the last day on which the option may be exercised (and for American-style options, the end of the exercise window). An option is a wasting asset with a printed shelf life: after the expiration date the contract is gone, worth whatever final settlement paid — usually zero for out-of-the-money options.

The specified date on which the principal (face value) of a debt instrument such as a bond is scheduled to be repaid to the investor; for futures, 'maturity' refers to the period within which the contract can be settled by delivery. The maturity date is the loan's end date: it is when the borrower's promise to hand back the principal comes due.

The price the buyer of an option pays (and the writer receives) for the rights granted by the contract; it is the market price of the option itself, composed of intrinsic value plus time value. The premium is what you pay for the right-but-not-the-obligation: it is the cost of insurance or of a leveraged bet, paid up front and never refundable.

The value an option would have if exercised immediately: the amount by which the underlying price exceeds the strike for a call, or by which the strike exceeds the underlying price for a put; only in-the-money options have intrinsic value. Intrinsic value is the cash you could capture right now by exercising and trading out of the underlying — everything above that in the premium is hope, not substance.

The portion of an option's premium in excess of its intrinsic value, reflecting the market's payment for the possibility that the option gains value before expiration; in standard usage it is synonymous with time value, though it embeds volatility, carry, and dividend effects as well as time. Extrinsic value is the 'maybe' premium: the extra amount buyers pay over immediate-exercise value for the chance the underlying moves favorably before expiry.

That portion of an option's premium that exceeds its intrinsic value; it reflects the probability that the option will move (further) into the money before expiration, so the longer the time remaining, the greater the time value, all else equal. Time value is the price of possibility: with more days left, there is more chance for the underlying to move in your favor, and the market charges for that chance.

An option that the holder may exercise at any time on or before the expiration date; all standardized U.S. exchange-traded equity options use American-style exercise. An American option is a standing offer: any day before expiry, the holder can invoke the strike and take or deliver the underlying.

An option that may be exercised only on its expiration date; most (but not all) U.S. index options use European-style exercise. A European option is a single-day right: you can trade the contract any time, but you can invoke the strike only on expiration day itself.

a: Bermuda option mid-Atlantic option quasi-American option
x: An exotic option that can be exercised only on a specified set of predetermined dates during its life, an exercise style intermediate between American (any time) and European (at expiry only). A Bermudan option opens the exercise window on a schedule — say, the first business day of each month — rather than every day (American) or just once at the end (European).

The act by which the holder of an option invokes the contractual right to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying at the strike price, converting the option position into a transaction or position in the underlying. Exercising is cashing in the ticket: instead of selling the option, you use it to force the trade at the strike.

The designation by the clearing organization of an option writer who must fulfill the contract — selling the underlying at the strike (assigned call) or buying it at the strike (assigned put) — when a holder exercises. Assignment is the other side of exercise: when a holder invokes the ticket, a writer is tapped on the shoulder and must honor the deal.

A provision in a futures or other derivative contract requiring delivery of the actual underlying commodity or asset (or a delivery instrument such as a warehouse receipt) to satisfy the contract at maturity. With physical settlement, holding the contract to the end means real goods or securities change hands — not just a check for the price difference.

A method of settling futures, options, and other derivatives whereby the seller pays the buyer the cash value of the underlying, or a cash amount based on the level of an index or price, according to a procedure specified in the contract, instead of delivering the asset itself. Cash settlement settles the score in money only: at expiry the contract simply pays out the difference, so no barrels, shares, or bonds ever move.

a: final settlement value expiry settlement price
x: The price at which a cash-settled futures (or option) contract is settled at maturity, determined pursuant to a procedure specified by the exchange. The final settlement price is the official last mark of a contract's life — the single number that decides the terminal cash flows for everyone still holding it.

The official daily price at which the clearing organization clears all trades and settles all accounts between clearing members for each contract month; it is the benchmark used for marking positions to market, computing margin calls, and invoicing deliveries. The daily settlement price is the exchange's official 'score' for the day: everyone's futures P&L and margin requirements are recomputed against it every session.

The specified month within which a futures contract matures and can be settled by delivery, or within which the delivery period begins, as defined in the contract specification. The delivery month is the contract's calendar label: 'December corn' means the corn future whose obligations fall due in December.

The first day on which notices of intent to deliver the actual commodity against open short futures positions can be issued (received by longs); the date varies by commodity and exchange. First notice day is when holding a long futures position stops being purely financial: from then on, a long can be handed a delivery notice and be obliged to pay for and take the goods.

The final day on which a futures or options contract may be traded on the exchange; after the close of the last trading day, remaining open positions proceed to settlement or delivery. The last trading day is the deadline for closing a position on your own terms — miss it, and the contract's settlement machinery decides the outcome for you.

a: notice of intent to deliver notice of delivery
x: The written notice given by a futures seller of the intention to make delivery against an open short position on a particular date, delivered through the clearing organization; it is separate and distinct from the warehouse receipt or other instrument used to transfer title. The delivery notice is the short's formal 'I will deliver' declaration — the document that starts the physical settlement process and lands on some long's desk.

A document certifying possession of a commodity in a licensed or exchange-approved warehouse, recognized for delivery purposes in settlement of futures contracts. The warehouse receipt is the paper (or electronic) title to goods sitting in an approved silo or vault — delivering the receipt is delivering the commodity.

a: notional amount notional principal contract value reference amount
x: The total face or reference value of the underlying exposure controlled by a derivative contract — the amount to which prices, rates, or percentage changes are applied to compute payments or P&L — as distinct from the much smaller premium or margin actually exchanged. Notional value is the size of the position you economically control, not the cash you put up: a small margin deposit can steer a very large notional ship.

a: face value principal value nominal value
x: The principal amount of a bond or note that the issuer promises to repay at maturity, and the base on which coupon interest is calculated; the bond trades at a premium, at par, or at a discount depending on whether its price is above, equal to, or below this amount. Par value is the loan amount printed on the bond: whatever the market price does day to day, par is what comes back at the end (absent default).

a: coupon stated interest rate nominal rate
x: The fixed rate of interest a bond pays, stated as a percentage of its principal (par) value per year and typically paid in semiannual installments; it equals the annual coupon divided by the face value. The coupon rate is the bond's built-in paycheck formula, fixed at issuance: it tells you the dollar interest you get each year per $100 of face value, regardless of what the bond's price does later.

Interest earned on a security but not yet paid to the investor; specifically, the portion of the next coupon payment that has accumulated since the last coupon date, which a bond buyer pays to the seller at settlement. Coupons arrive only on payment dates, but interest builds every day: accrued interest is the seller's share of the coming coupon for the days they held the bond.

The standard quoted market price of a bond, stated net of accrued interest — the price shown on screens and used for price comparison, as distinct from the full amount actually paid at settlement. The clean price strips out the mechanical day-count drift so price changes reflect real market moves, not just time passing between coupon dates.

a: full price invoice price gross price
x: The actual total amount paid for a bond at settlement, equal to the quoted (clean) price plus accrued interest since the last coupon date; also called the full or invoice price. The dirty price is the real check the buyer writes: the quoted price plus the seller's earned-but-unpaid slice of the next coupon.

The annual rate of return an investor earns if a bond is bought at its current price and held to maturity, with all coupons reinvested at that same rate; equivalently, the single discount rate that equates the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows to its current price. YTM is the bond's all-in interest rate: it folds the coupon stream and the gain or loss to par into one annualized number, letting different bonds be compared on equal footing.

The ratio of a bond's annual interest (coupon) payments to its current market price, stated as a percentage — a simple income-on-price measure that ignores the gain or loss to par at maturity. Current yield answers only 'how much income per dollar of price right now?' — like a dividend yield for bonds, with no regard for what you get back at the end.

A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to changes in interest rates, expressed in years; formally, the Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time to receipt of the bond's cash flows, and it serves as the basis for the price-sensitivity (modified duration) measure. Duration compresses maturity, coupon, and yield into one number that approximates how many percent a bond's price moves when rates move one percent — the bond's interest-rate speedometer.

The Macaulay duration adjusted for the bond's yield, giving the approximate percentage change in a bond's full price for a one-percent (100 basis point) change in yield to maturity — the direct price-sensitivity measure used in practice. If duration is the weighted-average timing of cash flows, modified duration is the translation of that timing into an actual price-risk number: MD 5 means roughly 5% price change per 1% rate change.

The curvature in the relationship between a bond's price and its yield: the second-order measure of how a bond's duration itself changes as yields change, quantifying the error in the linear duration approximation. Duration draws a straight line through a curved price-yield relationship; convexity measures the bend, and positive convexity means the bond falls less than duration predicts when rates rise and gains more when rates fall.

A blockchain is a shared, append-only database maintained by many computers in a network, in which transaction data is grouped into blocks and each block cryptographically references its parent, so that altering past data requires redoing all subsequent blocks and network consensus. Think of it as a public ledger copied onto thousands of computers: everyone holds the same history, and no single party can quietly rewrite it.

A distributed ledger is a database that is replicated, shared and synchronized across multiple nodes or institutions, with updates agreed through a consensus process rather than written by a single central administrator. Instead of one bank keeping the master copy of the books, every participant keeps an identical copy and they all agree on each new entry.

A consensus mechanism is the complete stack of protocols, incentives and ideas that allows a distributed network of nodes to agree on a single state of a blockchain, including Sybil resistance, block author selection and a chain-selection (fork-choice) rule. It is the rulebook that lets thousands of strangers agree on one version of history without a referee.

Proof of work (PoW) is a Sybil-resistance and block-author-selection mechanism in which miners compete to find a nonce that makes a block's hash fall below a difficulty target, expending real-world computation; the chain with the most accumulated work is treated as canonical. Miners burn electricity on a lottery; the winning ticket lets them write the next page of the ledger, and cheating would require out-computing the whole honest network.

Proof of stake (PoS) is a Sybil-resistance and block-author-selection mechanism in which validators lock capital (stake) that can be destroyed (slashed) for dishonest behavior, and are pseudo-randomly selected to propose and attest to blocks. Instead of proving you burned electricity, you post a bond: misbehave and your bond is burned, so cheating costs you directly.

A validator is a node participant in a proof-of-stake network that has deposited stake and is responsible for checking new blocks, attesting to the head of the chain, and occasionally proposing new blocks, earning rewards for honest work and penalties or slashing for failures or misbehavior. A validator is like a juror with money on the table: it votes on what the true chain is, and loses money if it lies or sleeps.

A miner is a network participant in a proof-of-work blockchain that expends computation to find valid block hashes, collecting new coins (block subsidy) and transaction fees in exchange for extending the chain. Miners are the bookkeepers of a PoW chain who pay for their write access with electricity instead of collateral.

A node is any computer running blockchain client software that connects to peers, propagates transactions and blocks, and verifies data against the protocol's consensus rules. Every node keeps its own copy of the ledger and checks the math itself — 'don't trust, verify'.

A wallet is an application or device that manages a user's cryptographic keys and uses them to view balances, sign transactions and interact with blockchain applications; the assets themselves live on the ledger, not inside the wallet. A wallet is a keychain plus a window into the blockchain, not a purse that 'holds' coins.

A private key is a secret 256-bit number that controls an externally owned blockchain account: whoever knows it can sign transactions and spend the account's funds, so it must never be revealed. The private key is the one true password to your coins — there is no recovery desk if it leaks or is lost.

A public key is the openly shareable half of an account's cryptographic key pair, derived one-way from the private key and used by the network to verify signatures and derive the account address. It is like your email address for money: anyone can know it and send you funds, but only the matching private key can spend them.

a: recovery phrase mnemonic phrase backup phrase
x: A seed phrase (recovery phrase) is a human-readable list of typically 12 or 24 words that encodes the entropy from which all of a wallet's private keys are deterministically derived, serving as the master backup for the wallet. It is the master key written in words: anyone who reads it owns everything the wallet controls, forever.

A smart contract is a program deployed to a blockchain — a collection of code (functions) and data (state) at a specific address — that executes automatically and exactly as written when called by a transaction. A vending machine for logic: given the right inputs and fee, a guaranteed, unstoppable output, with no operator able to intervene.

A gas fee is the payment, denominated in the chain's native currency, that compensates the network for the computational resources a transaction consumes, priced per unit of 'gas' — the protocol's measure of computational effort. Gas is the meter on the world's shared computer: every operation you run ticks up a bill you must pay, whether or not the transaction succeeds.

Block space is the finite capacity of each block to include transactions, measured in gas (Ethereum) or bytes/weight (Bitcoin); it is the scarce resource that gas markets price. Each block is a truck with a fixed cargo hold leaving at fixed intervals — when more freight shows up than fits, shippers bid up the price of space.

The mempool (memory pool) is each node's local holding area for valid broadcast transactions that have not yet been included in a block; block producers select transactions from it, typically by fee offered. It is the public waiting room for transactions — and because everyone can read it, predators can see your trade before it executes.

Transaction finality is the point at which a transaction's inclusion in the chain becomes irreversible — on proof-of-stake Ethereum, when the block containing it sits under checkpoints justified and finalized by ≥2/3 of staked ETH, so reversal would require burning at least one-third of all stake. Finality is when 'pending' becomes 'set in stone' — before it, the chain can still be rewritten; after it, reversal would cost attackers billions.

A confirmation is the inclusion of a transaction in a mined/validated block; each additional block built on top counts as another confirmation and exponentially reduces the probability that the transaction is reversed. Each confirmation is another layer of concrete poured over your transaction — one layer can be broken through, six is conventional vault-grade.

A layer 1 (L1) is the base blockchain network itself — such as Ethereum or Bitcoin — that provides its own consensus, data availability and settlement, and on which layer-2 systems anchor their security. The L1 is the bedrock courthouse of record: slower and expensive, but its rulings are final and everything built above ultimately defers to it.

A layer 2 (L2) is a protocol built on top of a layer-1 blockchain that handles transactions off the base chain to increase speed and throughput while deriving its security from the L1's consensus — chiefly via rollups, state channels, or related constructions. An L2 is an express lane that does the fast driving elsewhere but files the paperwork at the L1 courthouse, so the L1's security still backs every transaction.

A rollup is a layer-2 scaling solution that executes transactions off the layer-1 chain and then posts the transaction data (and a state commitment) back to the L1, so that the L1's consensus secures and finalizes the rolled-up state. A rollup runs thousands of transactions on a fast side system, then drops one summarized receipt onto Ethereum — the L1 keeps the evidence needed to check or reconstruct everything.

An optimistic rollup is a layer-2 rollup that assumes offchain transaction batches are valid by default and relies on a fraud-proof scheme: anyone can challenge a posted state transition during a challenge period, and proven fraud reverts the batch and slashes the operator's bond. It is an honor system with a bounty: transactions are accepted unless someone can prove cheating within a week, and the cheater's deposit pays for the mistake.

A zero-knowledge rollup (ZK-rollup) is a layer-2 rollup that executes transactions offchain and submits a succinct cryptographic validity proof (ZK-SNARK or ZK-STARK) to the layer-1 contract, which verifies the proof and finalizes the new state without re-executing the transactions.
