Instead of 'trust me, challenge me if I cheat' (optimistic), a ZK-rollup posts mathematical proof that every transaction in the batch was executed correctly — verified on L1 in one step.

A blockchain bridge is a mechanism that transfers assets, messages or arbitrary data between otherwise isolated blockchain networks, typically by locking or burning assets on the source chain and minting a representation on the destination chain. Bridges are ferries between islands that cannot naturally talk to each other — but the ferry company is often the weakest security link in the whole trip.

a: blockchain oracle price oracle price feed
x: A blockchain oracle is a service that sources, verifies and transmits off-chain data (prices, events, computation results) onto the blockchain so that smart contracts — which cannot access external data themselves — can act on it. Contracts are sealed in a deterministic box and can't browse the internet; the oracle is the courier that slips verified notes under the door.

A decentralized exchange (DEX) is a trading venue implemented as smart contracts — usually an automated market maker — that lets users swap tokens directly from their own wallets without depositing funds with an intermediary. A DEX is a currency-exchange kiosk run by code: open 24/7 to anyone, and your money never leaves your pocket until the exact moment of the swap.

A centralized exchange (CEX) is a trading platform operated by a company that takes custody of user deposits, runs an off-chain central limit order book to match buyers and sellers, and settles trades on its internal ledger. A CEX is a bank crossed with a stock exchange: fast and familiar, but you are trusting the operator with your money the whole time.

a: AMM constant function market maker CFMM
x: An automated market maker (AMM) is a decentralized exchange design that replaces the order book with smart-contract liquidity pools: traders swap against pooled reserves and prices are set algorithmically by a pricing function of those reserves. Instead of matching your buy order with someone's sell order, the AMM is a robot counterparty that always quotes a price from the contents of its vault.

A constant-product market maker (CPMM) is the canonical AMM pricing rule in which the product of a pool's two token reserves must remain constant across trades (x·y=k), so the marginal price is the ratio of reserves and each trade moves the price along a hyperbola. The pool is a balanced scale: remove some of one token and the other must grow so their product never shrinks — which is why big orders get progressively worse prices.

Concentrated liquidity is the Uniswap v3/v4 mechanism that lets liquidity providers allocate capital to a custom price range instead of uniformly across all prices, so the same capital provides deeper liquidity (and earns more fees) where trading actually occurs. Rather than spreading butter thinly from price 0 to infinity, LPs spread it thickly on the slice of the curve where the market actually trades.

A liquidity pool is a smart contract holding reserves of two (or more) tokens that an AMM uses as the counterparty for swaps; traders trade against the pooled reserves and liquidity providers fund them in exchange for a share of fees. It is a communal vault of token pairs: everyone chips in inventory, the vault quotes prices from its contents, and depositors split the toll every trader pays.

A DeFi liquidity provider (LP) is a user who deposits tokens into an AMM liquidity pool (or lending pool) and in return holds a pro-rata claim on the pool's reserves and the fees those reserves generate. LPs are the inventory suppliers of on-chain markets: they rent out their tokens to the pool and get paid a cut of every trade — while silently selling winners and buying losers as prices move.

Impermanent loss is the difference in value between depositing tokens into an AMM liquidity pool and simply holding those same tokens: as relative prices change, arbitrage rebalances the pool so the LP ends up with less of the appreciating asset and more of the depreciating one. The pool automatically sells your winners and buys your losers; if prices snap back the 'loss' vanishes — but if you withdraw while prices have diverged, it becomes real.

Slippage tolerance is the maximum deviation a user accepts between the expected price of an on-chain swap and the price it actually executes at; if execution would exceed this bound, the transaction reverts. It is the 'don't fill me worse than X' dial on a DEX trade — your insurance against the price moving between signing and execution.

Price impact is the change in a pool's token price caused by a trader's own swap: under the constant-product rule, larger trades relative to pool depth execute at progressively worse prices, and the impact is deterministic given pool reserves. It is how much your own order moves the market against you — the bigger the bite you take from the pool, the worse the price of the last bite.

A sandwich attack is an MEV strategy in which an attacker sees a victim's pending DEX trade in the mempool, inserts a buy immediately before it (front-run) and a sell immediately after it (back-run), profiting from the price movement the victim's own trade creates. A predator spots your big market order in the waiting room, jumps the queue to buy ahead of you, lets your purchase push the price up, then dumps on you — you become their exit liquidity.

Blockchain front-running is the practice of observing a profitable pending transaction (in the public mempool or via privileged ordering access) and inserting one's own transaction ahead of it to capture the opportunity first. It is the on-chain version of a broker trading ahead of a client's order — except the order flow is broadcast publicly to everyone, so bots do it at machine speed.

Back-running is an MEV strategy in which a bot places its transaction immediately after a target transaction in the same block, profiting from the state change the target creates — most commonly arbitraging a price dislocation right after a large trade or an oracle update. Instead of jumping the queue, the bot waits for your transaction to move the market, then cleans up the mispricing you left behind in the very same block.

Maximal extractable value (MEV) is the maximum value that can be extracted from block production — beyond the standard block reward and gas fees — by including, excluding, or reordering transactions within a block. Whoever decides the order of transactions in a block holds a printing press: they can see the future of the block and sell positions in it.

A flash loan is an uncollateralized loan that must be borrowed and repaid (plus fee) within a single blockchain transaction; if repayment does not complete, the entire transaction reverts as if the loan never happened. It is a loan that exists only for the duration of one atomic operation — millions of dollars, no collateral, but you must hand it back before the transaction closes or everything unwinds.

A lending protocol is a set of smart contracts (e.g. Aave, Compound) that pools supplied assets and lets borrowers draw loans against deposited collateral, with interest rates, collateral requirements and liquidations enforced automatically by code. It is a pawnshop run by a robot: depositors earn interest, borrowers post more collateral than they take, and the robot seizes and sells the collateral the moment the loan turns unsafe.

The collateral factor is the per-asset parameter that determines how much borrowing power a unit of deposited collateral confers, expressed as a percentage of the collateral's value; in Aave V3 this concept is split into LTV (borrowing power for new loans) and liquidation threshold (the undercollateralization trigger). It is the haircut the protocol applies to your collateral: $100 of a blue-chip asset might count as $80 of borrowing power, while a volatile token counts as far less.

Loan-to-value (LTV) is the ratio of the borrowed amount to the value of the collateral securing it; in DeFi lending, each asset's maximum LTV caps how much can be newly borrowed against it. LTV is the leverage dial on a collateralized loan: 75% LTV means every $100 of collateral backs at most $75 of new borrowing.

The health factor is Aave's numeric measure of how safe a borrow position is: the collateralization of the account weighted by liquidation thresholds, divided by total borrows — a value below 1 means the position can be liquidated. It is a fuel gauge for your loan: comfortably above 1 is green, approaching 1 is the warning light, below 1 liquidators take the car.

The liquidation threshold is the per-asset percentage of collateral value at which a borrow position is deemed undercollateralized and becomes eligible for liquidation — effectively the maintenance margin of a DeFi loan. It is the tripwire on your collateral: once your debt exceeds this share of what you posted, the protocol declares the loan unsafe and lets liquidators step in.

The liquidation bonus (or penalty) is the discount at which a liquidator can claim a borrower's collateral when repaying their debt — the economic incentive that makes third-party liquidation profitable. It is the bounty for the repo agent: repay part of a failing loan and you get to buy the borrower's collateral at a few percent below market.

An overcollateralized loan is a loan whose collateral value exceeds the borrowed amount — the standard structure of DeFi lending, where borrowers must post more than they take because there is no credit assessment or recourse beyond the collateral. Borrow $70 by locking up $100: the lender never checks your credit because your collateral is already worth more than the debt and can be seized instantly.

An under-collateralized loan is a loan where the borrower's collateral is worth less than the outstanding debt — either by design (credit-based or flash loans) or by deterioration (a liquidated-too-late position that becomes protocol bad debt). It is lending on trust rather than on locked value — normal in banking, but the exception in DeFi, where code cannot chase a borrower for the difference.

Staking is the act of depositing a network's native token to activate validator software that secures a proof-of-stake chain — proposing and attesting to blocks — in exchange for protocol rewards, with penalties (slashing) for misbehavior or downtime. Staking is posting a performance bond to become part-time infrastructure: do the work honestly and you earn a yield on your deposit; cheat or sleep and part of the deposit burns.

a: LST staking derivative liquid staking derivative (LSD)
x: A liquid staking token (LST) is a transferable token issued by a liquid staking protocol (e.g. Lido's stETH) that represents a claim on staked assets plus accruing rewards, letting stakers stay liquid and use their stake in DeFi while validators do the work. It is a receipt for your staked ETH that trades like ETH itself — you earn staking yield while still being able to sell, lend or LP the receipt.

Restaking is the reuse of already-staked ETH or liquid staking tokens as cryptoeconomic security for additional services (Actively/Autonomously Verifiable Services, AVSs), letting those services borrow Ethereum's trust while stakers earn extra rewards and accept extra slashing conditions. It is posting the same collateral as bail for multiple jobs at once: more income from one deposit, but any job can trigger forfeiture of the shared stake.

Yield farming is the practice of deploying crypto assets across DeFi protocols — lending pools, liquidity pools, staking — to maximize returns from interest, trading fees and token incentives, often moving capital frequently to chase the highest rates. It is rate-chasing on steroids: farmers shuttle capital to wherever the combination of fees, interest and reward tokens pays the most this week.

Liquidity mining is a token incentive program in which a protocol distributes its governance tokens to users who provide liquidity (or other desired behavior), subsidizing early liquidity and decentralizing token ownership. It is paying suppliers in company stock to stock the shelves: the protocol rents liquidity with newly minted tokens instead of cash.

Tokenomics is the economic design of a crypto token: its supply schedule (issuance, burns, caps), distribution (allocations, vesting, airdrops), utility (fees, governance, staking) and the incentive structures that determine how value and behavior accrue around it. It is the monetary policy plus cap table plus business model of a token — the rules that decide who gets tokens, when, and why anyone should hold them.

Circulating supply is the number of tokens currently issued and available to the market — excluding locked, vested, escrowed or not-yet-minted tokens — and is the supply basis for the conventional market capitalization. It is the float: the tokens that could actually change hands today, not the ones still locked in team vaults or scheduled for future emission.

Total supply is the total number of tokens that have been created (minted) so far, minus any that have been verifiably burned — i.e. all tokens in existence whether or not they are circulating. It is the full headcount of minted tokens: circulating plus everything still locked in vesting contracts, treasuries and escrow.

Maximum supply is the hard upper bound on the number of tokens that can ever exist under a protocol's issuance rules, where such a cap exists — most famously Bitcoin's 21 million. It is the ceiling written into the monetary constitution: no matter what happens, there will never be more than this many coins.

Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is a token's price multiplied by its total (or maximum) supply — the market capitalization the asset would have if every token that can ever exist were already circulating at today's price. FDV is the sticker price of the whole company if all shares, including locked insider shares, traded at today's price — often a fantasy number for low-float tokens.

Crypto market capitalization is the total USD value of an asset's supply, conventionally computed as current price multiplied by circulating supply (Coin Metrics' on-chain variant uses all issued native units). It is the price tag of the entire network at today's price — the standard yardstick for comparing the size of cryptoassets.

A token unlock is the scheduled release of previously locked tokens (team, investor, advisor or ecosystem allocations) into transferable circulation under a project's vesting terms — a predictable supply shock that markets typically front-run. It is the day the dam gate opens on insider stock: a known date when a tranche of supply becomes sellable for the first time.

A vesting schedule is the pre-committed timetable by which locked token allocations (team, investors, advisors) become transferable, typically combining a cliff (no tokens for an initial period) with linear or batched releases thereafter. It is a golden-handcuffs calendar: insiders earn their tokens over years instead of getting them on day one, aligning them with the project's survival.

A token burn is the permanent, verifiable removal of tokens from supply by sending them to an unspendable destination or destroying them in-protocol, reducing total supply. It is shredding banknotes on-chain: the tokens provably cease to exist, making each remaining token a larger share of the whole.

Minting is the creation of new tokens on-chain, increasing total supply — whether as protocol issuance (block rewards to miners/validators) or as application-level token creation by smart contracts. It is the printing press of a token economy: new units come into existence by rule, either paying for security or instantiating new assets.

An emission schedule is the predetermined rule governing the rate and timing of new token issuance over time — the protocol's monetary policy expressed as supply growth per block, epoch or era. It is the central-bank timetable baked into code: exactly how many new tokens are printed, when, and for whom, years into the future.

An airdrop is the free distribution of tokens to a set of wallet addresses, typically to reward past users, bootstrap a community, or decentralize governance ownership, with eligibility usually set by an on-chain snapshot. It is a retroactive thank-you payment and marketing campaign in one: wake up, check your wallet, and there are tokens because you used the protocol before a cutoff date.

A governance token is a token whose primary utility is voting power over a protocol's decisions — parameter changes, treasury spending, upgrades — typically exercised through a DAO's proposal-and-vote contracts. It is a shareholder ballot in token form: holding it gives you a say in how the protocol runs, weighted by how much you hold.

Protocol revenue is the portion of the fees a protocol collects that is kept by the protocol entity itself — flowing to its treasury or governance token holders — as distinct from fees passed through to liquidity providers or other suppliers. If fees are the till, protocol revenue is what the house actually keeps after paying the market makers who stocked the shelves.

Protocol fees are all charges and value a protocol collects from its operation — swap fees, borrow interest, liquidation penalties, management fees — excluding the gas costs users pay to the underlying network. Fees are the gross till of the protocol: everything users pay in, before it is split between liquidity suppliers, the treasury and token holders.

Total value locked (TVL) is the aggregate USD value of assets deposited by users into a protocol's own smart contracts — the standard gauge of how much capital a DeFi protocol or chain secures. TVL is the size of the vault: how much money users have parked in the protocol's contracts at this moment.

Stablecoin supply is the total outstanding issuance of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies designed to hold a stable value against a reference asset, usually the US dollar — and is tracked as a proxy for dry powder and fiat liquidity in the crypto economy. It is the pile of dollar chips sitting at the crypto casino's tables: when it grows, new fiat-backed buying power is entering; when it shrinks, capital is cashing out.

Exchange inflow is the volume of coins transferred on-chain into wallets attributed to centralized exchanges over a period, watched as a leading indicator of intent to sell or trade. Coins moving onto an exchange are like goods carried into a pawnshop — they are positioned to be sold, even if the sale hasn't happened yet.

Exchange outflow is the volume of coins withdrawn on-chain from exchange-attributed wallets over a period, commonly read as accumulation or movement to self-custody and reduced immediate sell pressure. Coins leaving the exchange are goods carried home from the market — they are being put back into storage rather than offered for sale.

Exchange reserve (exchange balance) is the total amount of a coin held in wallets attributed to centralized exchanges — the immediately sellable inventory sitting on trading venues. It is the stock of goods on shop shelves: a bulging shelf means plenty of potential supply for sale; emptying shelves mean holders have taken their coins home.

Realized capitalization (realized cap) values each coin at the price when it last moved on-chain, rather than at the current price — approximating the aggregate cost basis of the network and the value 'stored' in the asset. Instead of pricing every coin at today's quote, realized cap asks: what did the market actually pay for all these coins when they last changed hands?

MVRV (market-value-to-realized-value) is the ratio of an asset's market capitalization to its realized capitalization, comparing the market's current valuation to the aggregate on-chain cost basis. MVRV asks whether holders are, on average, sitting on big paper gains (ratio high, temptation to sell) or paper losses (ratio low, capitulation territory).

SOPR (Spent Output Profit Ratio) is the ratio of the fiat value of spent coins at the time they are spent to their value when they were created, measuring whether coins moving on-chain are, on average, being sold at a profit or a loss. SOPR is the market's daily P&L receipt: above 1, spenders are cashing out winners; below 1, they are realizing losses.

NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss) measures the network's total paper profit or loss as a share of market cap: the difference between market cap and realized cap, divided by market cap. NUPL answers: if every holder sold today, what fraction of the market's value would be profit? It is the aggregate sentiment dial from capitulation to euphoria.

Coin Days Destroyed (CDD) is an on-chain activity metric that weights coin movements by dormancy: each unspent coin accumulates one 'coin day' per day, and spending it destroys those accumulated days, so movements of old coins count far more than churn of young ones. Moving 10 BTC held for a decade rings a louder bell than moving 10 BTC bought yesterday — CDD measures the age-weighted significance of what moved.

a: HODL wave age bands UTXO age distribution
x: HODL waves are a visualization of the age distribution of the coin supply: colored bands show what fraction of all coins last moved within each age bucket (from <1 day to >10 years), revealing accumulation and distribution cycles. It is a geological cross-section of holder behavior: warm young layers swell when coins churn, cool old layers thicken when conviction holders sit tight.

Active addresses is the count of unique addresses that participated in the network as a sender or receiver in successful transactions over a period — the standard on-chain proxy for network usage and user activity. It is the daily foot-traffic count of a blockchain: how many distinct addresses actually showed up and transacted.

Transaction count is the total number of successful on-chain transactions over a period — the basic measure of how much settlement activity a blockchain processes. It is the number of checks the ledger cleared today, regardless of their size.

Hash rate is the estimated total computational power that miners devote to a proof-of-work network, expressed in hashes per second; it is the primary gauge of PoW security expenditure. It is the horsepower of the mining fleet: the more hashes per second the network throws at the puzzle, the costlier it is for an attacker to rewrite history.

Staking ratio is the percentage of a proof-of-stake network's eligible token supply that is actively staked, indicating how much capital currently secures consensus and how much remains liquid. It is the share of the town's wealth posted as security bonds: higher means more skin in the game, but also less free capital circulating in the economy.

The funding rate is a periodic payment exchanged directly between long and short holders of a perpetual futures contract, sized by the gap between the perpetual's price and the underlying spot index, designed to pull the perpetual price back toward spot. Perpetuals have no expiry to force convergence, so the market rents a tether instead: whoever is on the crowded, premium side pays the other side every few hours.

The predicted (estimated) funding rate is the exchange's real-time forecast of the funding rate that will apply at the next funding timestamp, computed from the premium index samples collected so far in the current interval. It is the meter running on the next funding bill: it shows what longs or shorts would pay if the interval ended right now.

The funding interval is the fixed period between funding payments on a perpetual futures contract — the clock that determines how often the funding rate is applied to open positions. It is the billing cycle of the perp tether: every interval, the payment between longs and shorts settles and the meter resets.

The perpetual basis is the price difference between a perpetual futures contract and the underlying spot (index) price, typically expressed as a percentage; the funding mechanism exists to keep this basis mean-reverting around zero. It is how far the tail (perp) wags from the dog (spot): positive when perp buyers pay a premium, negative when perps trade at a discount.

A liquidation cascade is a self-reinforcing chain of forced position closures: falling prices trigger liquidations whose forced market sells push prices lower still, triggering the next tier of liquidations in rapid succession. It is an avalanche on a leveraged mountainside: each margin call knocks loose more snow, and the falling snow triggers the margin calls below.

a: OI/market cap ratio estimated leverage ratio
x: The open-interest leverage ratio compares total derivatives open interest to the underlying market's size (spot market cap or exchange reserves), gauging how much leveraged positioning the market carries relative to its real capital base. It is the debt-to-equity ratio of the whole market: how big the tower of leveraged bets is compared to the pile of actual coins it leans on.

The long-short ratio is the proportion of long to short positioning in a derivatives market — reported by exchanges either by account count or by position size — used as a sentiment and crowding gauge. It is the seating chart of the derivatives arena: how many traders are on the bullish side versus the bearish side, and how lopsided the crowd has become.

Cross margin is a margin mode in which all available balance in the margin/futures account is shared as collateral across every open position, so unrealized profits and the whole account equity support each position's maintenance margin. It is one shared life raft for all your trades: a losing position can drain the entire account to stay afloat — and if it sinks, everything goes down with it.

Isolated margin is a margin mode in which each position carries its own dedicated collateral allotment, capping the maximum loss of that position at the margin assigned to it and ring-fencing the rest of the account. It is a fire door between trades: each position burns with only the fuel you loaded into it, never spreading to the rest of the account.

A curve that plots the yields of bonds of the same credit quality (typically government securities) against their times to maturity at a given point in time. The U.S. Treasury's official version is a par yield curve relating the par yield on a Treasury security to its time to maturity, derived daily from market price quotations. It is a snapshot of what it costs to borrow money for different lengths of time, showing how the market prices time, risk, and expectations about future rates.

a: upward-sloping yield curve positive yield curve
x: A yield curve configuration in which longer-maturity yields are higher than shorter-maturity yields, giving the curve an upward slope. It is the historically most common configuration, reflecting term premia and typical expectations that rates will not fall sharply. Lenders usually demand more compensation for tying up money longer, so longer loans carry higher rates — that is the 'normal' state of the curve.

A yield curve configuration in which shorter-maturity yields exceed longer-maturity yields, giving the curve a downward slope. The U.S. Treasury notes that short-term rates can exceed longer-term rates when market expectations about future rates and monetary policy shift; inversions have historically preceded U.S. recessions, though the relationship is a statistical regularity, not a causal law. Investors accept lower yields on long bonds because they expect rates to fall in the future — often because they expect the central bank to cut rates in a slowdown.

A yield curve configuration in which yields are approximately equal across maturities, so the term spread is near zero. It typically appears as a transitional state between an upward-sloping (normal) curve and an inverted curve, or vice versa. The market is charging roughly the same rate to borrow for one year as for ten years — a sign that expectations about the future are unusually uncertain or in transition.

The curve of yields on zero-coupon instruments across maturities — the set of rates at which a single future cash flow is discounted to today. It is built by bootstrapping coupon-bearing bond prices so that each instrument is repriced without error, and it is the curve used for present-value calculations. Instead of one blended yield per bond, the spot curve gives a separate 'pure' interest rate for every single future date, like a price tag for money delivered at each point in time.

The curve of interest rates implied today for borrowing or lending over future periods, derived from the spot (zero-coupon) curve so that investing to a long horizon equals rolling over at the shorter rate plus the forward rate. The U.S. Treasury's curve construction bootstraps instantaneous forward rates at input maturities as an intermediate step. If you know the 1-year rate and the 2-year rate, the market is implicitly quoting a rate for year two alone — the forward curve is the set of all such implied future-period rates.

a: present value factor price of a zero-coupon bond
x: The present value of one unit of currency received at a specified future date, equivalently the price today of a risk-free zero-coupon payment of 1 at that date. The full set of discount factors across dates is the discount function, which is derived from the spot rate curve. A discount factor answers: how much is a dollar delivered on a given future date worth right now?

The yield earned on an investment that makes a single payment at maturity with no intermediate coupons, for a specific maturity. It is the building block of the spot (zero-coupon) curve used to discount individual future cash flows. It is the pure interest rate for money delivered at one exact future date, with nothing paid in between — like the rate on a Treasury bill or a STRIP.

The coupon rate at which a hypothetical bond of a given maturity would price exactly at par (100% of face value), given the current discount function. The U.S. Treasury's official daily yield curve is a par yield curve, and its constant-maturity (CMT) rates are par yields read from that curve. It is the coupon a brand-new bond of a given maturity would have to pay today for investors to accept it at full face value.

The difference between two yields, typically expressed in basis points. Depending on context it may compare maturities on the same curve (term spread, e.g. 10-year minus 2-year Treasury), or securities of different credit quality at the same maturity (credit spread). It is the extra (or lesser) yield one instrument offers relative to another, summarizing how the market prices the difference in time, risk, or liquidity between them.

The difference between the yield on the debt securities of a particular corporate or sovereign borrower (or a rating class of borrowers) and the yield on similar-maturity Treasury securities. It compensates investors for bearing default and credit-migration risk, plus a liquidity component. It is the extra interest a risky borrower must pay over the government to persuade investors to lend to it.

The constant spread added to a benchmark spot curve that makes the model value of a security's cash flows — adjusted for the value of embedded options such as calls or prepayment rights — equal to its market price. It is the standard spread measure for callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It is the yield premium a bond pays over Treasuries after stripping out the value of any options hidden in the bond, leaving a cleaner measure of credit and liquidity compensation.

The constant spread that, when added to each point of the Treasury (or benchmark) spot rate curve, makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its market price. Unlike a nominal spread measured at a single maturity, it accounts for the entire term structure; unlike OAS, it does not adjust for embedded options. It is the single number of extra yield the bond must offer at every point along the curve for its promised cash flows to be worth today's price.

The spread over the floating benchmark in an asset swap — a package in which an investor buys a fixed-rate bond and simultaneously enters an interest rate swap, paying the bond's fixed coupons and receiving a floating rate plus a spread. It expresses the bond's yield relative to the swap curve rather than to government bonds. It measures how much extra return a bond offers once its interest-rate exposure has been swapped away, isolating the credit and liquidity premium versus the derivatives market's benchmark.

The difference between the fixed rate on a plain-vanilla interest rate swap of a given maturity and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity. It reflects the relative pricing of the derivatives and government bond markets, including intermediation and funding costs. It compares the cost of exchanging fixed-for-floating payments in the swap market with the government's borrowing cost — a gauge of how dealers price balance-sheet usage and of relative supply and demand in the two markets.

a: dollar value of a basis point PVBP basis point value BPV
x: The change in a bond's (or portfolio's) value, in currency units, for a one-basis-point (0.01%) change in yield. In the U.S. it is also called the dollar value of an 01; it is essentially the price value of a basis point (PVBP), often written PV01. It answers the trader's core question: how many dollars do I make or lose if yields move by one basis point?

a: present value of a basis point PVBP price value of a basis point
x: The change in the present value (full price) of a bond or swap for a one-basis-point change in yield. It is the same quantity as PVBP and the U.S. market term DV01; in swap markets PV01 is the standard sensitivity measure per basis point of the swap rate. It is the cash value gained or lost when the relevant rate ticks up or down by a single basis point.

A measure of a bond's or portfolio's price sensitivity to a change in yield at one specific maturity point on the curve, holding other points fixed. The set of key rate durations across maturities decomposes total interest-rate sensitivity, and they sum (approximately) to the effective duration. Instead of asking 'what if all rates move?', it asks 'what if only the 5-year rate moves?' — locating where along the curve a portfolio's risk actually sits.

A bond's price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve, computed numerically by repricing the bond at higher and lower yields while allowing cash flows to change (e.g. via call or prepayment options). It is the appropriate duration measure for bonds with embedded options, where cash flows are not fixed. It measures how much a bond's price actually moves when rates move, recognizing that for callable or mortgage bonds the payments themselves change when rates change.

The weighted-average time until a bond's cash flows are received, with each cash flow weighted by its share of the bond's present value. Expressed in years, it equals maturity for a zero-coupon bond and is always shorter than maturity for a coupon bond; it is the foundation from which modified and effective duration are derived. It is the 'center of gravity' of a bond's payments — the single point in time at which the average dollar of the bond's value arrives.

A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is concave: prices rise less when yields fall and fall more when yields rise than duration alone predicts. It is typical of callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities, whose cash flows shorten when rates decline (calls/prepayments) and lengthen when rates rise. The bond works against you both ways: it stops appreciating just when rates fall (because it gets called or prepaid) and keeps falling when rates rise.

A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is convex: prices rise more when yields fall and fall less when yields rise than duration alone predicts. All standard non-callable fixed-rate bonds exhibit positive convexity; the effect grows with longer maturity and lower coupons. The bond's price accelerates in your favor: you gain a bit extra when rates fall and lose a bit less when rates rise, compared with the straight-line duration estimate.

A unit of measure for interest rates and yields equal to one one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). It is the standard unit for quoting yield changes, spreads, and rate moves. It is the 'cent' of interest rates: saying 'up 25 basis points' unambiguously means up 0.25 percentage points.

The short-term interest rate that a central bank sets (or targets) to implement monetary policy. In the United States it is the Federal Open Market Committee's target range for the federal funds rate, which the New York Fed's trading desk defends through open market operations and administered rates. It is the central bank's main dial: raising it tightens financial conditions to cool the economy, lowering it loosens conditions to stimulate activity.

The interest rate on loans or deposits with a maturity of one business day, typically traded between financial institutions to manage daily reserve or cash positions. Key U.S. overnight rates include the effective federal funds rate (unsecured) and SOFR (secured by Treasury collateral). It is the price of borrowing money until tomorrow — the shortest-maturity interest rate in the financial system and the anchor for all longer rates.

A broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities, published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It is the principal U.S. dollar benchmark that replaced LIBOR for derivatives and loans. It is the going rate for a one-day loan backed by Treasuries — essentially a near-risk-free overnight borrowing cost built from actual repo market transactions.

a: fed funds rate EFFR (effective federal funds rate)
x: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight, uncollateralized. The FOMC sets a target rate or range for it, and the New York Fed publishes the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) as the volume-weighted median of actual transactions. It is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of their reserve balances at the Fed — the rate U.S. monetary policy directly targets.

The implicit interest rate on a repurchase agreement, a transaction in which one party sells securities and agrees to repurchase them later at a slightly higher price — economically a loan collateralized by securities. The rate is set by the difference between the sale and repurchase prices relative to the term. It is the cost of borrowing cash against bonds: you hand over the securities, get cash, and pay back a bit more later — that bit more, annualized, is the repo rate.

The percentage reduction applied to the market value of collateral when determining how much cash can be borrowed against it. In a repo, the haircut is the gap between the collateral's value and the cash lent, protecting the lender against a fall in collateral value before it could be sold. If you pledge $1 million of bonds with a 5% haircut, the lender only gives you $950,000 — the haircut is the lender's safety cushion.

The extra yield investors demand for holding a longer-term bond instead of rolling over a series of short-term instruments — compensation for the risk that future rates and inflation differ from expectations. It is the difference between a long-term yield and the expected average of future short rates, and it is not directly observable. Locking your money up for ten years is riskier than renewing a one-year loan ten times; the term premium is the extra pay for bearing that risk.

The inflation rate that would make an investor indifferent between holding a nominal Treasury and a same-maturity Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS), computed as the nominal yield minus the real (TIPS) yield. It is a market-based measure of expected average inflation over the horizon, though it also embeds inflation risk and liquidity premia. If nominal bonds pay 4.5% and inflation-protected bonds pay 2.0%, the market is pricing roughly 2.5% average inflation — that gap is the breakeven.

A derivative in which one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays the realized change in an inflation index (e.g. U.S. CPI-U) on a notional amount, transferring inflation risk. In the standard zero-coupon form, both legs are compounded and exchanged as a single payment at maturity. It is a bet or hedge on inflation itself: one side pays a pre-agreed inflation rate, the other pays whatever inflation actually turns out to be.

The first currency in a currency-pair quotation, i.e. the currency being priced. The quoted exchange rate expresses how many units of the quote (counter) currency are needed to buy one unit of the base currency, as in EUR/USD 1.2500 meaning one euro exchanges for 1.25 US dollars, with EUR as the base. The base currency is the 'thing being bought or sold' in an FX quote; the number tells you its price in the other currency.

The second currency in a currency-pair quotation, i.e. the currency in which the price of one unit of the base currency is expressed. In EUR/USD 1.2500, USD is the quote (counter) currency and the rate states that 1 euro is exchanged for 1.25 US dollars. The quote currency is the 'money you pay with' in the pair — the quoted number is an amount of it.

An exchange rate quotation expressed from the home country's perspective as the number of units of home currency per one unit of foreign currency. For example, from the euro area's perspective, EUR 0.8989 = USD 1.00 is a direct quotation; it is the convention used in most countries. Direct quotation treats the foreign currency as the 'good' and states its price in your own money.

An exchange rate quotation expressed from the home country's perspective as the number of units of foreign currency per one unit of home currency. For example, from the euro area's perspective, USD 1.11 = EUR 1.00 is an indirect quotation; the convention is common in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and the euro area. Indirect quotation states how much foreign money one unit of your own currency buys.

a: percentage in point price interest point
x: The conventional smallest whole-unit increment of an FX exchange rate quote. For most major currency pairs (priced to four decimal places) one pip is one unit of the fourth decimal place (0.0001); for yen pairs one pip is one unit of the second decimal place (0.01). A pip is the FX market's standard 'cent' for talking about exchange-rate moves and spreads.

a: fractional pip point (tenth of a pip)
x: One tenth of a pip, i.e. the additional decimal place (the fifth decimal for most pairs, the third for yen pairs) that electronic FX platforms added to quotes. Pipettes allow finer pricing than the traditional four-decimal convention. A pipette is the extra digit beyond the pip that lets platforms quote spreads in tenths of a pip.

a: spot foreign exchange spot FX transaction
x: A transaction for the exchange of two currencies at a rate agreed on the trade date for settlement on the standard spot value date, normally two business days later (T+2). Spot is one of the core OTC FX instrument categories in the BIS Triennial Survey and accounted for 28% of the $7.5 trillion average daily global FX turnover in April 2022. A spot FX deal is 'buy currency now at today's rate', with the actual exchange of funds settling a couple of business days later.

An over-the-counter contract to exchange one currency for another at a rate fixed today for settlement on a specific future date beyond the spot value date. Outright forwards are used mainly to hedge future currency payments and receipts, and accounted for 15% of global OTC FX turnover in April 2022. An FX forward locks in today the exchange rate for a currency trade you will make weeks or months from now.

A contract combining a spot purchase (sale) of one currency against another with a simultaneous offsetting forward sale (purchase) of the same amounts. In the spot leg one party lends one currency and borrows the other at the spot rate; in the forward leg the exchange is reversed at a pre-agreed forward rate, making the instrument economically similar to collateralized borrowing and lending. FX swaps were the most traded FX instrument, at $3.8 trillion per day (51% of global turnover) in April 2022. An FX swap is like a repo with a currency instead of a security: you swap currencies today and swap them back later at a pre-set rate.

A strategy of borrowing (funding) in a low-interest-rate currency and investing in a high-interest-rate currency without hedging the exchange-rate exposure, aiming to earn the interest rate differential. Its profitability violates uncovered interest parity, and research documents that carry-trade returns are negatively skewed — subject to sudden crash risk when funding liquidity falls and positions unwind en masse. Collect the interest-rate gap between two currencies and hope the exchange rate doesn't move against you before you exit.

The difference between the forward exchange rate and the spot exchange rate for a given tenor, i.e. the adjustment added to or subtracted from the spot rate to obtain the outright forward rate. FX swaps are typically quoted in forward points rather than outright rates. Forward points are the 'time value' of a currency pair — how much the forward rate differs from spot because of the interest-rate gap.

The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is above its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a premium for future delivery (equivalently, positive forward points). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward premium when its interest rate is below that of the other currency in the pair. A currency at a forward premium costs more in the forward market than in the spot market — the mirror image of its lower interest rate.

The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is below its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a discount for future delivery (equivalently, negative forward points for that currency). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward discount when its interest rate is above that of the other currency in the pair. A currency at a forward discount costs less forward than spot — the arithmetic counterpart of its higher interest rate.

The family of equilibrium conditions linking spot and forward exchange rates to interest rate differentials between two currencies. It comprises covered interest parity — a no-arbitrage condition tying the forward premium to the interest differential — and uncovered interest parity, which relates the interest differential to the expected change in the spot rate. Money should earn the same total return wherever it is parked once currency effects are accounted for; IRP is the statement of that idea, hedged (covered) or unhedged (uncovered).

The no-arbitrage condition that interest rates on two otherwise identical assets in different currencies must be equal once the foreign currency risk is hedged in the forward market: the interest rate differential should equal the differential between the forward and spot exchange rates. Often described as the closest thing to a physical law in international finance, it has been systematically violated since the 2008 financial crisis, visible in a persistent cross-currency basis. If you fully hedge the currency risk, borrowing dollars to invest in yen (or vice versa) should earn nothing extra — CIP is what makes that true.

a: UIP uncovered interest rate parity UIRP
x: The hypothesis that the interest rate differential between two currencies equals the expected change in their exchange rate, so that the higher-yielding currency is expected to depreciate just enough to offset its yield advantage for an unhedged investor. Empirically UIP fails: high-interest-rate currencies tend to appreciate rather than depreciate, a puzzle that underlies carry-trade profitability. UIP says there's no free lunch from chasing higher foreign interest rates — the exchange rate should move to cancel the extra yield. In practice it often doesn't.

An exchange rate between two currencies that does not directly involve the home reference currency — in market practice, a pair not involving the US dollar (e.g. EUR/GBP, GBP/JPY). Because most currencies are quoted primarily against the dollar, cross rates are typically derived by multiplying or dividing the two currencies' dollar rates. A cross rate is the exchange rate between two 'non-anchor' currencies, usually computed through their rates against the dollar.

a: triangular arbitrage cross currency arbitrage three-point arbitrage
x: The practice of exploiting a pricing discrepancy among three currencies by executing three trades — exchanging an initial currency for a second, the second for a third, and the third back into the initial — when the quoted cross exchange rate diverges from the implicit cross rate derived from the other two pairs. High-frequency studies find such opportunities are rare, small (often ~1 basis point) and fleeting (mostly lasting seconds or less). If EUR/USD and USD/JPY imply one EUR/JPY rate but a bank quotes another, you can cycle through the three pairs and end up with more than you started.

A proprietary index, designed and published by ICE Data Indices, measuring the value of the US dollar as a weighted geometric mean against a fixed basket of six currencies: euro (57.6%), yen (13.6%), pound sterling (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%) and Swiss franc (3.6%). Set at 100.000 at its March 1973 start, it rises when the dollar strengthens against the basket; futures on the index trade on ICE. DXY is the standard single number summarizing how strong the dollar is overall against other major currencies.

A trade-weighted index of a currency's value against a basket of partner currencies, adjusted for relative price levels — in the BIS methodology, derived by adjusting the nominal effective exchange rate by relative consumer prices. An increase in the REER indicates a real appreciation of the currency, interpreted as a loss of price competitiveness. The REER tells you whether your currency is really getting more expensive abroad, after accounting for inflation differences — not just what the nominal rate says.

A trade-weighted index of a currency's nominal value against a basket of trading-partner currencies — in the BIS methodology, calculated as a geometric trade-weighted average of bilateral exchange rates. An increase in the NEER indicates a nominal appreciation of the currency; it is the building block from which the real effective exchange rate is derived by adjusting for relative prices. The NEER collapses a currency's many bilateral exchange rates into one number weighted by how much you trade with each partner.

The date on which the counterparties to a foreign exchange trade actually exchange the funds, i.e. when the traded amounts become effective (delivered). For a spot FX transaction the value date is normally two business days after the trade is agreed (T+2); for forwards and swaps it is the agreed future delivery date of each leg. The trade date is when you agree the deal; the value date is when the money actually changes hands.

A short-dated FX swap used to roll a currency position forward by one day: the holder buys (or sells) a foreign currency amount settling tomorrow and simultaneously does the opposite transaction settling the day after (the spot value date). Institutions use tom-next swaps at the end of each day to close out and re-institute foreign balances, thereby collecting or paying the overnight interest differential (cost of carry) without holding an open FX position. Tom-next is the daily 'roll' that keeps a spot FX position from ever settling, in exchange for paying or receiving one day of the interest-rate gap.

A reference exchange rate determined at a set time each trading day from market transactions and orders around a fixing window, used to value portfolios, settle contracts and execute customer 'fix orders' at a common published price. The most prominent is the London WM/Reuters 4 p.m. fixing in the interbank forex market. A fixing is the market's agreed 'official' exchange rate for a given moment each day, so that funds and contracts everywhere can be valued on the same number.

a: WM/Reuters 4pm fix WMR 4pm fix London fix
x: The daily reference exchange rate computed from market activity in a window around 4:00 p.m. London time, historically administered as the WM/Reuters benchmark. It is the most widely used FX fixing for valuing funds, settling derivatives and executing customer orders, and was the focus of the 2013-15 benchmark-manipulation investigations and the subsequent 2015 reform that widened the fixing window. The 4 p.m. London fix is the FX market's global 'closing price' — the single rate the world's asset managers use to value and convert currencies.

The set of prices of futures contracts on the same underlying asset across successive delivery months, plotted as price against time to maturity. Its shape (upward-sloping, downward-sloping, or mixed) summarizes how the market prices near-term versus deferred delivery. It is the price 'map' of the same commodity or asset at different future delivery dates — like reading the market's price tag for delivery in each coming month.

a: futures term structure price term structure
x: The relationship between the prices (or yields) of contracts on the same underlying asset and their times to maturity or delivery. In futures markets it is synonymous with the futures curve; in rates markets it refers to the yield curve across maturities. It answers the question: how does price change purely as a function of when delivery or maturity occurs, holding the asset itself constant?

A market situation in which prices in succeeding delivery months are progressively higher than in the nearest delivery month, i.e. the futures curve slopes upward. For physically delivered contracts, contango typically reflects storage, financing, and insurance costs of carrying the commodity; it is the opposite of backwardation. The further out in time you buy delivery, the more you pay — because someone has to store, finance, and insure the goods until then.

A market situation in which futures prices are progressively lower in the more distant delivery months than in the nearer months or spot, i.e. the futures curve slopes downward. It is the opposite of contango and often signals tight near-term supply or a high convenience yield on holding the physical commodity. Buyers pay a premium to get the commodity now rather than later — immediacy is worth more than future delivery.

The difference between the spot or cash price of a commodity and the price of the nearest futures contract for the same or a related commodity, typically calculated as cash minus futures. It is usually computed against the futures contract next to expire and may reflect differences in time, product form, grade, or location. Basis is the local truth adjustment: what you actually pay or receive at your elevator, hub, or grade versus the exchange's quoted futures price.

A market-neutral strategy that combines buying an asset in the cash (spot) market with selling a futures contract on the same asset, to exploit a futures price that is high relative to the spot price plus carrying costs. The arbitrageur holds ('carries') the asset until futures expiration and delivers it against the short futures position. If the futures price overpays for future delivery relative to what it costs to buy, store, and finance the goods today, you can lock in that overpayment by buying now and selling forward.

The mirror image of cash-and-carry arbitrage: a market-neutral strategy that shorts the asset in the cash market while buying its futures contract, exploiting a futures price that is low relative to spot, a condition associated with backwardation. At maturity the arbitrageur takes delivery against the long futures and uses it to cover the short position. If the market prices future delivery cheaply compared with today's spot, sell high now and lock in cheap re-purchase later through the futures contract.

The cost of storing a physical commodity or holding a financial instrument over a period of time, including insurance, storage, and interest on the funds committed, plus other incidental costs. A market in which futures prices rise with each successive maturity by at least these charges is called a carrying-charge market; if the charges fully reimburse the holder, the carry is 'full'. It is the total bill for holding an asset from today until a future delivery date — rent for the warehouse, insurance premiums, and the interest on the money tied up.

The implied benefit or return from physically holding a commodity inventory — for example, keeping a production process running or avoiding stockouts — rather than holding a futures contract on it. It is inversely related to inventory levels: when stocks are high the convenience yield is low, and when stocks are low it is high. Owning the actual barrel or bushel has an option value a paper contract does not: you can use it, sell it, or keep your plant running when supply is tight.

The return generated when a futures position is rolled from a near-term expiring contract into a longer-dated contract, arising from the price difference between the two contracts as the near contract converges toward spot. It is positive for long positions in backwardation and negative in contango. Because a futures price must meet the spot price at expiry, holding and renewing a position earns (or costs) the gap between the expiring contract and the next one, even if the spot price never moves.

a: calendar spread time spread horizontal spread interdelivery spread
x: The simultaneous purchase of one delivery month of a futures contract and sale of a different delivery month of the same futures contract. The position is a bet on the change in the price relationship between the two months (the term structure) rather than on the outright direction of the market. Instead of betting on whether the price goes up or down, you bet on whether near delivery gets more expensive or cheaper relative to later delivery.

A spread in which the long and short legs are in two different but generally related commodity markets — for example, corn versus soybeans or crude oil versus gasoline. In interest-rate futures, yield curve spread trades are treated by CME Group as intercommodity spreads. You trade the price relationship between two linked commodities — betting that one gains value relative to the other — rather than the direction of either market alone.

A spread involving two different delivery months of the same commodity — the CFTC glossary defines the interdelivery spread as exactly this and notes it is also called an intracommodity spread. It is functionally identical to the futures calendar spread: the trader is long one month and short another of the same contract. Same commodity, different months: you trade the shape of one market's own curve rather than its level.

In energy futures, the simultaneous purchase of crude oil futures and sale of petroleum product futures (or the reverse) to establish a refining margin; also the calculated theoretical market value of the refined products obtainable from a barrel of crude after it is 'cracked'. Common variants are the gasoline crack, heating oil crack, and the 3-2-1 crack spread of three crude contracts against two gasoline and one heating oil contract. It is the refinery's gross margin traded as an instrument: what you can sell the gasoline and diesel for, minus what the crude cost you.

a: soybean crush board crush gross processing margin
x: In the soybean futures market, the simultaneous purchase of soybean futures and sale of soybean meal and soybean oil futures to establish a processing margin (the reverse — selling beans and buying products — is the reverse crush). It expresses the value added by crushing raw soybeans into meal and oil. It is the soybean processor's gross profit line turned into a trade: what meal and oil sell for, minus what the beans cost.

The difference between the price received by a generator for electricity produced and the cost of the natural gas needed to produce that electricity — a common metric for estimating the profitability of natural gas-fired generation. It is typically calculated from daily spot prices for power and gas at regional trading points, using a benchmark heat rate. It is the gas power plant's gross margin per megawatt-hour: the electricity price minus the fuel bill to generate it.

The difference between the price received by a generator for electricity produced and the cost of the coal needed to produce it — the coal-fired analogue of the spark spread, used to estimate returns over fuel costs of coal generation. It can be computed from current spot prices or from forward prices. It is the coal plant's gross margin per megawatt-hour: the power price minus the coal bill (including getting the coal to the plant).

The spread between the 3-month LIBOR based on US dollars and the 3-month US Treasury bill yield, historically used as a gauge of perceived credit risk in the interbank market versus risk-free government debt. The FRED series (TEDRATE) was discontinued in January 2022 when 3-month USD LIBOR ceased publication; SOFR-based spreads are the suggested modern analogue. It measures how much extra interest banks demand to lend to each other compared with what the US government pays — a fear gauge for bank credit risk.

A three-month futures spread that combines a near-term spread and a longer-term spread: the trader buys two different delivery months and sells an intermediate month twice (or the reverse), in a 1:-2:1 ratio. The position expresses a view that the middle month — the 'whipping post' or belly — will underperform or outperform the two outer months (the wings). It bets on the curvature of the futures curve: whether the middle of the curve is too cheap or too rich relative to its neighbors, while largely cancelling out outright and simple calendar-spread exposure.

A yield curve spread trade that gains when the yield differential between longer-maturity and shorter-maturity rates increases (the curve steepens). It is executed long the front (shorter-maturity) leg and short the back (longer-maturity) leg, typically with Treasury futures or cash bonds weighted to be DV01-neutral. You are betting the gap between long-term and short-term interest rates widens — whatever happens to the overall level of rates.

A yield curve spread trade that gains when the yield differential between longer-maturity and shorter-maturity rates decreases (the curve flattens or inverts). It is executed short the front (shorter-maturity) leg and long the back (longer-maturity) leg, typically DV01-neutral using Treasury futures or cash bonds. You are betting the gap between long-term and short-term rates shrinks — again, independent of whether the overall rate level rises or falls.

A steepening of the yield curve driven by short-term interest rates falling faster than long-term rates. It is called 'bull' because falling yields mean rising bond prices, and this pattern often appears when the central bank is expected to cut short-term rates. The curve steepens from the front end rallying: short rates drop (short bonds rise) faster than long rates.

A steepening of the yield curve driven by long-term interest rates rising faster than short-term rates. It is called 'bear' because rising yields mean falling bond prices, and the pattern often appears when inflation expectations pick up and the market anticipates tighter policy to follow. The curve steepens from the long end selling off: long rates rise (long bonds fall) faster than short rates.

A flattening of the yield curve driven by long-term interest rates falling faster than short-term rates. It is called 'bull' because falling yields mean rising bond prices, and the pattern often appears in flight-to-safety episodes or when inflation expectations decline. The curve flattens from the long end rallying: long rates drop faster than short rates.

A flattening of the yield curve driven by short-term interest rates rising faster than long-term rates. It is called 'bear' because rising yields mean falling bond prices, and the pattern typically appears when the central bank is raising short-term policy rates. The curve flattens from the front end selling off: short rates rise faster than long rates, usually as the central bank hikes.

a: change in open interest delta OI
x: The day-over-day (or period-over-period) change in open interest — the total number of futures contracts, long or short, in a delivery month or market that have been entered into and not yet liquidated by an offsetting transaction or fulfilled by delivery. Rising open interest indicates new positions being created; falling open interest indicates positions being closed. Volume counts how many contracts changed hands; the change in open interest tells you whether hands are entering or leaving the market.

a: volume and OI analysis price-volume-OI framework
x: A technical-analysis framework for futures markets that interprets price trends jointly with trading volume and open interest to judge whether a move is supported by new positioning or by liquidation of existing positions. It is an analytical framework or heuristic, not a proven predictive law. Price tells you where the market went; volume tells you how much business was done; open interest tells you whether traders are staying or leaving — read together, they describe the 'conviction' behind a move.

A weekly report published by the CFTC providing a breakdown of each Tuesday's open interest for markets in which 20 or more traders hold positions at or above CFTC-established reporting levels. The legacy report separates open interest into commercial, non-commercial, and non-reportable holdings; disaggregated and TFF variants provide finer categories. It is a weekly census of who is long and who is short in each major futures market — hedgers versus speculators versus small traders.

In the CFTC's legacy Commitments of Traders report, a reportable trader whose futures positions are commercially motivated — traditionally producers, merchants, processors, and users of the physical commodity who manage business risks by hedging, plus swap dealers offsetting OTC risk in the futures market. In the Disaggregated COT this group is split into Producer/Merchant/Processor/User and Swap Dealers. Commercials are the industry players using futures to insure their real business, not to bet on price direction.

In the CFTC's legacy Commitments of Traders report, a reportable trader who does not qualify as commercial — encompassing professional money managers such as CTAs, CPOs, and hedge funds as well as a wide array of other non-commercial (speculative) traders. In the Disaggregated COT this group is split into Managed Money and Other Reportables. Noncommercials are the market's risk-takers: participants trading futures for profit rather than to hedge a physical business.

A trader category in the CFTC's Disaggregated Commitments of Traders report comprising registered commodity trading advisors (CTAs), registered commodity pool operators (CPOs), and unregistered funds identified by the CFTC — traders engaged in managing and conducting organized futures trading on behalf of clients. It is the 'fund money' line in the COT report: positions run by professional managers trading other people's capital.

A trader category in the CFTC's Disaggregated Commitments of Traders report: an entity that predominantly engages in the production, processing, packing, or handling of a physical commodity and uses the futures markets to manage or hedge risks associated with those activities. These are the true commercials of the physical supply chain — the farmers, elevators, crushers, and end-users hedging real inventory and inputs.

A trader category in the CFTC's Disaggregated Commitments of Traders report: an entity that deals primarily in swaps for a commodity and uses the futures markets to manage or hedge the risk associated with those swaps transactions, whether its counterparties are speculators such as hedge funds or traditional commercial clients. These are banks and dealers whose futures positions are the warehouse for risk they took on from OTC swap clients — the futures leg is the hedge, not the bet.

The unweighted arithmetic mean of the last n observations (usually closing prices), recomputed each period as the window slides forward; the most basic trend-following overlay. A rolling average that smooths day-to-day noise so the underlying trend is easier to see. Every observation in the window counts equally.

A recursively computed moving average whose weights decay geometrically with age, giving recent observations more influence and reducing lag relative to a same-length simple moving average. Like a simple average, but today's price counts more than last week's, so it reacts faster to new information.

a: WMA Linearly weighted moving average LWMA
x: A moving average that weights observations linearly by recency — the newest price gets weight n, the next n-1, down to 1 — so recent data dominates while the window length stays fixed. A compromise between the SMA and EMA: recent prices matter more, but the weights decline in a straight line rather than exponentially.

a: SMMA Modified moving average Running moving average MMA
x: A recursive moving average (also called modified or running moving average) equivalent to an EMA with smoothing constant 1/n, so it smooths far more heavily than a same-length standard EMA. The gentlest common average: each new price is absorbed at only 1/n weight, so the line moves slowly and filters a great deal of noise.

Alan Hull's moving average (2005), engineered to nearly eliminate lag while retaining smoothness by combining weighted moving averages of different lengths with a lag-canceling correction term. An average designed to hug price closely without becoming jagged — fast like a short WMA, smooth like a long one.

A double-smoothed simple moving average — an SMA of an SMA — whose effective weights form a triangle that peaks at the middle of the window, giving mid-window data the most influence. Averaging an average: extra smooth at the cost of extra lag, with the middle of the window weighted most.

Tushar Chande's Variable Index Dynamic Average: an exponential-style moving average whose smoothing constant is scaled each bar by a volatility index — the absolute Chande Momentum Oscillator — so it reacts faster in decisive, volatile markets and slower in quiet ones. An adaptive average that automatically speeds up when the market is moving decisively and slows down when it is drifting.

Perry Kaufman's adaptive moving average, which varies its smoothing constant with an Efficiency Ratio measuring how directional (versus noisy) recent price movement has been, hugging price in trends and going flat in chop. An average that asks how much of the recent movement is real trend versus random wiggle, and speeds up only when the answer is mostly trend.

A lag-corrected EMA (John Ehlers and Ric Way, 'Zero Lag (Well, Almost)', TASC 2010): an EMA applied to de-lagged data — price plus the difference between the current price and the price (n-1)/2 bars ago — compensating for the EMA's inherent lag. Pre-correct the data for the lag you know the EMA will add, so the smoothed output lands close to the current price.

Patrick Mulloy's Double Exponential Moving Average (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, January 1994): a composite of a single and a double EMA that subtracts the extra lag of the double-smoothed series from the single-smoothed one to track price more closely. Measure how much double-smoothing lags single-smoothing, and add that gap back to the fast EMA as a correction.

Patrick Mulloy's Triple Exponential Moving Average, which extends DEMA with a third smoothing layer, combining single, double, and triple EMAs to remove even more lag for short-term trading. DEMA with one more correction term — closer still to price, noisier still.

A signal framework in which a shorter-period moving average crossing a longer-period one (or price crossing a moving average) is read as a shift in trend direction; John Murphy calls the two-average version the double crossover method. It is an analytical convention, not a proven predictive law. When the fast average overtakes the slow one, recent prices have moved enough to bend the trend measure — a simple, mechanical trend-change rule.

A bullish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing above the 200-day SMA — interpreted by technicians as confirmation of a long-term uptrend. It is a widely watched analytical convention, not a proven predictive law. The market's medium-term average climbing above its long-term average suggests that upward momentum has been sustained long enough to matter.

A bearish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing below the 200-day SMA — read as confirmation of a long-term downtrend; the mirror image of the golden cross and equally a convention rather than a proven law. The medium-term average sinking below the long-term average suggests the decline has been deep and persistent enough to bend long-term trend measures.

Gerald Appel's Moving Average Convergence/Divergence oscillator (late 1970s): a momentum indicator built from the difference between a fast and a slow EMA (default 12 and 26) with a 9-period EMA signal line, combining trend-following and momentum information in one unbounded oscillator. When the fast average pulls away from the slow one, momentum is accelerating; when they converge, the move is running out of steam.

The core series of the MACD: the fast (default 12-period) EMA minus the slow (default 26-period) EMA of closing prices, oscillating around zero as the two averages converge and diverge. The spread between a fast and a slow average: positive and widening means upside momentum is building.

A 9-period EMA of the MACD line, plotted alongside it; crossovers of the MACD line through this signal line are the most common MACD trading signal. A moving average of the MACD itself, smoothing its turns so crossovers are easier to read.

The bar plot of the MACD line minus its signal line, visualizing the distance between them; it expands and contracts ahead of crossovers and is used to spot momentum shifts early. Instead of waiting for the two MACD lines to cross, watch the gap between them shrink or grow.

J. Welles Wilder's momentum oscillator (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978) comparing smoothed average gains to smoothed average losses over a look-back period (default 14), bounded between 0 and 100. A speedometer for price: it shows how persistently and strongly the market has been closing up versus down.

George Lane's momentum indicator (late 1950s) measuring where the close sits within the high-low range of the look-back period, bounded 0-100 and published in Fast, Slow, and Full versions. Lane's premise: momentum changes direction before price. In an uptrend prices tend to close near the top of their recent range; the stochastic quantifies that tendency.

Chande and Kroll's oscillator (The New Technical Trader, 1994) that applies the stochastic formula to RSI values instead of price, measuring where the current RSI sits within its own high-low range over the look-back period; an indicator of an indicator, bounded between 0 and 1. RSI can drift between 80 and 20 for weeks without reaching its classic extremes; StochRSI restores sensitivity by tracking RSI's position within its recent range rather than its absolute level.

Larry Williams' momentum oscillator showing where the close sits relative to the highest high of the look-back period, plotted on an inverted 0 to -100 scale; mathematically the inverse of the fast stochastic %K line. It answers 'how close is the latest close to the top of the recent range?': readings near 0 mean closes at the range top, readings near -100 mean closes at the bottom.

a: ROC Price rate of change PROC
x: A pure momentum oscillator measuring the percentage change between the current close and the close n periods ago, plotted as an unbounded line around zero; the StockCharts ROC page notes the indicator is also referred to simply as Momentum. It is rise over run for prices: positive while the price is higher than n periods ago, negative while lower, with distance from zero showing how fast the move is.

The simplest momentum measure: the absolute point difference between the current close and the close n periods ago, plotted as an unbounded oscillator around zero; the unscaled sibling of the rate-of-change, which expresses the same comparison as a percentage. It tracks how many points price gained or lost over the window, ignoring the price level, so its slope shows acceleration or deceleration of the move.

Donald Lambert's oscillator (Commodities magazine, 1980) measuring how far the typical price has deviated from its moving average, expressed in units of mean absolute deviation scaled by 0.015 so that roughly 70-80% of readings fall between -100 and +100. CCI normalizes 'how stretched is price from its own average?' - excursions beyond +/-100 mark statistically unusual strength or weakness that can flag a new trend or an extreme.

Welles Wilder's trend-strength gauge (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): the Wilder-smoothed average of the Directional Movement Index (DX), which measures the spread between +DI and -DI relative to their sum; ADX quantifies trend strength on a 0-100 scale regardless of direction. ADX answers 'is the market trending at all?', not which way - Wilder suggested readings above 25 indicate a strong trend and below 20 the absence of one.

The positive half of Wilder's Directional Movement System: 100 times the ratio of smoothed positive directional movement (upward range expansion beyond the prior bar's high) to smoothed True Range over 14 periods, measuring the strength of upside directional movement. +DI tracks how much of the recent true-range movement was upside expansion; when +DI is above -DI, buyers hold the directional edge.

The negative half of Wilder's Directional Movement System: 100 times the ratio of smoothed negative directional movement (downward range expansion beyond the prior bar's low) to smoothed True Range over 14 periods, measuring the strength of downside directional movement. -DI tracks how much of the recent true-range movement was downside expansion; when -DI is above +DI, sellers hold the directional edge.

Welles Wilder's volatility measure (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): the Wilder-smoothed average of True Range, where True Range is the greatest of the current high-low span, |high - prior close|, and |low - prior close| - capturing gap and limit-move volatility that a plain high-low range misses. ATR tells you how much an instrument typically moves per bar, with no directional content: it expands in violent markets and contracts in quiet ones.
