John Bollinger's volatility bands: a 20-period simple moving average flanked by upper and lower bands set k standard deviations (default 2) of price above and below it, so the envelope widens as volatility rises and contracts as it falls. The bands define 'relatively high' and 'relatively low' statistically: price at the upper band is high relative to recent volatility, at the lower band relatively low - without implying a reversal by itself.

A Bollinger-derived indicator measuring the percentage width between the upper and lower bands relative to the middle band, tracking volatility expansion and contraction on a normalized scale comparable across securities and timeframes. It turns the visual 'pinch' of the bands into a number: falling BandWidth means volatility is drying up; the famous Squeeze is BandWidth at the low end of its own historical range.

A Bollinger-derived indicator expressing the close's position within the bands as a percentage of band width: 100 at the upper band, 0 at the lower band, 50 at the middle band, and beyond those values when price is outside the bands. %B states exactly where price sits inside the Bollinger envelope, making band tags, divergences and pattern confirmations quantifiable and comparable across securities.

Volatility envelopes around an exponential moving average, with channel lines set a multiple of Average True Range above and below the EMA; the modern version popularized by Linda Raschke replaces Chester Keltner's 1960 10-day typical-price SMA plus/minus high-low range with EMA plus/minus ATR. Like Bollinger Bands but built from ATR instead of standard deviation, Keltner Channels are smoother and more constant in width, which suits trend identification and breakout detection.

Richard Donchian's price channel plotting the highest high and lowest low of the last n periods (commonly 20) as upper and lower bands, with an optional midline at their average; the basis of classic breakout systems such as the Turtle Traders' rules. The channel shows the extremes of the recent trading range; a close outside it is by definition a new n-period high or low, which breakout traders treat as trend initiation.

A channel built on a least-squares linear regression line through the last n closes, with parallel upper and lower lines plotted a set number of standard deviations (typically 2) of price away from the regression line. The regression line is the best-fit trend through the window and the bands mark statistically typical deviation around it - about two-thirds of observations within +/-1 sigma if deviations were normal.

a: MA envelopes Percentage envelope Trading bands
x: Parallel bands set a fixed percentage above and below a simple or exponential moving average, creating a constant-width channel used for trend confirmation and, in flat markets, as overbought/oversold references. Unlike volatility-adaptive bands, the percentage offset never changes, so a touch of the envelope always means 'price is x% stretched from its average.'

a: PSAR SAR Parabolic stop and reverse
x: Welles Wilder's stop-and-reverse system (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): a trailing stop plotted as dots below price in uptrends and above price in downtrends, accelerating toward price as the trend extends and flipping sides when price crosses it. It behaves like a trailing stop that tightens the longer a trend runs - the acceleration factor pulls the dots toward price, forcing an exit when momentum stalls.

An ATR-based trend-following overlay (Olivier Seban, 2009) that plots a single line below price in uptrends and above it in downtrends, at a distance of multiplier x ATR from the bar midpoint, flipping sides when price closes through the line. It is a volatility-adjusted trailing stop: wider when the market is volatile, tighter when calm, so ordinary noise does not stop you out but a genuine reversal does.

Goichi Hosoda's 'one-look equilibrium chart' (published 1969): a five-line system of high-low midpoint averages - Conversion Line, Base Line, two Leading Spans forming the cloud (Kumo), and a Lagging Span - designed to show trend, momentum, and support/resistance at a glance. Price above the cloud means uptrend, below means downtrend, inside means no trend; the cloud projected ahead sketches where support or resistance is expected to lie.

The fastest Ichimoku line: the midpoint of the 9-period high-low range, (9-period high + 9-period low)/2, used as the short-term equilibrium level and the faster line in Ichimoku crossover signals. Rather than averaging closes, it averages the range extremes, so it sits at the center of recent price action and flattens immediately when the market goes quiet.

The slower Ichimoku line: the midpoint of the 26-period high-low range, serving as the medium-term equilibrium level, signal-confirmation line, and a common trailing reference. It marks the recent balance point of the market; price far above it is extended, and pullbacks to a flat Kijun are watched as equilibrium tests.

The faster cloud boundary: the average of Tenkan-sen and Kijun-sen, plotted 26 periods ahead of the current bar, forming the top of the Kumo (cloud) when above Senkou Span B and the bottom when below it. It averages the short and medium equilibria and projects them forward, marking the near edge of expected future support or resistance.

The slower cloud boundary: the midpoint of the 52-period high-low range, plotted 26 periods ahead, forming the long-term equilibrium edge of the Kumo. The slowest Ichimoku line, it moves rarely and marks durable long-term balance; flat, thick sections of cloud built on Span B are watched as major support or resistance.

The Ichimoku confirmation line: today's close plotted 26 periods back on the chart, so it can be compared directly with where price and the cloud stood 26 bars ago. By shifting the close into the past, you see at a glance whether the current price is above or below the price and cloud of 26 periods ago - a built-in momentum comparison.

Joe Granville's cumulative volume indicator (Granville's New Key to Stock Market Profits, 1963): a running total that adds the period's volume when the close rises and subtracts it when the close falls, tracking cumulative buying versus selling pressure. Granville's thesis is that volume precedes price - if volume consistently flows in on up days, the OBV line rises even before price breaks out.

Marc Chaikin's cumulative money-flow line: each period's volume is weighted by where the close falls within the high-low range (the Money Flow Multiplier) and added to a running total, measuring cumulative buying and selling pressure. Closing near the high on big volume means buyers dominated the session; the A/D line accumulates that evidence and often diverges from price before reversals.

Marc Chaikin's oscillator version of the Accumulation/Distribution concept: the sum of Money Flow Volume over n periods (typically 20 or 21) divided by the sum of volume, oscillating between +1 and -1 around a zero line. It compresses the A/D logic into a fixed window: positive CMF means closes have clustered in the upper half of their ranges, volume-weighted, over the look-back.

Gene Quong and Avrum Soudack's volume-weighted momentum oscillator: an RSI-style 0-100 calculation applied to typical-price money flows, so both the direction and the volume of each bar feed the reading. It is RSI with volume mixed in - an overbought reading requires not just rising prices but rising prices backed by rising dollar volume.

Richard Arms' oscillator relating midpoint change to volume and range: it measures how much price moved per unit of volume, rising when prices advance with ease (large range, light volume) and falling when they decline with ease. If a big price move needs little volume, movement is 'easy'; if heavy volume produces a tiny range, movement is labored - EMV quantifies the effort-versus-result idea behind Arms' Equivolume charts.

Alexander Elder's oscillator (Trading for a Living) multiplying the close-to-close price change by volume, combining direction, extent, and participation into one measure of the force behind a move; the smoothed 13-period EMA form is the standard version. A one-point gain on huge volume shows more conviction than the same gain on a trickle - Force Index scores moves by both size and participation.

Paul Dysart's cumulative index (1930s; popularized by Norman Fosback in Stock Market Logic) that accumulates percentage price changes only on periods when volume declines, on the theory that informed 'smart money' acts on quiet days while the crowd trades on high-volume days. Strip out the noisy high-volume days and watch what remains: if price grinds higher on falling-volume days, quiet accumulation is presumed.

The complement of the Negative Volume Index: Dysart's cumulative index (in Fosback's formulation) that accumulates percentage price changes only on periods when volume increases, tracking what the volume-driven 'crowd' is doing. High-volume days are when the crowd trades; PVI isolates those days to show the crowd's cumulative net effect on price.

The average price of a security weighted by volume, computed intraday as cumulative (typical price x volume) divided by cumulative volume from the session open; the benchmark institutions use to judge execution quality and intraday fair value. It is the day's center of gravity of trading: above VWAP the average buyer is in profit, below it the average seller is.

Volume-weighted average price computed from a user-chosen anchor bar - a significant high or low, earnings release, gap, or other event - rather than the session open, extending the VWAP logic across days and timeframes. Markets reprice after events; anchoring VWAP to the event measures whether buyers or sellers have won all the volume traded since that moment.

A moving average of successive VWAP values over a user-chosen number of periods, producing a volume-weighted average that flows continuously from day to day instead of resetting each session. Classic VWAP dies at the close; MVWAP keeps a rolling volume-weighted memory, giving longer-horizon traders a VWAP-like reference across days.

A moving average in which each price is weighted by its bar's volume - bars traded on heavy volume pull the average toward them, so the line tracks where business was actually done rather than treating all bars equally. An SMA answers 'average price of the last n bars'; a VWMA answers 'average price weighted by how much traded in each of those bars.'

The ratio of current trading volume to average volume over a look-back (typically 10-20 sessions), often time-of-day adjusted so that, say, 10:30 a.m. volume is compared with prior 10:30 a.m. volumes; a reading of 1.0 means perfectly normal participation. Raw volume is meaningless without context - five million shares is quiet for a mega-cap and extraordinary for a small-cap; RVOL normalizes it.

a: PVO Percentage Volume Oscillator Volume Oscillator (VO)
x: A MACD-style oscillator applied to volume: the difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average of volume, usually expressed as a percentage of the slow average (the Percentage Volume Oscillator, defaults 12, 26, 9). It shows whether participation is expanding or drying up: positive and rising means short-term volume is running above its longer norm.

Marc Chaikin's momentum-of-money-flow oscillator: the MACD formula applied to the Accumulation/Distribution Line - the 3-day EMA of the ADL minus its 10-day EMA - designed to anticipate turns in accumulation and distribution. It is an indicator of an indicator: instead of watching the ADL's slow drift, you watch its momentum cross zero, flagging shifts in buying and selling pressure earlier.

Tushar Chande's 1995 indicator measuring how recently price made a new n-period high, expressed as a 0-100 percentage: 100 when the high occurred in the current period, decaying toward 0 as it recedes into the past. Instead of asking how far price moved, Aroon-Up asks how long ago the latest high was - frequent new highs keep it pinned near 100.

The downside counterpart in Chande's Aroon system: a measure of how recently price made a new n-period low, on a 0-100 scale where 100 means the low was set in the current period. It tracks the freshness of new lows; a market printing new lows today has Aroon-Down at 100, and sustained 70-100 readings mark strong downtrends.

The difference between Aroon-Up and Aroon-Down, compressing Chande's pair into one line bounded between -100 and +100; positive when new highs are more recent than new lows, negative when new lows are more recent. It nets the two Aroon lines: +100 means today's bar made a new n-period high while the low is as old as possible; the zero line is the bull-bear divide.

Tushar Chande's momentum oscillator: 100 times the difference between summed up-moves and summed down-moves over n periods divided by their total, bounding raw, unsmoothed momentum between -100 and +100. It is a tug-of-war score between up days and down days: if all movement over the window was up, CMO is +100; all down, -100.

Larry Williams' three-timeframe momentum oscillator (1976; Stocks & Commodities, 1985): a weighted blend (4:2:1) of buying-pressure-to-true-range ratios over 7, 14, and 28 periods, designed to reduce the false divergences of single-timeframe oscillators. Short-term momentum dominates the blend but is checked by two longer frames, so a divergence must show weakness across multiple horizons to count.

Jack Hutson's momentum oscillator (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, early 1980s): the one-period percentage rate of change of a triple-smoothed exponential moving average (EMA of EMA of EMA), engineered to filter out price moves too small to matter. Three rounds of smoothing strip out noise; what remains turning up or down is, in theory, the significant trend cycle.

An oscillator that strips trend from price by subtracting a displaced (effectively centered) moving average: the close (n/2 + 1) periods ago minus the n-period SMA, designed to isolate cycle highs and lows rather than momentum. Comparing a past price against a moving average centered on it cancels the trend component, leaving the shorter cycle around the trend visible.

a: KST Know Sure Thing Pring's KST
x: Martin Pring's summed rate-of-change oscillator (Stocks & Commodities, 1992): four rate-of-change series over different periods, each SMA-smoothed, then combined with weights 1-2-3-4 so the longest cycle counts most. Instead of one momentum look-back, KST blends four cycles - short-term turns nudge it, but only broad multi-timeframe momentum swings really move it.

Edwin Coppock's long-term momentum indicator (Barron's, October 1965): a 10-period weighted moving average of the sum of the 14-period and 11-period rates of change, designed to flag major stock-market bottoms on monthly charts when it turns up from below zero. Coppock reportedly chose 11-14 months after hearing that grief over a loss typically runs about that long; the indicator waits out the mourning period and signals when the market has 'recovered.'

John Ehlers' transform (Stocks & Commodities, November 2002) that maps normalized prices through the Fisher function so the output has an approximately Gaussian distribution, producing sharper, better-defined turning points than the raw price series. Price extremes are rare and squashed on a normal scale; the Fisher transform stretches the tails so that turning points stand out as crisp spikes.

A price filter rather than a true indicator: it draws straight legs between swing points, ignoring all moves smaller than a set percentage (traditionally 5%), to reveal the significant highs and lows through the noise. It answers 'what would this chart look like if every wiggle under x% were deleted?' - exposing the skeleton of swings for trend, pattern, and Elliott Wave analysis.

Bill Williams' five-bar reversal marker: an up fractal is a series of at least five successive bars with the highest high in the middle and two lower highs on each side, and a down fractal is the mirror image with lows; one of the five indicators of his Trading Chaos system. A fractal flags a local extreme where the market pushed to a level and was rejected on both sides - a candidate swing point.

Bill Williams' trend-detection overlay: three smoothed moving averages of the median price - Jaw (13-period, shifted 8 forward), Teeth (8, shifted 5), and Lips (5, shifted 3) - whose entanglement signals a sleeping (range) market and whose fanning signals a feeding (trend) phase. In Williams' metaphor, when the three balance lines intertwine the alligator sleeps and you do not trade; when they open and order by speed, it hunts and you follow the trend.

Bill Williams' momentum histogram: the 5-period simple moving average of bar midpoints minus the 34-period SMA of bar midpoints - effectively a MACD of the median price computed with simple, not exponential, averages. It compares very recent momentum with background momentum using midpoints rather than closes, so the intraday range feeds the reading.

Bill Williams' companion to the Alligator: a dual histogram showing the convergence and divergence of the Alligator's balance lines - the upper histogram is |Jaw - Teeth| and the lower is -|Teeth - Lips| - used to time the 'sleeping, awakening, eating, sated' phases. Instead of eyeballing whether the Alligator's mouth is opening or closing, the Gator plots the mouth's spread directly: expanding bars mean feeding, contracting bars mean sleep.

a: Elder-Ray Bull Power and Bear Power
x: Alexander Elder's two-part oscillator: Bull Power = period high minus a 13-period EMA of closes, and Bear Power = period low minus the same EMA, measuring how far buyers and sellers can push price above and below the market's consensus of value. The EMA is the agreed value; the high shows the maximum buyers could reach and the low the maximum sellers could reach - their distances from the EMA are the two camps' power.

Donald Dorsey's volatility indicator: a 25-period sum of the ratio of a 9-period EMA of the high-low range to a double-smoothed 9-period EMA of that range, designed to spot 'reversal bulges' when the daily range expands abnormally. When the range EMA swells relative to its own smoothing, the sum bulges - Dorsey's warning that the current trend may be about to reverse.

Etienne Botes and Douglas Siepman's trend indicator (2010, inspired by Wilder's DMI): +VI and -VI compare 14-period sums of inter-bar directional movement - current high versus prior low and current low versus prior high - to the 14-period sum of True Range. Where Wilder's DMI measures movement beyond the previous bar, the Vortex measures the connection between consecutive bars' extremes - the 'flow' between them.

John Ehlers' Relative Vigor Index: an oscillator comparing a smoothed close-minus-open to a smoothed high-minus-low, on the premise that closes tend to exceed opens in uptrends and fall below them in downtrends, so the ratio moves in phase with the price cycle. A bar's 'vigor' is how much of its range the close captures from the open; persistently positive vigor means an uptrend.

Larry Connors' composite short-term mean-reversion oscillator: the average of a 3-period RSI of closes, a 2-period RSI of the up/down streak length, and the 100-period percent rank of the one-day rate of change. It blends three flavors of stretched-ness - price momentum, streak duration, and the size of today's move versus recent history - into one 0-100 short-term extreme gauge.

A purchase or sale for delivery and payment on the market's standard near-term settlement date at the current spot price. It defines the legal and economic claim being traded, including who must perform and when.

A privately negotiated agreement obligating two parties to exchange a specified asset or cash amount on a future date at terms fixed today. It defines the legal and economic claim being traded, including who must perform and when.

A standardized exchange-traded agreement obligating parties to buy or sell an underlying interest at a future time under contract terms, commonly settled through offset or delivery and cleared with daily margining. It defines the legal and economic claim being traded, including who must perform and when.

A contract giving its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying interest at a strike price by or at expiration, while the writer bears the corresponding obligation if exercised. It defines the legal and economic claim being traded, including who must perform and when.

The market for the physical or cash commodity (or asset) itself, as contrasted with futures or other derivative contracts on it. It may take the form of an organized central market, a decentralized over-the-counter market, or a local organization serving a small region, and trades settle with prompt delivery and payment through customary market channels. The cash market is where the actual thing changes hands now, not a promise about the future. Its price is the reference point to which futures and forward prices are compared.

A futures-style derivative contract, predominant in cryptoasset markets, that has no expiry or settlement date, so a position can be held indefinitely. Its price is kept anchored to an underlying spot index price through periodic funding payments exchanged between long and short position holders. A perpetual is a futures contract you never have to roll. A funding fee paid by the more crowded side keeps its price tethered to spot.

A derivative in which two counterparties agree to exchange streams of cash flows over a specified period, computed by applying agreed rates, prices, or formulas to a notional amount. Under the detailed statutory definition in the Commodity Exchange Act (as amended by the Dodd-Frank Act), the term includes interest rate swaps, commodity swaps, currency swaps, equity swaps, and credit default swaps. A swap lets two parties trade one kind of payment obligation for another — for example, exchanging a fixed interest bill for a floating one — without trading the underlying asset itself.

A swap in which the two counterparties agree to exchange interest rate cash flows on a specified notional principal. In the standard plain-vanilla form, one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays a floating rate tied to a reference rate on a series of payment dates; the principal itself is not exchanged. Two parties swap the character of their interest payments — fixed for floating — so each ends up with the rate exposure it wants.

A swap that involves the exchange of one currency for another on a specified schedule. Counterparties typically exchange principal amounts in two currencies at inception, exchange interest payments in each currency during the life of the contract, and re-exchange the principals at maturity at the pre-agreed rate. Each party borrows in the currency where it has an advantage, then swaps the proceeds and the interest obligations, so each ends up servicing debt in the currency it actually needs.

A swap in which one party (the total return payer) transfers the full economic performance of a reference asset — its income plus any price appreciation or depreciation — to the other party, which in return pays a financing rate (a reference rate plus a spread) on the notional. It transfers the asset's returns without transferring ownership and is classed among the common credit derivatives. A total return swap lets you collect everything a stock, bond, or index pays and earns — as if you owned it — while posting only a fraction of its value as margin and paying a financing charge.

A bilateral over-the-counter credit derivative in which the protection seller agrees to make a payment to the protection buyer in the event of a specified credit event (such as a default or bankruptcy) of a reference entity, in exchange for a fixed payment or series of fixed payments. It is the most common type of credit derivative. A CDS works like default insurance on a borrower: you pay a periodic premium, and if the borrower suffers a credit event, you are compensated for the loss in value of its debt.

A leveraged over-the-counter derivative between a client and a provider in which the parties exchange the difference between the opening and closing price of an underlying asset — a share, index, currency, or commodity — without either party owning the underlying. The FCA classifies CFDs as complex, high-risk products that carry a considerable risk of substantial losses. A CFD is a cash-settled bet on a price move: you gain or lose the full change in the asset's price while posting only a fraction of its value as margin.

An exchange-traded investment product that must register with the SEC as an open-end investment company (or sometimes as a unit investment trust). It pools investor money into a portfolio of assets and its shares trade on a national securities exchange throughout the day at market prices, like a stock. An ETF packages a whole portfolio into a single share you can buy or sell any time the market is open, combining mutual-fund-style pooling with stock-style trading.

An unsecured, senior debt obligation of a financial institution that trades on a national securities exchange and whose payment terms are linked to the performance of a reference index or benchmark. Unlike an ETF, an ETN holds no underlying assets, so investors bear the issuer's credit risk, and ETNs can result in the loss of the entire investment. An ETN is essentially a promise from a bank to pay you the return of an index. You get index-linked payoff with bond-like exposure to the bank's solvency.

An SEC-registered open-end investment company that pools money from many investors and invests it in stocks, bonds, short-term money-market instruments, other securities, or assets. Its shares are redeemable: investors can sell them back to the fund on any business day at the fund's next-computed net asset value. A mutual fund is a shared portfolio: many investors chip in, a manager runs the money to a stated objective, and each investor owns a slice priced once a day.

A closed-end investment company — one of the three basic types of investment company — that issues a fixed number of shares in a one-time public offering. The shares then trade on an exchange at market prices determined by supply and demand, which can be above (a premium) or below (a discount) the fund's net asset value. A closed-end fund is a sealed pool of money: after the initial offering, the only way in or out is to trade the fund's shares with other investors, so the share price can drift away from the value of what the fund holds.

A security representing a share of ownership in a company. Common stock entitles its owners to vote at shareholder meetings and to receive dividends when declared, and it represents the residual claim on the company's assets after creditors and preferred stockholders. Common stock is the basic unit of company ownership: you get a vote, a shot at dividends, and whatever value is left after everyone with a senior claim has been paid.

A class of stock whose holders usually do not have voting rights but receive dividend payments before common stockholders and have priority over common stockholders if the company goes bankrupt and its assets are liquidated. Dividends are typically set at a fixed rate on a stated par value. Preferred stock trades away voting power and unlimited upside for a senior, more bond-like income stream.

a: ADR American Depositary Receipt GDR DR
x: A negotiable security issued by a depositary bank that represents an ownership interest in shares of a (typically foreign) company held in custody by the bank. American Depositary Receipts let shares of foreign companies trade in U.S. markets in U.S. dollars, with each receipt representing one or more shares, or a fraction of a share, of the foreign stock. A depositary receipt is a stand-in certificate: the foreign shares sit in a bank's vault abroad, and you trade the bank-issued receipt at home in your own currency and market hours.

A bond issued by a company to raise money for purposes such as funding operations or expansion. The issuer promises to pay interest (the coupon) and repay the principal at maturity, and corporate bonds span credit qualities from investment grade to high yield. A corporate bond is an IOU from a company: you lend it money, it pays you interest on schedule, and it owes you your principal back at maturity — if it stays solvent.

A debt security issued by a national government to finance its operations. U.S. Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government and span marketable instruments from short-term bills to notes and long-term bonds. A government bond is a loan to the state, repaid out of its taxing and money-issuing power, which is why its yield in its own currency is treated as the benchmark 'risk-free' rate.

A short-term U.S. Treasury marketable security with terms from 4 weeks up to 52 weeks. Bills are sold at face value or at a discount from face value and pay no periodic interest; the investor is paid the face value at maturity. A T-bill is a short-term loan to the U.S. government where the interest is built into the discount: you pay a bit less than face value now and collect the full face value in a few weeks or months.

A U.S. Treasury marketable security issued with maturities of 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years. Notes pay interest every six months and repay the face value at maturity. A Treasury note is the middle of the government yield curve: multi-year lending to the U.S. government with a steady semiannual coupon.

A long-term U.S. Treasury marketable security — historically a 30-year investment and now offered in 20-year terms as well — that pays interest every six months and is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. A Treasury bond is the longest-term loan to the U.S. government: decades of fixed semiannual coupons, which makes its price the most rate-sensitive of the marketable Treasuries.

A bond whose principal is adjusted for changes in a price index so that its payments keep pace with inflation. U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) are marketable securities whose principal is adjusted by changes in the Consumer Price Index; they pay interest every six months and are issued in terms of 5, 10, and 30 years. An inflation-linked bond grows your principal with the cost of living, so the fixed coupon you receive is paid on an ever-adjusting, inflation-protected base.

A bond that pays no periodic interest; it is issued or created at a deep discount to face value, and the investor's entire return comes from accretion to the full face value at maturity. U.S. Treasury STRIPS create zero-coupon securities by separately trading the individual interest and principal components of Treasury notes, bonds, and TIPS. A zero-coupon bond bundles all its interest into the purchase discount: you pay a fraction of face value today and receive one certain payment on one known future date.

A security — usually a bond or preferred stock — that can be converted into a different security, typically shares of the issuing company's common stock, at the holder's option under preset terms. A convertible bond combines fixed-income coupon payments with an embedded equity conversion option. A convertible is a bond with a stock option stapled to it: you collect coupons with downside seniority, but if the stock runs, you can swap the bond for shares.

Short-term promissory notes issued in bearer form by large corporations, with maturities typically ranging from 5 to 270 days. Because the notes are unsecured, the commercial paper market is generally dominated by large corporations with strong credit ratings. Commercial paper is how big, blue-chip companies borrow for a few weeks or months at money-market rates instead of drawing a bank loan.

A time deposit with a specific maturity, traditionally evidenced by a certificate: the depositor commits a fixed amount for a fixed period — such as six months, one year, or five years — and in exchange the issuing bank or credit union pays a stated rate of interest. Large-denomination CDs are typically negotiable and can trade in secondary markets. A CD is a locked savings box: you lend the bank a fixed sum for a fixed term at a fixed rate, and you pay a penalty if you break the lock early.

A transaction in which one party sells securities to another while agreeing to repurchase them at a later date at an agreed price. A repo is economically similar to a loan collateralized by securities, with the interest rate — the repo rate — implied by the difference between the sale and repurchase prices. A repo is a pawnshop loan for securities: hand over your bonds today for cash, buy them back tomorrow for slightly more — the difference is the interest.

A reverse repurchase agreement is the mirror side of a repo: one party buys securities from a counterparty subject to an agreement to resell them at a later date at an agreed price. It is economically similar to lending cash collateralized by securities; the New York Fed's Overnight Reverse Repo (ON RRP) facility temporarily reduces reserve balances and helps provide a floor under overnight interest rates. In a reverse repo you are the lender: you take securities as collateral, hand over cash overnight, and get your cash back with interest the next day.

As defined in the Commodity Exchange Act, the agricultural commodities enumerated in Section 1a(9) plus all other goods and articles (onions excepted) and all services, rights, and interests in which contracts for future delivery are presently or in the future dealt in. In everyday market usage, a physical commodity is a fungible raw good — an agricultural product, metal, or energy product — traded in standardized grades, as opposed to a financial instrument. A commodity is a standardized raw input: one bushel of No. 2 yellow corn or one troy ounce of gold is interchangeable with another, which is what makes them tradeable in bulk.

a: FX pair Currency cross Cross rate
x: The quotation convention of the foreign exchange market, in which an exchange rate expresses how much of one currency (the quote or counter currency) is needed to buy one unit of another (the base currency). Every FX transaction simultaneously buys one currency and sells the other, so currencies always trade in pairs; a pair quoted via a third country's market convention is a cross rate. You can never buy 'a currency' outright — you always pay for it with another currency, so every FX price is a ratio of two monies.

a: Crypto-asset Cryptocurrency Digital asset Virtual currency
x: A type of private-sector digital asset that depends primarily on cryptography and distributed ledger technology (or similar technology) as part of its perceived or inherent value — the working definition used by the FSB and fellow standard-setting bodies. The category spans unbacked assets such as bitcoin as well as tokens used for platform access or in decentralized finance, and is distinguished from stablecoins by the absence of a stabilization mechanism. A cryptoasset is digital value secured by cryptography and recorded on a shared ledger rather than by an issuer's promise — its worth rests on what the network and its users make of it.

A crypto-asset that aims to maintain a stable value relative to a specified asset — typically a fiat currency such as the U.S. dollar — or a pool or basket of assets, using a stabilization mechanism such as reserve backing. A 'global stablecoin' (GSC) is a stablecoin with potential reach and adoption across multiple jurisdictions. A stablecoin tries to be the steady dollar of the crypto world: a token engineered to be worth the same tomorrow as today, usually by backing each token with reserves.

A token on one blockchain that represents, and is intended to be backed one-for-one by, a crypto-asset locked with a custodian or smart contract, so the underlying asset can be used in environments where it does not natively exist. Wrapped bitcoin (wBTC), for example, makes bitcoin usable as collateral in Ethereum-based DeFi protocols. A wrapped token is a coat-check ticket for a coin from another blockchain: you lock the original, get a ticket that circulates elsewhere, and redeem the ticket to get the original back.

An instrument constructed to replicate the payoff of another asset without holding it. In traditional finance this is a replicating portfolio of derivatives and cash instruments (e.g., a long call plus a short put at the same strike and expiry creates a synthetic long futures position); in DeFi, synthetic assets are collateral-backed on-chain tokens whose oracle-driven prices track off-chain assets such as the U.S. dollar or equities (as in Maker or Synthetix). A synthetic asset fakes exposure to something you don't own: combine the right building blocks — options, collateral, oracles — and you get the target's price behavior without the asset itself.

a: Digital option All-or-nothing option Fixed-return option
x: A type of option whose payoff is either a fixed amount or zero, depending on the outcome of a yes/no proposition — typically whether the price of an asset will be above or below a strike at a specified time. It is also called a digital option. A binary option is a fixed-odds bet on a market event: pick the right side of the line and you collect the full payout; pick wrong and you get nothing.

A path-dependent exotic option that either comes into existence (knock-in) or ceases to exist (knock-out) if the underlying's price reaches a specified barrier level during the option's life. In standard FX market documentation, 'Barrier Option' means a knock-in option or a knock-out option, with a designated barrier determination agent deciding whether the trigger event occurred. A barrier option is a regular option with a tripwire: cross the price barrier and the option is either switched on or killed outright, which makes it cheaper than a plain option.

a: Average price option Average rate option
x: An exotic option whose payoff depends on the average price of the underlying asset during some portion of the life of the option, rather than on the underlying's price at a single date. An Asian option pays on the average price over time instead of the price on one day, smoothing out spikes and dips — useful when your real exposure is to an average cost or rate.

An exotic option whose payoff depends on the minimum or maximum price of the underlying asset during some portion of the life of the option, allowing the buyer to pay or receive the most favorable underlying price observed during the lookback period. A lookback option gives you perfect hindsight: it settles as if you had traded at the best price the market offered during the option's life.

An over-the-counter forward contract on the realized variance of an underlying's returns: at maturity one party pays the difference between the variance realized over the contract period and a pre-agreed variance strike, scaled by the variance notional. It gives pure exposure to realized variance without directional exposure to the underlying. A variance swap is a bet on how violently an asset will actually move, settled on measured squared daily moves — no view on direction needed.

A forward contract on realized volatility — the standard deviation of an underlying's returns — settling at maturity on the difference between realized volatility and a pre-agreed volatility strike, times the vega notional. Because its payoff is linear in volatility rather than variance, it is described in the canonical literature as the cleanest and easiest way to trade volatility. A volatility swap is a pure bet on how much an asset will move, measured in plain volatility points rather than squared ones.

An OTC forward contract on a short-term interest rate. The buyer of a FRA is a notional borrower who commits to pay a fixed rate of interest on a notional amount that is never actually exchanged, while the seller agrees notionally to lend; settlement exchanges the value of the difference between the contracted rate and the realized reference rate. A FRA locks in today the interest rate on a loan you will take (or make) in the future — only the rate difference ever changes hands, never the principal.

A standardized, exchange-traded futures contract whose underlying is an interest rate or an interest-bearing instrument — such as U.S. Treasury, SOFR, or Fed Funds futures — used to hedge or express views on interest rates at maturities from one week to 30 years. An interest rate future lets you lock in or bet on where rates will be months or years from now, in a standardized, centrally cleared contract.

a: Stock index future Index future E-mini
x: A standardized, exchange-traded futures contract on a stock index — such as the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 — that provides cash-settled exposure to the index level without holding any of the constituent stocks. An equity index future is the whole stock market in one leveraged ticket: you gain or lose the index's move times a fixed multiplier, cash-settled, with no shares ever changing hands.

A futures contract on a physical commodity: a standardized, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a specified quantity and grade of an agricultural product, metal, or energy product at a price set at initiation, for delivery or cash settlement in a specified future month. A commodity future locks in today the price of wheat, oil, or gold for a future month, letting producers and users shift price risk to those willing to bear it.

A standardized, centrally cleared futures contract on the exchange rate between two currencies, traded on a regulated FX marketplace. It fixes today the rate at which one currency will be exchanged for another on a specified future settlement date, offering a cleared, transparent alternative to over-the-counter forwards. An FX future is a currency forward repackaged as an exchange product: standard sizes, standard dates, a clearinghouse guarantee, and a public price.

The total value of the final goods and services produced within a country during a given period. In the United States it is estimated quarterly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis as the signature measure of the National Income and Product Accounts. GDP is the economy's scoreboard: it tells you how much the country actually produced in a quarter or year, and its growth rate is the standard gauge of whether the economy is expanding or contracting.

Gross domestic product adjusted to remove the effects of price changes, so that output in different periods can be compared in constant purchasing-power terms. When media report 'GDP growth' they almost always mean the percent change in real GDP. Real GDP answers: did the country actually produce more stuff, or did prices just go up? It strips out inflation so growth reflects volume, not price changes.

Gross domestic product measured at the market prices prevailing during the period being measured, without adjustment for inflation. It moves with both the quantity of output and the price level. Nominal GDP is the raw dollar size of the economy; it grows even if the country produces the same amount, simply because everything costs more.

A sustained increase in the general level of prices for goods and services over time, equivalently a decline in the purchasing power of money. In the U.S. it is most commonly measured by the 12-month percent change in the Consumer Price Index or the PCE price index. Inflation means your dollar buys less this year than last year; central banks target a low, stable rate (the Fed aims for 2%) because both very high inflation and deflation damage the economy.

A measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services, published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The headline series is the CPI for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). The CPI is a giant shopping basket whose total cost is tracked every month; how fast that basket's cost rises is the most-watched U.S. inflation reading.

A family of indexes published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics measuring the average change over time in selling prices received by domestic producers of goods and services. It measures price change from the seller's perspective, in contrast to the CPI's purchaser perspective. PPI tracks what producers charge at the factory gate or for their services; because it captures price pressure before the retail level, traders watch it as a possible early signal of consumer inflation.

a: Core CPI Core PCE Inflation excluding food and energy
x: An inflation measure that excludes the volatile food and energy components, intended to reveal the underlying, persistent trend in prices. In the U.S. the standard readings are 'all items less food and energy' in the CPI and the core PCE price index. Gasoline and grocery prices whipsaw month to month; stripping them out gives a cleaner read on whether inflation is really embedded in the economy, which is what central banks care about.

A sustained general decline in the prices of goods and services, equivalently an increase in the purchasing power of money. It is typically associated with contracting money and credit or collapsing aggregate demand and is considered more dangerous than moderate inflation because it raises the real burden of debt and encourages delayed spending. When prices fall broadly, cash gains value just by sitting still, so consumers postpone purchases and borrowers must repay debts with more valuable money — a self-reinforcing drag on the economy.

A decrease in the rate of inflation — prices are still rising, but at a slower pace. It is distinct from deflation, which is an actual decline in the price level. Disinflation is easing off the accelerator, not going in reverse: inflation falling from 9% to 3% is disinflation even though everything still costs more than before.

The simultaneous occurrence of high or rising inflation with stagnant output and elevated unemployment — a combination that contradicts the simple Phillips-curve trade-off. The term is identified with the 1970s U.S. experience, when inflation and unemployment rose together after the oil shocks. Stagflation is the worst of both worlds: the economy stops growing and jobs disappear while prices keep climbing, leaving policymakers with no painless option.

The percentage of the civilian labor force that is jobless, actively seeking work, and available to take a job. In the United States it is estimated monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics from the Current Population Survey of about 60,000 households and published in The Employment Situation report. It is the best-known single gauge of labor-market slack: a low rate means most people who want work have it, while a rising rate signals a weakening economy.

a: NFP Non-farm payrolls Payroll employment Establishment survey employment
x: The monthly change in the number of workers on U.S. nonfarm business and government payrolls, estimated by the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Current Employment Statistics (CES) survey of establishments. Released with the unemployment rate in The Employment Situation, it is the first major hard-data read on the U.S. economy each month. It answers 'how many jobs did employers actually add last month' from the business side, making it the market's favorite single labor-market number.

The share of the U.S. civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over that is either working or actively seeking work. It is computed monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics from the Current Population Survey. It measures how much of the working-age population is actually engaged in the labor market, separating 'no job but looking' from 'out of the labor force entirely.'

a: PMI ISM Manufacturing Index ISM Purchasing Managers Index
x: A monthly diffusion index compiled from surveys of purchasing and supply executives that summarizes whether business conditions in manufacturing or services are expanding or contracting relative to the prior month. The best-known U.S. versions are ISM's Manufacturing PMI and Services PMI (formerly the Report On Business). Because purchasing managers feel order flow before it shows up in output statistics, the PMI is one of the earliest monthly reads on the economy's direction.

a: Advance retail sales Retail trade MARTS
x: The monthly estimate of receipts at U.S. retail and food-services establishments, published by the Census Bureau through the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS) and the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS). It is the earliest broad indicator of consumer spending on goods. Because consumer spending is the largest component of GDP, the retail-sales report is a fast proxy for the health of household demand.

A monthly index of the real output of U.S. manufacturing, mining, and electric and gas utilities, published by the Federal Reserve in its G.17 release. It measures the volume of industrial output relative to a base year, currently expressed as a percentage of its 2017 average. It tracks the factory-and-resource side of the economy, which swings much harder than services over the business cycle.

The percentage of an industry's productive capacity actually being used, published monthly by the Federal Reserve alongside industrial production for manufacturing, mining, and utilities. It is computed as actual output divided by an estimate of sustainable maximum capacity. It shows how much slack the industrial economy has: high utilization foreshadows bottlenecks and price pressure, while low utilization signals idle plants and weak investment.

a: Consumer Confidence Index CCI Consumer sentiment
x: A monthly survey-based index of U.S. household attitudes about current business and labor-market conditions and expectations for income, business activity, and jobs, published by The Conference Board with 1985 as the base year (1985=100). It comprises the Present Situation Index and the Expectations Index. Confident consumers tend to spend more freely, so the index is watched as a leading indicator of consumption, the largest part of GDP.

a: Inverted yield curve Negative term spread
x: A condition in which short-term Treasury yields exceed long-term yields, inverting the normally upward-sloping term structure of interest rates. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York measures the term spread as the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury rate and uses its slope to estimate the probability of a recession twelve months ahead. Inversion signals that markets expect the central bank to cut rates because of coming weakness, so a negative spread has preceded nearly every modern U.S. recession with few false alarms.

The actions and communications of a central bank to influence the availability and cost of money and credit in pursuit of macroeconomic goals. In the United States, the Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy under its congressional mandate of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates. It is the economy's thermostat: the central bank tightens to cool demand and inflation, and eases to support growth and employment.

The use of government taxation and spending to influence the economy, set in the United States by Congress and the President through the federal budget. Its outcomes are tracked as revenue, outlays, and the deficit - the annual gap between spending and revenue, financed by issuing Treasury debt. Where monetary policy moves the price of money, fiscal policy moves money itself: cutting taxes or boosting spending injects demand, while raising taxes or cutting spending withdraws it.

Large-scale purchases of longer-term securities - Treasuries, agency debt, and mortgage-backed securities - by a central bank to ease financial conditions when the policy rate is near zero. The Federal Reserve ran several such large-scale asset purchase programs from late 2008 to 2014 and again in 2020-21. When the overnight rate cannot go lower, the central bank instead pushes down longer-term rates directly by becoming a huge buyer of bonds.

a: QT Balance sheet normalization Balance sheet runoff
x: The reduction of a central bank's securities holdings - by letting maturing bonds roll off without full reinvestment or, more rarely, selling them - which drains reserve balances and tightens financial conditions. It is the reverse of quantitative easing. If QE steps on the gas by adding reserves and holding down long rates, QT gently lifts off, letting the balance sheet shrink so bond markets stand on their own.

Communication by a central bank about the likely future course of monetary policy, used to shape public expectations and thereby influence financial conditions today. The FOMC has used forward guidance in its postmeeting statements since the early 2000s, most intensively when the funds rate was pinned near zero. Telling markets where rates are heading does some of the tightening or easing for you: long-term rates move on expectations, not just on today's rate.

a: Interest rate increase Policy tightening Tightening
x: An increase in a central bank's policy interest rate - in the United States, an upward move in the FOMC's target range for the federal funds rate - intended to restrain demand and inflation. Hikes are typically delivered in 25-basis-point steps, with larger moves when inflation is urgent. Raising the overnight rate makes borrowing costlier across the economy, cooling spending and price pressure at the cost of slower growth.

a: Interest rate reduction Easing Policy easing
x: A decrease in a central bank's policy interest rate - in the United States, a downward move in the FOMC's target range for the federal funds rate - intended to stimulate borrowing, spending, and employment. Cuts may be gradual 'insurance' moves or emergency responses to crises. Cheaper overnight money cascades into cheaper loans, encouraging firms and households to spend and invest when the economy needs support.

A monetary-policy stance, or a description of a policymaker, that prioritizes controlling inflation - favoring higher interest rates and restraint even at some cost to growth and employment. The opposite stance is dovish. A hawk would rather risk a cool economy than let inflation expectations escape; the hawk's nightmare is 1970s-style entrenched inflation.

A monetary-policy stance, or a description of a policymaker, that prioritizes supporting growth and employment - favoring low interest rates, easing, and tolerance of inflation risk. The opposite stance is hawkish. A dove worries more about the jobless than about a few tenths of extra inflation; the dove's nightmare is a weak economy left to stagnate.

a: Citi Economic Surprise Index CESI Economic Surprise Index
x: An index that aggregates how economic data releases compare with consensus forecasts, turning 'better or worse than expected' into a single daily time series. The best known is the Citigroup Economic Surprise Index, a rolling three-month, weighted measure of data surprises versus Bloomberg survey medians. Markets move on surprises, not levels - the index tracks whether the flow of data is beating or disappointing what economists had already priced in.

A public company's net profit divided by its number of common shares outstanding, reported as basic EPS on weighted-average shares and as diluted EPS including the potential shares from options, warrants, and convertibles. It is the standard per-share measure of profitability shown on the income statement. EPS turns total profit into an amount 'per share of ownership,' making companies of different sizes comparable and forming the denominator of the P/E ratio.

The total amount of money a company brings in from selling its products or services during a period, before any expenses are deducted - the 'top line' of the income statement. It is typically reported as net revenue after subtracting returns, allowances, and discounts. Revenue is the raw scale of a business's sales engine; every margin and profit figure ultimately starts from it.

Revenue remaining after subtracting the direct costs of producing the goods or services sold, expressed as a percentage of revenue. The SEC's investors' guide describes gross profit - sometimes called gross margin - as net revenues minus the cost of sales. It measures how much markup the core product carries before overhead: the first test of whether a business model works.

Income from operations as a percentage of net revenues - the share of each sales dollar left after production costs and operating expenses, but before interest and taxes. The SEC's investors' guide defines it exactly as income from operations divided by net revenues. It captures the profitability of the core business itself, independent of how the company is financed or taxed.

a: Net margin Profit margin Bottom-line margin
x: Net income as a percentage of revenue - the final 'bottom-line' share of each sales dollar remaining after all costs, interest, and taxes have been deducted. It is the most complete single-margin summary: what ultimately falls to shareholders out of each dollar of sales.

a: FCF Free cash flow to the firm FCFF FCFE
x: The cash a business generates from operations after the capital expenditures needed to maintain and grow its asset base - the cash genuinely available to debt and equity holders. In Damodaran's framework, valuation discounts cash flows to equity (after interest, principal, and reinvestment) or to the firm (after taxes and reinvestment but before debt payments). Accounting profit is an opinion; free cash flow is what is actually left to pay dividends, buy back stock, or pay down debt.

a: P/E ratio PE Price-to-earnings ratio Earnings multiple
x: A company's share price divided by its earnings per share - how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual earnings. The SEC's investors' guide and Damodaran both define it as market price per share over EPS, with variants depending on which earnings period and share count are used. P/E is the market's price tag on earnings: high ratios imply investors expect growth or see low risk, while low ratios imply the opposite - or neglect.

The price-earnings ratio computed using expected earnings per share - for the next fiscal year or the next four quarters - rather than trailing earnings. Damodaran classifies both of those forward-EPS variants as forward P/E ratios. Since investing is about the future, forward P/E prices what a company is expected to earn, giving the market's growth-adjusted valuation snapshot.

Market capitalization - or price per share - divided by the book value of shareholders' equity: what investors pay per dollar of net asset value on the balance sheet. Damodaran's consistency rule for multiples requires equity value in the numerator to be paired with equity book value in the denominator. P/B asks whether the market values the business above or below the accumulated accounting value of what it owns minus what it owes.

Market capitalization divided by trailing revenue - equivalently price per share over revenue per share - the amount investors pay per dollar of a company's sales. It remains usable when earnings are negative, which the P/E ratio is not. Sales are the hardest income-statement line to fake and exist even for loss-making firms, so P/S is the multiple of last resort for young or distressed companies.

The total economic value of a business - what an acquirer would effectively pay: market value of equity plus total debt (and other claims such as preferred stock and minority interest) minus cash and cash equivalents. It measures the value of the operating business independent of how it is financed. Buying a company means assuming its debts and receiving its cash, so the true price tag is the equity value plus net debt - enterprise value is that price tag.

a: EV/EBITDA Enterprise multiple EV to EBITDA
x: Enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization - a capital-structure-neutral multiple showing how many years of pre-financing operating earnings the whole business costs. It is widely used to compare takeover values across firms with different debt levels and tax regimes. Because both the numerator and the denominator are pre-financing, EV/EBITDA puts a leveraged firm and a debt-free firm on equal footing.

Annual dividends per share divided by the current share price - the dividend-only rate of return on a stock at today's price. Holding the dividend constant, the yield rises when the price falls and falls when the price rises. It is the stock-market analog of a bond's yield: the cash income you collect per dollar invested, ignoring price changes.

Earnings per share divided by the share price - the reciprocal of the P/E ratio - expressing how much annual earnings the company generates per dollar invested. It allows direct comparison of equity valuations with bond yields. If P/E is the price of a dollar of earnings, the earnings yield is the 'interest rate' a stock's current earnings represent on its price.

An intrinsic valuation method that estimates an asset's worth as the present value of its expected future cash flows, discounted at a rate reflecting their risk. Damodaran states the principle directly: assets that generate cash flows have value equal to the sum of those expected cash flows discounted back to today. A dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today; DCF simply adds up all future dollars after shrinking each one for time and risk.

The estimated value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast horizon in a DCF model, computed either as a growing perpetuity or as an exit multiple. It typically dominates the valuation, often contributing well over half of total present value. Since a business presumably outlives any five- or ten-year forecast, terminal value is the compressed answer to 'and then what?' - and where most of the value hides.

A structural competitive advantage that lets a company defend its profits against rivals for an extended period - the concept popularized by Warren Buffett and operationalized by Morningstar as its Economic Moat Rating of wide, narrow, or none. Morningstar grants a wide moat when advantages are expected to last more than 20 years and a narrow moat for about 10. A moat is what stops competition from grinding a great business's returns down to average: the difference between a temporary profit spike and a durable cash machine.

a: Earnings beat Earnings miss EPS surprise
x: The difference between a company's reported earnings and the consensus analyst estimate - positive when profits beat expectations, negative when they miss. Since prices embed consensus beforehand, the surprise rather than the earnings level is what moves the stock. Markets price in what everyone expects; only the unexpected part of an earnings report is genuinely new information.

a: Earnings guidance Company guidance Forward outlook
x: A public company's own forecast of its future performance - typically revenue and EPS for the coming quarter or year - issued voluntarily alongside earnings reports and discussed on analyst calls. It shapes the consensus against which actual results are later judged. Guidance is management's answer to 'what should we expect?' - and it often matters more to the stock than the quarter just reported.

A company's repurchase of its own shares on the open market or via tender offer, reducing shares outstanding. Repurchased shares are retired or held as treasury stock, raising each remaining share's claim on earnings. It is the flexible cousin of the dividend: another way to return cash to shareholders, but one that also shrinks the share count and lifts per-share metrics.

A corporate action that increases the number of outstanding shares by issuing new shares to existing holders in a set ratio, cutting the per-share price proportionally while leaving market capitalization unchanged. The most common forms are 2-for-1, 3-for-2, and 3-for-1 splits. A split is slicing the same pie into more pieces: your ownership stake and the company's value do not change, only the size of each slice.

A corporate action that consolidates shares - exchanging many old shares for one new share - to raise the per-share price proportionally while leaving market capitalization unchanged. It is most common among small or distressed companies trying to meet exchange minimum-price rules or attract institutional investors. It is the same pie cut into fewer, bigger slices: economically neutral by itself, but usually a symptom that the share price fell low enough to become a problem.

A distribution of a portion of a company's profits to shareholders in cash, typically declared by the board on a fixed schedule such as quarterly. Investor.gov defines a dividend as a portion of a company's profit paid to shareholders, with unscheduled payments known as special dividends. It is the most direct way a company hands owners their share of the profits: cash in the account rather than a claim on future growth.

The first trading day on which a stock trades without the right to its declared dividend: buy on or after the ex-date and the seller, not you, receives the payment. It is set by stock-exchange rules, normally on the record date or one business day before if the record date is not a business day. Because trades take a day to settle, the ex-date is the practical cutoff: it answers 'how late can I buy and still get the dividend?'

The date set by a company's board on which a shareholder must appear on the company's books to receive a declared dividend; shareholders of record are also the ones sent proxy statements, financial reports, and other corporate information. It is the company's administrative snapshot: whoever the transfer records show as owner on this date gets the dividend.

An issue giving existing shareholders the right - but not the obligation - to buy additional shares pro rata to their holdings at a discount to the market price within a set window, usually 16 to 30 days. The rights are often transferable and tradable like ordinary shares until they expire. It is a loyalty-preserving capital raise: current owners get first claim on new shares cheaply, and those who do not want in can sell the right itself.

A corporate action in which a company separates a division into an independent company by distributing new shares in it to existing shareholders, generally pro rata. Holders end up owning shares in both the parent and the spun-off entity. A spin-off unbundles a conglomerate so each business can be managed - and valued - on its own merits.

a: Risk arbitrage Risk arb Deal arbitrage
x: An event-driven strategy that seeks to profit from the spread between a takeover target's trading price and the announced deal price: typically buying the target's stock - and, in stock-for-stock deals, shorting the acquirer's - to capture the discount that reflects the risk the deal fails. Also called risk arbitrage. After a $50-per-share cash bid the target might trade at $48; the arbitrageur buys the $2 gap, earning it if the deal closes and losing heavily if it breaks.

A disruptive order-book practice in which a trader rapidly submits and cancels very large numbers of bids or offers to overload a trading venue's quotation system, delay other participants' market data or executions, or create misleading impressions of market activity. The CFTC has described submitting or cancelling bids or offers to overload a registered entity's quotation system as conduct 'of the character of' spoofing, which Dodd-Frank made unlawful as a disruptive practice under CEA section 4c(a)(5). Imagine shouting thousands of fake orders into a market every second and instantly retracting them, just so everyone else's screens and systems choke on the noise while you exploit the confusion.

Bidding or offering with the intent to cancel the bid or offer before execution, an explicitly prohibited disruptive trading practice under CEA section 4c(a)(5)(C) as added by the Dodd-Frank Act. The spoofer places visible orders it never intends to fill in order to deceive other participants about supply or demand and profit from the induced price movement. You wave a huge fake buy order in front of the market so prices tick up, then you sell into the move and yank the fake order before anyone can hit it.

A variant of spoofing in which a trader submits multiple non-bona fide orders at successively different price levels on one side of the order book to create a false appearance of market depth and pressure, thereby moving the price so that a genuine order on the opposite side can execute advantageously. The CFTC's description of spoofing-type conduct includes submitting or cancelling multiple bids or offers to create an appearance of false market depth. Instead of one big fake order, you stack a whole staircase of fake orders at different prices so the book looks deep on one side and the market walks straight into your real trade on the other side.

a: wash sale (manipulative sense) round trip trading
x: Entering into, or purporting to enter into, transactions that give the appearance that purchases and sales have been made without incurring market risk or changing the trader's market position; the Commodity Exchange Act prohibits wash trading, and Section 9(a)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibits transactions involving no change in beneficial ownership (and matched orders) done to create a false or misleading appearance of active trading. You sell to yourself — the asset never really changes hands and you take no risk, but the tape lights up with 'activity' that lures in real traders.

With respect to commodity futures and options, taking a futures or option position based on non-public information regarding an impending transaction by another person in the same or a related future or option; in securities markets, the analogous practice of a broker or adviser trading ahead of a known customer order to profit from its expected price impact. It misappropriates order information and disadvantages the customer whose order is anticipated. You know a giant buy order is about to hit the market, so you buy first, let the customer's order push the price up, and sell into their demand.

A manipulative or disruptive trading practice whereby a trader buys or sells a large number of futures contracts during the closing period of a contract — the period in which the settlement price is determined — in order to benefit an even larger position in an option, swap, or other derivative that is cash-settled based on that day's settlement price. You shove the price around in the last minutes of trading not because you want the position, but because today's official closing price sets the payoff on a much bigger bet you hold elsewhere.

Engaging in a series of transactions — typically wash trades or matched orders — designed to create a false or misleading appearance of active trading or of price movement in a security, so that the publicly reported 'tape' attracts other investors. Section 9(a)(1)-(2) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibits effecting such transactions for the purpose of inducing purchases or sales by others. You manufacture busy-looking trades and rising prints on the ticker so the crowd thinks something is happening and piles in — the activity is theater, not genuine demand.

Illegal insider trading refers generally to buying or selling a security, in breach of a fiduciary duty or other relationship of trust and confidence, on the basis of material, nonpublic information about the security. Not all trading by corporate insiders is illegal: insiders may lawfully trade when they do so without using material nonpublic information and report their transactions as required. If you trade using secret, market-moving information that you were entrusted with and weren't supposed to use, you're stealing an unfair edge from everyone on the other side of your trade.

Information about a security or its issuer that is both material — meaning there is a substantial likelihood a reasonable investor would consider it important in making an investment decision — and not yet disseminated to the public. Trading on such information in breach of a duty of trust or confidence is the core of illegal insider trading. It's the kind of secret that would obviously change someone's mind about buying or selling — like an unannounced merger or an earnings collapse — and that the market hasn't been told yet.

Intentional conduct that artificially affects the supply, demand, or price of a security or commodity rather than letting prices reflect genuine market forces — for example, wash trades, matched orders, spoofing, marking the close, or spreading false information to move a price. Section 9 of the Securities Exchange Act and CEA section 4c/6(c) prohibit specific manipulative acts, and Rule 10b-5 reaches manipulative schemes generally. It's rigging the scoreboard: instead of predicting where prices will go, the manipulator makes the price move and cashes in on the fake signal everyone else is reacting to.

A fraud in which promoters boost ('pump') the price of a stock — typically a little-known microcap — through false or misleading positive statements, then sell ('dump') their own holdings into the inflated price, after which the hype stops, the price collapses, and later investors lose their money. The operators buy a cheap stock quietly, shout spectacular lies about it until the crowd bids it up, and then unload everything on the crowd before the truth catches up.

Excessive trading of a customer account by a person who controls the account (typically a broker with discretion or de facto control), done for the purpose of generating commissions or fees while disregarding the customer's interests. FINRA's quantitative-suitability doctrine reaches the same conduct even without formal discretion when the broker effectively controls the account. The broker trades your account like a hamster wheel — every spin pays them a commission, whether or not any of it makes sense for you.

Securing such relative control of a commodity or its deliverable supply that its price can be manipulated at the cornerer's will — in the extreme, holding contracts requiring delivery of more of the commodity than is available for delivery. A successful corner forces shorts to cover or settle at prices dictated by the cornerer. You quietly buy up nearly everything there is to deliver, so when the sellers must come to market to fulfill their contracts, you're the only shop in town and you name the price.

An illegal manipulation scheme that is the bearish mirror image of a pump and dump: the perpetrator establishes a short position in a stock, then spreads false or unsubstantiated negative rumors to drive the price down, and covers the short at the lower price for a profit. Spreading false information to move a price and manipulative short selling violate the antifraud provisions of the securities laws. Bet that a stock will fall, then poison the well with scary lies so it actually falls, and buy back cheap while everyone else panics.

A market term for concerted heavy short selling of a stock, typically combined with spreading negative rumors about the company, intended to drive the price down quickly so the short sellers profit when covering at lower prices. When the selling is collusive or the rumors false, a bear raid constitutes market manipulation; heavy short selling based on genuine analysis is lawful. A pack of short sellers attacks a vulnerable company all at once — selling hard and whispering bad news — hoping to start a stampede they can ride to profit.

The monitoring of order, trade, and position data by exchanges, self-regulatory organizations, and regulators to detect potentially violative conduct such as manipulation, spoofing, wash trading, insider trading, and rule breaches, and to enforce compliance with exchange rules and securities laws. At NYSE, for example, the Surveillance and Investigations group surveils and preliminarily investigates members for market- and trading-related violations. It's the market's referee system: software and analysts watch every order and trade for patterns that look like cheating, then flag them for investigation.

The set of procedures by which financial institutions verify the identity of customers and understand the nature of their activities, anchored in the U.S. by Section 326 of the USA PATRIOT Act (31 U.S.C. § 5318(l)), which requires minimum standards for verifying the identity of persons opening accounts, maintaining verification records, and screening against government lists of known or suspected terrorists. Before a firm lets you move money or trade, it must actually know who you are — name, address, ID documents — so criminals can't hide behind anonymous accounts.

a: AML controls AML/CFT program BSA/AML program
x: The program of internal policies, procedures, and controls that financial institutions must establish to guard against money laundering and the financing of terrorism. Under 31 U.S.C. § 5318(h) each financial institution must maintain an AML program including, at a minimum, internal policies/procedures/controls, a designated compliance officer, ongoing employee training, and an independent audit function, applied on a risk basis. Banks and brokers must build a filter that makes it hard to wash dirty money through the financial system — and prove to examiners that the filter actually works.

The FINRA Rule 2111 obligation that a broker-dealer or associated person have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer, based on reasonable diligence to ascertain the customer's investment profile — including age, other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, objectives, experience, time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance. For retail customers, suitability has been superseded by Regulation Best Interest (SEA Rule 15l-1), to which Rule 2111 no longer applies. A broker can't sell you just anything that isn't fraudulent — the recommendation has to fit who you are, what you can afford, and what you're trying to do.

The obligation, owed under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by an investment adviser to its client, to act in the client's best interest; per the SEC's 2019 interpretation it comprises a duty of care (including advice in the client's best interest, best execution, and advice and monitoring over the relationship) and a duty of loyalty (not subordinating the client's interests to the adviser's own, with full and fair disclosure of material conflicts). A fiduciary must run your money the way a careful, honest trustee would — putting your interests first, telling you about conflicts, and never secretly profiting at your expense.

The standard of conduct established by the SEC's Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1, adopted 2019) requiring a broker-dealer, when making a recommendation of a securities transaction or investment strategy to a retail customer, to act in the retail customer's best interest without placing its own financial or other interests ahead of the customer's. It is implemented through disclosure, care, conflict-of-interest, and compliance obligations.
