When a broker recommends something to a retail customer, they must recommend what's good for the customer — not what's lucrative for the broker — and prove their house rules back that up.

The maximum position, net long or net short, in one commodity future (or option) or in all futures (or options) of one commodity combined, that may be held or controlled by one person (other than a person eligible for a hedge exemption), as prescribed by an exchange and/or the CFTC. A position limit (in the strict sense) is a speculative position limit whose exceedance violates exchange rules and triggers predefined penalties. It's a speed limit on market size: no single trader may pile up a futures position so big that they can bully the price or endanger delivery.

A position threshold set by an exchange which, when exceeded, triggers a notification to the exchange and gives it authority to inquire into, limit, or order a reduction of the trader's position — but which, unlike a position limit, is not itself a violation of exchange rules when exceeded. It's a tripwire rather than a fence: crossing it doesn't break a rule, but it tells the exchange 'watch this trader' and lets them demand answers or cuts if the position looks dangerous.

The CFTC's reporting system under which futures commission merchants, clearing members, foreign brokers, and traders must report positions at or above CFTC-set reporting levels — sizes of positions set by the exchanges and/or the CFTC at or above which traders or brokers must make daily reports of position size by commodity and delivery month and whether the position is controlled by a commercial or non-commercial trader. Once your position gets big enough to matter to the whole market, you can no longer stay anonymous — the regulator gets a daily look at exactly what you hold.

a: Rule 201 short sale price test circuit breaker
x: A rule limiting when or at what price short sales may be executed, the current U.S. form being Rule 201 of Regulation SHO: when a stock's price falls at least 10% from the prior day's close, trading centers must prevent the execution or display of short-sale orders at prices at or below the national best bid for the rest of that day and the following day. When a stock is already crashing, this rule makes short sellers wait their turn above the bid so they can't keep hammering the price down tick after tick.

The Regulation SHO requirement (Rule 203(b)(1)-(2)) that, before effecting a short sale in any equity security, a broker-dealer must have reasonable grounds to believe the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due, and must document that 'locate' before executing the short sale. Before you sell shares you don't own, your broker must point to a real, borrowable source of those shares — no selling into thin air.

The SEC's short-sale regulation (Rules 200-204 under the Exchange Act), adopted in 2004 with compliance beginning January 3, 2005, to update short-sale regulation and address abusive naked short selling and persistent failures to deliver. Its four pillars are order marking (Rule 200), the short-sale price test circuit breaker (Rule 201), the locate requirement (Rule 203(b)), and close-out requirements for fails to deliver (Rules 204 and 203(b)(3)). It's the rulebook that keeps short selling honest: mark your orders correctly, don't pile onto crashing stocks, line up shares before you sell, and actually deliver what you sold.

The FINRA margin rule regime under which a customer who executes four or more day trades within five business days in a margin account (a day trade being the purchase and sale, or sale and purchase, of the same security on the same day) is designated a 'pattern day trader' and becomes subject to special margin requirements, historically a $25,000 minimum equity requirement. If you day trade frequently with borrowed money, regulators make you keep a serious cash cushion in the account so a bad day doesn't sink the broker too.

The U.S. tax rule (IRC section 1091, detailed in IRS Publication 550) that disallows a loss deduction when stock or securities are sold at a loss and substantially identical stock or securities are bought (or an option or contract to buy them is acquired) within 30 days before or after the sale; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement position. You can't sell a stock for a tax loss on Friday and buy it right back on Monday — the IRS treats that as never having really sold, so the loss waits until you truly exit.

The profit realized when a capital asset — such as stocks or bonds held as investments — is sold for more than its adjusted basis; per the IRS, a capital gain is the excess of the amount realized on sale over the asset's adjusted basis. Gains are classified as short-term (asset held one year or less) or long-term (held more than one year), with long-term net gains generally taxed at preferential rates. Buy low, sell high — the positive difference between what you paid (your basis) and what you sold for is your capital gain, and the tax rate depends on how long you held it.

The loss realized when a capital asset is sold for less than its adjusted basis; per the IRS, you have a capital loss if you sell the asset for less than your adjusted basis. Capital losses offset capital gains, and if losses exceed gains, up to $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately) of the excess is deductible against ordinary income per year, with the remainder carried forward. Sell for less than you paid and you have a capital loss — painful, but it can shrink your tax bill by canceling out gains and a limited slice of ordinary income each year.

Trading volume is the total number of units of a security (shares, contracts, or coins) that changed hands in executed trades during a given period. It is the standard measure of market activity and is reported per instrument, per venue, or consolidated across venues. Volume counts how much of an asset actually traded. It tells you how active and liquid the market was, not which direction prices moved.

a: quote asset volume quote currency volume
x: Quote volume is trading volume denominated in the quote currency of a trading pair, i.e., the sum over trades of price times quantity. It is the standard volume field in crypto exchange data (e.g., Binance klines report base-asset volume and quote-asset volume side by side). Instead of counting how many units traded, quote volume tells you how much money (in the pair's pricing currency) changed hands.

a: dollar-volume liquidity value traded turnover value
x: Dollar volume is the total monetary value of shares traded during a period, computed as price multiplied by share volume. It measures how much capital actually changed hands and is the standard way to compare trading activity across instruments of different prices. A $5 stock trading 10 million shares moves less money ($50M) than a $200 stock trading 500,000 shares ($100M) — dollar volume captures that difference; share counts do not.

a: share turnover share turnover ratio velocity
x: Share turnover is a liquidity measure computed by dividing the total number of shares traded over a period by the number of shares outstanding during that period. It expresses how many times the share base effectively changed hands, indicating the relative ease of buying or selling the stock. Turnover normalizes volume by company size: trading 1 million shares is frenetic for a firm with 5 million shares outstanding but trivial for one with 5 billion.

The open price is the price of the first trade of an instrument within a given period — for a daily bar, the first transaction of the trading session, on many exchanges determined by an opening auction. It anchors one end of the bar's price path. The open is where trading started for the period. It summarizes where overnight or pre-period information got priced in at the first print.

The high price is the highest price at which any trade executed during a given period. It marks the upper extreme of the period's traded range and forms the top of an OHLC bar or candlestick wick. The high is the most anyone paid during the period — the peak of the price excursion.

The low price is the lowest price at which any trade executed during a given period. It marks the lower extreme of the period's traded range and forms the bottom of an OHLC bar or candlestick wick. The low is the least anyone received (or paid) for the asset during the period — the trough of the price excursion.

The close price is generally the last price at which a stock trades during a regular trading session (e.g., 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern for U.S. markets), often set by a closing auction. It is the most widely used single price for performance measurement, marking-to-market, and indicator input. The close is the market's final word for the period — the price at which the last trade printed before the session ended.

The adjusted close is the closing price amended to reflect the effects of corporate actions — stock splits and dividend distributions — so that the historical price series is internally comparable. Data vendors compute it by applying split and dividend adjustment factors to the as-traded close. A 2-for-1 split halves the share price overnight without making holders poorer; the adjusted close rewrites history so the chart and return calculations show continuity instead of a fake 50% crash.

An OHLC bar is a summary record of a period's trading containing the open (first trade), high (maximum trade), low (minimum trade), and close (last trade) prices. It is the canonical aggregated unit of price history and the basis of bar and candlestick charts. An OHLC bar compresses everything that happened in a period into four numbers: where trading started, the extremes it reached, and where it ended.

An OHLCV bar is an OHLC bar augmented with the total trading volume over the same interval. It is the standard record layout for aggregated market data; in finance literature the OHLCV data is sometimes called 'candles'. OHLCV adds 'how much traded' to the four price extremes, so each record captures both the price path summary and the activity level behind it.

a: tick-by-tick data trade and quote data TAQ data
x: Tick data is the unaggregated, event-level record of market activity: every executed trade (price, size, time, venue) and, in full feeds, every quote update (bid, ask, sizes), timestamped in sequence. It is the finest granularity of market data, from which bars of any type are derived. Tick data is the market's raw ledger — each individual trade and quote as it happened, rather than a summary.

a: time-based bar fixed-interval bar calendar bar
x: A time bar is an OHLC(V) bar built by aggregating all trades within a fixed clock interval (1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, etc.). It is the default sampling scheme in market data, in which bars are produced at uniform points in time regardless of how much trading occurred. Time bars chop the trading day into equal clock slices and summarize each slice — whether it contained three trades or three thousand.

A tick bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating a fixed number of consecutive trades (e.g., every 1,000 transactions), rather than a fixed clock interval. Sampling in transaction time aligns bar formation with market activity instead of the clock. A new bar appears after every N trades — busy markets produce bars rapidly, quiet markets slowly, so each bar contains a comparable amount of trading activity.

A volume bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating trades until a fixed cumulative quantity (e.g., 10,000 shares or 100 BTC) has traded. Bars are thus sampled in units of traded volume rather than time or trade count. Each bar represents the same amount of actual participation — the market 'votes' with quantity, and a new bar is cast once the vote count reaches the threshold.

A dollar bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating trades until a fixed cumulative dollar value (price × quantity, e.g., $1,000,000) has traded. Sampling in money terms keeps bar information content comparable even as an instrument's price level changes over time. Each bar represents the same amount of cash changing hands, which keeps the sampling meaningful across years during which the share price may have multiplied.

A range bar is a price-based chart element in which a new bar is created only after the price has moved by a user-specified fixed range, regardless of how much time passes. Every completed bar therefore has the same high-low span, and time is eliminated as a construction variable. Range bars print one bar per fixed price excursion — the chart advances only when price actually travels, so flat markets produce almost no bars.

A Renko chart is a Japanese-origin price chart built of fixed-size 'bricks': a new brick is drawn in the direction of the move only when price surpasses the previous brick's boundary by the brick size, and never adjacent on the same line. Like point-and-figure, time plays no role; it is a technical-analysis framework for filtering noise, not a proven predictive method. Renko stacks identical bricks in the direction of travel — you see a clean staircase of meaningful moves while small wiggles never make it onto the chart.

a: P&F chart point and figure P&F
x: Point-and-figure is a century-old technical-analysis charting technique that plots price against changes in direction rather than against time: rising prices are drawn as columns of Xs and falling prices as columns of Os, with columns reversing only after a set reversal amount. It is an analytical framework for trend and pattern study, not a proven predictive law. P&F ignores the clock and minor wiggles entirely — the chart only grows when price moves by a full box, and switches columns only on a meaningful reversal.

Heikin-Ashi (Japanese for 'average bar') is a candlestick variant in which each candle's OHLC values are computed as weighted averages of actual prices and the previous Heikin-Ashi candle, smoothing the displayed price series. It is a visualization/analytical technique for highlighting trend; its displayed values are not actual traded prices. Heikin-Ashi candles are 'pre-smoothed' candlesticks: trends look cleaner and reversals stand out, because each bar is averaged with its predecessor.

The typical price is the arithmetic mean of a bar's high, low, and close: (H+L+C)/3. It is a standard single-price summary of a trading bar, used as the price input of indicators such as the Money Flow Index and the Commodity Channel Index. Typical price collapses a bar into one number that represents where trading happened, giving equal weight to the extremes and the close.

The median price is the midpoint of a bar's trading range: (H+L)/2. It summarizes a bar by the center of its extremes and, when averaged over periods, forms a smoother trend line than close-based averages because it is less affected by close-to-close fluctuations and outliers. Median price is the halfway point of the bar's range — a quick measure of the bar's center of gravity that ignores where within the range the close landed.

The weighted close is the average of a bar's high, low, and close with the close counted twice: (H+L+2C)/4. It is a bar-summary price that emphasizes the close — reflecting its importance for mark-to-market — over the bar's extremes. Weighted close is the typical price with extra weight on the closing print, on the view that where the bar settled matters more than where it wandered.

In bar data, the average price is the arithmetic mean of a bar's four OHLC prices: (O+H+L+C)/4. It is the most neutral single-number summary of a bar — it is, for example, exactly the Heikin-Ashi close — though in session-level contexts 'average price' can instead mean a volume-weighted average over the period. Average price treats all four of a bar's reference prices equally, giving a balanced 'center' of the period's action.

True range is a volatility measure introduced by J. Welles Wilder Jr. (1978) that extends the bar's high-low range to capture gaps relative to the previous close. It is the largest of: current high minus low, |high − previous close|, and |low − previous close|; its smoothed average is the Average True Range (ATR). Plain range misses overnight gaps. True range asks: how far did price actually travel, including any jump from yesterday's close to today's extremes?

a: rolling max moving maximum trailing maximum
x: The rolling maximum is the highest value of a series within a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It underlies channel indicators such as Donchian channels and breakout systems. At each point, look back over the last N bars and ask: what was the highest price seen? That level moves as old extremes drop out of the window.

a: rolling min moving minimum trailing minimum
x: The rolling minimum is the lowest value of a series within a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Together with the rolling maximum it defines the lower boundary of channel indicators such as Donchian channels. At each point, look back over the last N bars and ask: what was the lowest price seen? The level ratchets as time passes and old lows expire from the window.

a: rolling average simple moving average SMA moving average
x: The rolling mean is the arithmetic average of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Applied to prices it is the simple moving average (SMA), the most common trend-smoothing statistic in market analysis. The rolling mean smooths out bar-to-bar noise by averaging the last N values, so the line rises when recent values are generally higher than the ones dropping out.

The rolling median is the median value of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It is a robust alternative to the rolling mean, insensitive to extreme values within the window. Instead of averaging the last N bars, take the middle one — a single spike can pull a mean around but cannot move the median much.

a: rolling volatility rolling std moving standard deviation
x: The rolling standard deviation is the sample (or population) standard deviation of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Applied to returns it is the standard estimator of realized volatility and the width driver of Bollinger Bands. It measures how spread out the last N returns (or prices) were — a live gauge of how violently the market has been moving recently.

Rolling correlation is the Pearson correlation coefficient between two series computed over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It tracks how the co-movement of two assets (typically their returns) evolves through time. Instead of one correlation number for the whole history, you get a time series showing when two markets moved together and when they decoupled.

Rolling beta is the regression slope of an asset's returns on a benchmark's returns — covariance divided by benchmark variance — estimated over a trailing window that slides forward one observation at a time. It tracks how an asset's market sensitivity evolves rather than assuming a single static beta. Beta asks 'when the market moves 1%, how much does this asset typically move?'; rolling beta shows that answer changing through time as the asset's risk profile shifts.

The rolling z-score standardizes each observation of a series by the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation of its trailing window: how many recent-standard-deviations the current value sits from the recent mean. It converts levels into a locally normalized scale used by mean-reversion and Bollinger-style analyses. A z-score of +2 says 'today's value is unusually high compared with the recent past' — unusual measured in units of the recent volatility, not absolute price.

An organized or decentralized arrangement in which participants exchange financial assets, funds, and risk exposures and thereby establish prices. Financial markets perform two core functions: channeling savings to issuers in the primary market and providing liquidity and price discovery through secondary trading. It is where people who have money meet people who need it, and where people holding risk trade it to people willing to bear it; the byproduct of all that trading is a price.

An organized, regulated marketplace that provides a centralized facility for trading standardized instruments under a published rulebook covering membership, listing, order matching, surveillance, and clearing. The CFTC defines a board of trade as any organized exchange or other trading facility for the trading of futures, swap, and/or option contracts (7 USC 1a(6)). A regulated bazaar: everyone agrees to the same rulebook, and the venue matches buyers with sellers under surveillance.

A decentralized market in which counterparties negotiate transactions directly or through dealer networks rather than on a centralized exchange, allowing contract terms to be customized. Most foreign exchange, government and corporate bond, and swap trading occurs over the counter. Instead of meeting in one hall, buyers and sellers call dealers or message each other directly and agree their own deal terms.

a: Clearing organization Clearing house Central counterparty CCP
x: An entity through which futures, derivatives, and securities transactions are cleared and settled and that interposes itself between counterparties, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. A clearing organization registered with the CFTC is a Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO); in securities markets the same function is performed by a central counterparty such as NSCC. After a trade, the clearinghouse steps into the middle so that each trader faces the clearinghouse instead of each other — if one side defaults, the clearinghouse absorbs it.

The act that discharges the obligations created by a trade: the final transfer of securities or other assets from seller to buyer against the corresponding transfer of funds, occurring on a scheduled settlement date. A trade is only completed at settlement; execution creates the obligation, settlement fulfills it. Execution is shaking hands on the deal; settlement is actually handing over the shares and the cash.

The market in which newly issued securities are sold to investors for the first time and the issuer receives the proceeds. IPOs, follow-on offerings, and new bond issues are primary market transactions. This is where securities are born: money flows from investors to the issuer in exchange for brand-new shares or bonds.

The market in which previously issued securities are traded among investors, without the issuer receiving the proceeds. Secondary trading provides the liquidity and continuous pricing that make primary issuance possible. This is the resale market: investors trade existing shares with each other, and the company is not a party to the deal.

A market structure in which buyers and sellers trade directly with one another through a centralized matching process — orders compete and are matched by price-time priority rules or crossed at a single clearing price — rather than through a dealer acting as counterparty. Like an auction house: everyone shouts bids and offers into one room, and the matching rules pair the most willing buyer with the most willing seller.

A market structure in which dealers (market makers) stand ready to buy and sell from their own inventory at publicly quoted prices, so customers transact with a dealer as counterparty rather than directly with one another. Instead of trading with the person on the other side, you always trade with a shopkeeper who quotes a price to buy and a price to sell.

a: Order book market Central limit order book market CLOB
x: A market structure in which prices are formed by the interaction of participants' own orders: limit orders rest in a central order book and incoming orders execute against them by price-time priority, so no dealer intermediation is required. The CFTC describes the central limit order book as a single order book covering an entire market that accepts limit orders. The order book itself is the market — your limit order can become the best bid, and anyone in the world can trade against it.

A market structure in which dealers continuously or on request quote firm bid and ask prices at which they are prepared to trade as principal, and customer orders execute against those quotes rather than against other customers' orders. Prices come from dealers, not from a public book: you trade when you accept a dealer's quoted bid or offer.

A market structure combining elements of auction/order-driven trading and dealer/quote-driven trading — typically an electronic limit order book operating alongside designated market makers or a floor auction with assigned liquidity obligations. Part robot, part human: most orders match electronically, but assigned market makers still quote and can step in when the book is thin.

A trading mechanism in which orders are matched whenever they arrive during the trading session: an incoming order executes immediately against compatible resting orders in the order book, so trading proceeds continuously rather than at discrete crossing times. The market never waits — the moment your order can match something in the book, it trades.

A trading mechanism in which orders are collected over a specified period and then executed simultaneously at a single price — the clearing price that maximizes the volume of matched orders. The CFTC defines a call auction as one in which traders place limit bids and offers over a specified time period and those orders are subsequently matched, in contrast to a continuously available order book. Everyone writes down what they would trade at each price; at the appointed moment, the venue picks the one price that clears the most volume and all matched orders trade at that price.

The call auction that establishes a security's official opening price at the start of regular trading, concentrating overnight and on-open orders into a single-price cross before continuous trading begins. All the demand that built up since the last close is pooled and cleared at one price, which becomes the day's official open.

The call auction that establishes a security's official closing price at the end of regular trading, pooling market-on-close, limit-on-close, and continuous-book interest into a single-price cross. One final batch trade sets the closing print that indexes, funds, and performance reports all use as the day's price.

A temporary suspension of trading in a security imposed by an exchange or regulator, triggered by events such as pending material news, order imbalances, regulatory concerns, or volatility rules; trading resumes through a reopening process, often an auction. The referee stops the game so everyone can absorb new information or so order can be restored, then restarts it with an auction.

a: Market-wide circuit breaker Volatility trading curb
x: A system of coordinated trading halts and/or price limits on equity and equity-derivative markets designed to provide a cooling-off period during large intraday market declines; the term entered regulation via the 1988 Brady Report recommendations after the October 1987 crash. In U.S. equities, market-wide circuit breakers halt all markets when the S&P 500 falls 7%, 13%, or 20% from the prior close. When the whole market falls too far too fast, everything stops for a set period so panic cannot feed on itself uninterrupted.

A U.S. National Market System plan, approved by the SEC in 2012 and made permanent in 2019, that prevents trades in NMS stocks from occurring outside specified price bands set at a percentage level above and below the average price of the security over the preceding five minutes. Each stock has a moving corridor around its recent average price; trades may not print outside the corridor, and if the quote sits at the corridor edge too long, the stock pauses.

The process by which markets incorporate information into prices through the interaction of buy and sell interest, producing transaction and quotation prices that reflect participants' aggregate assessment of value. Auctions, continuous order books, and dealer quotes are all price discovery mechanisms; opening and closing crosses are explicitly designed as price discovery facilities. Nobody sets the price — it emerges from thousands of orders colliding, each carrying someone's information and opinion.

The dispersion of trading in the same instrument across multiple competing venues — exchanges, ECNs, dark pools, and internalizing broker-dealers — rather than concentration in a single marketplace. The SEC has described current U.S. equity market structure as dispersed and complex, with volume spread among many automated trading centers. The same stock trades in a dozen different rooms at once; no single room sees all the buyers and sellers.

a: Consolidated data feed Tape SIP feed
x: A high-speed electronic system that consolidates and reports the latest price and volume data on sales of exchange-listed stocks from all trading venues into a single stream. In the U.S. NMS, Securities Information Processors (CTA and Nasdaq UTP) operate the consolidated feeds under national market system plans. One combined ticker for the whole market: no matter which venue a trade happened on, it shows up on the tape.

The U.S. regulatory framework, mandated by Congress in Section 11A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and implemented chiefly through Regulation NMS (2005), that links competing securities markets through consolidated data, order protection, and access rules. Its statutory objectives include efficient execution, fair competition among markets, price transparency, best execution, and interaction of investor orders. Congress decided stocks should trade on many competing venues but behave like one connected market, with shared prices and rules that stop your order from being filled at a worse price than displayed elsewhere.

A defined period during which a venue accepts orders and executes trades, bounded by official open and close times and often segmented into pre-market, regular, and after-hours phases. Session boundaries determine which orders are active, which prices are official, and when settlement-relevant prints occur. Markets keep office hours; the session is the window in which your orders can actually trade and the prices 'count' as official.

a: RTH Core trading session Regular session
x: The principal daily trading session of a market; for U.S. exchange-listed stocks, regular trading hours run 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Official opening and closing prices, consolidated-volume statistics, and most regulatory protections are defined over this window. The main shift: when the market is fully staffed, liquid, and protected, and when the day's official prices are set.

Extended-hours trading that occurs before the regular session opens; in U.S. equities, pre-market trading typically begins as early as 4:00 a.m. ET and runs until the 9:30 a.m. open. It is part of what regulators call extended-hours or after-hours trading — trading outside regular trading hours. The warm-up window: overnight news gets traded before the official open, but with fewer participants and wider spreads.

a: After-hours trading Post-market session Late session
x: Extended-hours trading that occurs after the regular session closes; per the SEC, after-hours trading (also called extended-hours trading) is trading outside regular trading hours, which for U.S. exchange-listed stocks end at 4:00 p.m. ET. Late sessions on U.S. equity venues typically run until 8:00 p.m. ET. Trading continues after the closing bell, letting investors react to late news, but in a thinner, jumpier market.

a: Globex session Night session Evening session
x: Trading that occurs outside a market's daytime session, spanning the evening, night, and early morning; in U.S.-based futures markets, the overnight session on CME Globex runs from the evening open (e.g., 6:30 p.m. ET) through to the next day's close, encompassing Asian and European hours. Futures markets barely sleep: after the U.S. day ends, trading hands off to Asia and Europe before the next U.S. morning.

The price range established during the initial part of a trading session — commonly the first minutes or the first hour — used by traders as a reference for the session's early balance between buyers and sellers. The concept is institutionalized in exchange terminology (trades made 'on opening' occur within the opening price range) and in intraday frameworks such as opening range breakout analysis, which are analytical conventions rather than proven predictive laws. The high and low of the first stretch of trading sketch the day's initial battle lines; traders watch what happens when price later leaves that box.

In Market Profile analysis (developed by J. Peter Steidlmayer at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s), the price range established during the first hour of the regular trading session — the first two 30-minute TPO periods — taken to represent the range set by short-term, day-timeframe traders before longer-term participants extend it. It is an analytical convention within the Market Profile framework, not a proven predictive law. The first hour's high and low mark the territory day traders carve out; whether later trading holds or breaks that range tells you whether bigger money is participating.

The standard interval between the trade date and the settlement date for a class of transactions, conventionally written T+n (trade date plus n business days). The SEC shortened the standard settlement cycle for most U.S. broker-dealer securities transactions from T+2 to T+1, effective May 28, 2024. The plumbing delay between agreeing a trade and actually exchanging cash for securities — the shorter it is, the less can go wrong in between.

The offsetting of multiple obligations between parties so that only the net balance must be settled, replacing many gross transfers with a smaller number of net payments or deliveries. Netting may be bilateral (between two parties) or multilateral (across many participants, typically at a central counterparty). If I owe you $100 and you owe me $80, we settle $20 one way instead of moving $180 around — scaled up to thousands of trades, this shrinks what actually has to move.

The legal substitution, upon clearing, of the original contract between buyer and seller with two new contracts in which the central counterparty becomes the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer. Novation replaces mutual counterparty exposure among traders with exposure to the clearinghouse. Once your trade clears, the person on the other side legally disappears — your contract is now with the clearinghouse, and so is theirs.

A securities settlement mechanism that links the transfer of securities to the transfer of funds so that delivery occurs if and only if payment occurs, eliminating principal risk — the risk of delivering securities without receiving the money, or vice versa. The shares and the cash swap hands atomically: neither side can end up having given away its asset without receiving the other side of the deal.

A foreign exchange settlement mechanism that ensures the final transfer of one currency occurs if and only if the final transfer of the countercurrency occurs, eliminating FX settlement (Herstatt) risk — the loss of the full value of a currency paid without receiving the currency bought. Both currency legs of an FX trade move simultaneously; you can never wire your dollars away and get no euros back because the other bank failed that afternoon.
A displayed or communicated offer to buy a specified quantity at a stated price. It describes the immediately available terms and ease of trading in an order-driven market.
A displayed or communicated offer to sell a specified quantity at a stated price, also called an offer. It describes the immediately available terms and ease of trading in an order-driven market.

The difference between the best available ask price and best available bid price for the same instrument and quotation conditions. It describes the immediately available terms and ease of trading in an order-driven market.

The ability to buy or sell an asset promptly in meaningful size without causing a substantial adverse price change or incurring unusually high cost. It describes the immediately available terms and ease of trading in an order-driven market.

The difference between the best (lowest) quoted offer and the best (highest) quoted bid for a security at a point in time, i.e. the round-trip cost of immediacy at displayed prices. SEC Rule 600(b)(12) of Regulation NMS defines the average quoted spread as the share-weighted average of the national best offer minus the national best bid at the time of order receipt. It measures how far apart the best standing buy and sell prices are; the narrower the gap, the cheaper it is to trade immediately in small size.

A measure of the execution cost actually paid, defined relative to the midpoint of the national best bid and offer at the time of order receipt: for buy orders, twice the difference between the execution price and the midpoint; for sell orders, twice the difference between the midpoint and the execution price (SEC Rule 600(b)(8)). It captures what a liquidity demander really paid against the pre-trade benchmark price, so price improvement inside the quotes shows up as a smaller spread.

The execution cost measure recomputed with the NBBO midpoint at a specified interval after execution rather than at order receipt: for buys, twice the execution price minus the later midpoint; for sells, twice the later midpoint minus the execution price (SEC Rule 600(b)(13)). It estimates what a liquidity provider retains after prices adjust to the trade. It separates the liquidity provider's compensation from its losses to better-informed traders: if the price moves against the provider after the trade, the realized spread shrinks below the effective spread.

The arithmetic mean of the best bid and best offer, conventionally computed from the NBBO; Regulation NMS uses the NBBO midpoint as the reference price for effective and realized spread calculations. It is the standard benchmark for the unobserved transaction-cost-free value of a security between trades. It is the neutral point splitting the spread - neither side's concession - so it serves as the default fair-value reference for measuring execution quality.

The price of the most recently reported transaction in a security. Regulation NMS defines last sale data as price and volume data associated with a transaction, and consolidated last sale information as the price, volume, and market identification of the most recent transaction report disseminated under a national market system plan. It records where the asset last changed hands - a fact about the past, not a commitment about the price at which the next trade will occur.

The highest-priced bid currently quoted for a security; at the level of a single venue it is that market's best bid, and aggregated across protected venues it forms the national best bid. Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(15) defines best bid and best offer as the highest priced bid and the lowest priced offer. It is the most any displayed buyer is currently willing to pay - the price a seller can execute against immediately, up to the quoted size.

a: best offer lowest offer inside ask
x: The lowest-priced offer currently quoted for a security; at the level of a single venue it is that market's best offer, and aggregated across protected venues it forms the national best offer. Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(15) defines best bid and best offer as the highest priced bid and the lowest priced offer. It is the least any displayed seller is currently willing to accept - the price a buyer can execute against immediately, up to the quoted size.

The highest protected bid and the lowest protected offer for an NMS stock across all national securities exchanges, calculated and disseminated on a current and continuing basis under Regulation NMS; when market centers transmit identical bids or offers, they are ranked first by size, then by time (Rule 600(b)(60)). It is the single national reference for the best available displayed prices in a fragmented market where the same stock trades on many venues.

The collection of unexecuted buy and sell orders for a security maintained by a trading venue, organized by price level and priority. Its state evolves through order book events - limit-order submissions, market orders, and cancellations - which together drive short-horizon price changes (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 2014). It is the visible queue of supply and demand waiting to trade: who wants to buy, who wants to sell, at what prices, and how much.

An order book composed of limit orders ranked by price and by a secondary priority rule (time, size, or pro rata), against which incoming marketable orders are continuously matched - the operating mechanism of a continuous double auction on modern electronic exchanges. It is a standing electronic auction: unfilled limit orders wait in line, and anyone demanding immediacy trades against the front of the opposite queue.

A market structure in which order flow in an instrument is centralized in a single transparent electronic limit order book at one venue, where a matching engine automatically matches orders to buy and sell under uniform priority rules, providing a single point of price discovery and queue priority. Instead of liquidity being scattered across many venues, every order joins one consolidated queue, so all participants see and compete in the same book.

The best bid and best offer of an order book, together with their displayed sizes - the first price level on each side. Regulation NMS treats the best bid and best offer of each venue (and the NBBO across venues) as core market data elements. It is the headline of the book: the prices at which a small market order would execute right now.

The quantities of orders displayed at price levels beyond the best bid and offer - the size available as one moves away from the inside market. Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(31) defines depth of book data as the quotation sizes at each venue at each of the next five prices below the national best bid and above the national best offer. It shows how much size the book can absorb before the price has to move a given distance.

Trading interest that is visible to the public before execution - quotations and displayed orders included in consolidated quotation data. The SEC's equity market structure concept release classifies registered exchanges and ECNs as displayed trading centers, which executed about 74.6% of NMS share volume in late 2009. It is the liquidity everyone can see quoted before deciding to trade.

a: undisplayed liquidity dark liquidity non-displayed liquidity
x: Trading interest that is available for execution at a trading center but is not included in the consolidated quotation data disseminated to the public - encompassing reserve (iceberg) size, fully undisplayed order types, dark pool matching interest, and broker-dealer internalization (SEC Concept Release on Equity Market Structure). It is liquidity you discover only by executing against it: the orders are real but not advertised in the public quotes.

The order-matching rule under which orders at a better price execute first, and among orders at the same price the earliest-submitted order executes first. CME Group's FIFO algorithm uses price and time as the only criteria for filling an order. You earn execution priority by offering a better price or by getting in line earlier.

a: pro rata pro-rata matching allocation algorithm
x: An order-matching rule that divides an incoming order among the resting orders at the best price in proportion to their sizes, subject to rounding, minimum allocations, and often top-order or FIFO components. Under CME's Pro-Rata algorithm, an order's allocation percentage equals its quantity divided by the total quantity at that price. Everyone posting at the front price gets a slice of the incoming order, sized by how much they posted.

An order-matching priority in which size influences ranking among eligible orders and time breaks or contributes to the ranking, as used in specified non-displayed venue books. It describes the immediately available terms and ease of trading in an order-driven market.

a: random selection for service lottery allocation
x: An order-matching scheme in which the resting order(s) at the eligible price selected to trade with an incoming order are chosen at random rather than by time or size priority. Exchange system documentation (e.g. Euronext/Borsa Italiana migration guides to the Optiq platform) describes a random allocation scheme applied consistently with pro rata allocation or with a minimum allocation lot, and market-design literature has proposed randomized matching as an alternative to FIFO and pro rata. Instead of rewarding the earliest or largest order, the engine holds a lottery among eligible resting orders.

One of the classical dimensions of market liquidity identified by Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002): the presence of large-volume orders such that sizable trades can be executed with only a negligible effect on prices. In microstructure it denotes order-size capacity, distinct from the technical-analysis usage (advancers versus decliners). It answers: how wide is the river - can a whale trade without making a splash?

The volume of orders available in the book at or near the best prices - the size that can be executed with only limited price concession. It is one of the liquidity dimensions catalogued by Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002), and Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014) show the price response to order-flow imbalance is inversely proportional to it. It answers: how much can I trade before my own trading moves the price against me?

The speed at which prices and order-book liquidity return toward equilibrium after a trade or shock displaces them - one of the liquidity dimensions identified by Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002), who describe resiliency as the promptness with which price impacts from transactions are corrected. It measures how fast the market heals after being hit by a large order or news.

The ability to execute a transaction promptly at or near current prices - the time dimension of market liquidity in the Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002) framework, and the service for which liquidity demanders compensate liquidity providers through the spread. It answers: how fast can I get this trade done right now, and what do I pay for that speed?

The cost dimension of market liquidity in the Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002) framework: the ability to trade at low transaction cost, conventionally measured by the narrowness of the bid-ask spread, which compensates liquidity providers for offering immediacy in executing buy and sell orders. It answers: how little do I lose by buying and immediately selling again - the tightness of the round trip.

The condition in which some market participants possess payoff-relevant information that others lack. It is the foundational friction of market microstructure theory - in Kyle (1985) prices respond to the net order flow of an informed trader, and in Glosten and Milgrom (1985) the bid-ask spread exists because the specialist cannot distinguish informed from uninformed traders. When a dealer cannot tell whether the counterparty knows something, every trade is partly a gamble - so the dealer charges everyone a premium upfront.

The risk liquidity providers bear that their counterparties are better informed, so that executed trades systematically precede price moves against the provider. In Glosten and Milgrom (1985), the specialist sets bid and ask prices that are conditional expectations of value given the trade's direction, and the spread compensates for expected losses to informed traders. If you tend to get filled exactly when you are wrong, you must charge for that tendency before it happens.

The price risk a market maker bears on positions accumulated while quoting both sides of the market, because bids and offers are hit asymmetrically before price moves. In the Ho-Stoll lineage formalized by Avellaneda-Stoikov and solved under inventory constraints by Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013), the market maker's P&L from the spread is challenged by the price risk borne on inventory. Earning the spread means repeatedly holding stock you did not choose to hold; if the price moves while you hold it, the spread income can be overwhelmed.

The net excess of demand over supply at the best bid and ask, defined by Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014) from all order book events - limit orders, market orders, and cancellations - at the best prices. They show short-horizon price changes are largely driven by this imbalance, with an approximately linear relation whose slope is inversely proportional to market depth. Prices move on the net pressure of orders arriving and leaving the inside market, not on raw trade counts.

Trade volume classified by the direction of the initiating side: positive for buyer-initiated and negative for seller-initiated trades. It is the basic input to order-flow analysis, and Hasbrouck (1991) uses signed-volume innovations to measure the information content of stock trades from their impact on subsequent quote revisions. A trade at the ask is someone choosing to buy and a trade at the bid is someone choosing to sell; adding up these signs tracks net buying or selling pressure.

The identification of which side of a transaction demanded immediacy - buyer-initiated trades execute at or near the ask, seller-initiated trades at or near the bid. Because public data record price and volume but not the aggressor, initiation is inferred by classification algorithms such as those of Lee and Ready (1991). The party who crosses the spread is the one who started the trade; initiation asks who that was.

A trade-classification heuristic that signs a trade as buyer-initiated if its price is above the previous trade price (uptick) and seller-initiated if below (downtick), carrying the sign of the last nonzero price change through zero ticks. It is one of the component rules evaluated in Lee and Ready (1991). Rising prints suggest buyers are pushing the price up; falling prints suggest sellers are pushing it down.

A trade-classification heuristic that signs trades above the prevailing quote midpoint as buyer-initiated and trades below it as seller-initiated; trades exactly at the midpoint require a tie-breaking rule such as the tick test. It is the primary component of the Lee and Ready (1991) classification procedure. Paying more than the middle of the market means you were the buyer; receiving less means you were the seller.

The standard trade-classification procedure of Lee and Ready (1991) for inferring trade direction from intraday data: sign trades by the quote rule relative to the prevailing midpoint, sign midpoint trades by the tick rule, and match trades to quotes with an allowance for trade-reporting delay. Combine quote information with tick information to make the best guess about who initiated each trade.

The frequency per unit time at which new orders of a given type or side reach a trading venue. It is a core primitive of queueing-based microstructure and market-making models - in the Avellaneda-Stoikov lineage formalized by Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013), arrival rates of liquidity-consuming orders depend on the distance of the quote from the reference price. It measures how busy the order flow is - how many new orders show up each second at each price.

The rate or fraction at which resting orders are cancelled before execution. In automated markets the large majority of displayed orders are cancelled rather than executed - the SEC notes that high-frequency liquidity providers cancel a very high percentage of their orders, and the CFTC lists cancel-to-fill ratios among the objective measures of high message rates. Most quotes are withdrawn, not traded; the cancellation rate tells you how quickly the visible book evaporates and renews.

The ratio of cancelled orders (or cancelled quantity) to executed trades over a period - a standard metric of messaging intensity. The CFTC's Technology Advisory Committee working group listed cancel-to-fill ratios among the objective forms of measurement for the recurring high message rates characteristic of high-frequency trading. It counts how many quotes die for every trade that actually prints.

The ratio of order messages (submissions, modifications, and cancellations) to executed trades, computed in count or volume terms over a period. Exchanges use it to calibrate messaging load - for example Eurex computes order-to-trade ratios per product under its Excessive System Usage Fee framework, charging fees when a participant's ratio exceeds calibrated limits. It measures how much messaging chatter a participant generates for each actual transaction.

An order's rank in the priority sequence of resting orders at its price level, which determines how much incoming volume must trade (or cancel) ahead of it before it is executed. Under FIFO matching - where, per CME Group, the first order at a price level is the first matched - position is set by arrival time and lost if the order's price is changed, quantity increased, or account changed. It is your place in line at the front of the book.

The normalized difference between the displayed size at the best bid and the best ask, a short-horizon predictor of mid-price movements: when one side of the inside market is heavier, the price tends to move toward the lighter side. It is the state variable underlying Stoikov's (2018) micro-price and relates to the order-flow imbalance of Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov. A heavy bid queue and a thin ask queue mean sellers face little resistance - the price is more likely to tick up than down.

A size-weighted price between the bid and the ask that adjusts the midpoint for the imbalance of displayed quantities; Stoikov (2018) defines the micro-price as a high-frequency estimator of the short-horizon future price and shows empirically that it predicts near-term prices better than the mid-price or the weighted mid-price. If the bid queue is heavy relative to the ask, the fair price leans toward the ask - the microprice quantifies that lean.

An execution at a price inferior to a protected quotation displayed by another trading center - Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(105) defines a trade-through as the purchase or sale of an NMS stock during regular trading hours at a price lower than a protected bid or higher than a protected offer. Rule 611 (the Order Protection Rule) requires trading centers to maintain policies reasonably designed to prevent trade-throughs. It is trading at a worse price while a better displayed price is available somewhere else in the national market system.

A market state in which the national best bid equals the national best offer, so the displayed spread is zero. Regulation NMS Rule 610(e) requires exchanges and associations to maintain rules requiring members reasonably to avoid displaying quotations that lock any protected quotation and to assure the reconciliation of locked quotations. A buyer and a seller publicly agree on price, but their quotes sit on different venues and do not automatically interact.

A market state in which the best bid exceeds the best offer, producing a negative displayed spread. Regulation NMS Rule 610(e) requires exchange rules that members reasonably avoid displaying quotations that cross protected quotations, and Rule 611(b)(4) excepts from trade-through liability executions occurring while a protected bid is priced higher than a protected offer. Someone is publicly bidding more than someone else is asking - arbitrage on its face, usually an artifact of timing rather than a real opportunity.

The time delay between a market event and a participant's ability to observe and act on it - quoted in the CFTC's automated-trading concept release from Hasbrouck and Saar as the time it takes to learn about an event (e.g., a change in the bid), generate a response, and have the exchange act on the response. It is the lag between something happening in the market and your reaction actually landing at the exchange.

The elapsed time for an order message to travel from a participant's system to the exchange matching engine and for the acknowledgment or execution response to return. The CFTC's concept release cites industry data showing roundtrip trade times on one exchange group falling from 127 milliseconds in 2004 to 4.2 milliseconds in 2011. It is the order-to-answer time: send an order, and measure how long until the exchange confirms what happened.

The placement of a firm's trading servers in or near the exchange's own data center to minimize network latency to the matching engine; the CFTC defines co-location as connectivity solutions hosted by the exchange itself, with third-party equivalents termed proximity hosting. Physically sit your computers next to the exchange's computers so your messages arrive before everyone else's.

A connection arrangement that enables a market participant, often a broker's or clearing firm's client, to transmit orders directly to a trading platform without re-entry or prior review by the intermediary's systems; per the CFTC's concept release, DMA implies the participant's order flow is not routed through its clearing firm before reaching the platform. The client's orders ride the member's connection to the exchange at wire speed, without a human or broker system touching each order first.

A form of market access in which a customer or other person trades on an exchange or alternative trading system through the use of a broker-dealer's market participant identifier. SEC Rule 15c3-5 (the Market Access Rule) requires brokers providing such access to maintain, under their direct and exclusive control, risk management controls that prevent orders exceeding pre-set credit or capital thresholds and erroneous orders. The customer trades under the sponsoring broker's name and clearing umbrella, so the broker must police every order at the gateway.

A displayed quotation that no longer reflects current market value because prices have moved without the quote being updated, leaving it executable at an obsolete price. Bartlett and McCrary analyze how such stale quotes arise and how faster traders can arbitrage them when venues or feed systems update slowly. It is yesterday's price still posted in today's market - an offer to trade at terms the quoter would no longer choose.

A quotation that appears and disappears on extremely short timescales, produced by millisecond-lived limit orders that are cancelled almost immediately. Hasbrouck and Saar document such fleeting order and quoting behavior as a hallmark of low-latency trading, and Regulation NMS Rule 611(b)(8) accommodates it via the one-second flickering-quote exception to trade-through liability. These are quotes that blink in and out faster than slower participants can react to them.

A call option is a contract that gives its buyer (holder) the right, but not the obligation, to purchase a specified quantity of an underlying asset or to enter a long futures position at a specified strike price on or before a specified expiration date. The option writer (seller) has the corresponding obligation to sell the underlying if the holder exercises. Buying a call is like paying a small fee to lock in a purchase price: if the asset rises above that price you can buy it cheap, and if it doesn't you simply walk away, losing only the fee.

A put option is a contract that gives its buyer (holder) the right, but not the obligation, to sell a specified quantity of an underlying asset at a specified strike price on or before a specified expiration date. The put writer has the corresponding obligation to buy the underlying if the holder exercises. A put works like an insurance policy on an asset: you pay a premium for the right to sell at a guaranteed price, so a price collapse no longer hurts you beyond the premium.

Moneyness is the position of an underlying asset's price relative to an option's strike price, classifying the option as in-the-money (positive intrinsic value if exercised now), at-the-money (strike equals the current price), or out-of-the-money (zero intrinsic value). It can be measured against spot or against the forward price, and quantified numerically, e.g., by log-moneyness or by the option's delta. Moneyness tells you whether an option would be worth anything if it expired right now, and roughly how much 'cushion' it has.

An in-the-money (ITM) option is an option with positive intrinsic value: a call whose strike is below the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is above it. Its premium equals intrinsic value plus any remaining time value. An ITM option is already 'winning' — exercising it immediately would capture real value, so most of its price moves one-for-one with the underlying.

An at-the-money (ATM) option is an option whose strike price equals (or is nearest to) the current price of the underlying; in forward terms (ATMF) the strike equals the forward price. An ATM option has no intrinsic value — its entire premium is time value. The ATM option is the coin-flip strike: it sits exactly at the boundary between finishing valuable and finishing worthless, which makes it the most sensitive to volatility and time.

An out-of-the-money (OTM) option is an option with no intrinsic value: a call whose strike is above the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is below it. Its premium consists entirely of time value, and it expires worthless if still OTM at expiration. An OTM option is a lottery-like claim: cheap, but it only pays if the underlying moves far enough before time runs out.

A deep in-the-money option is an option whose strike is far enough inside the money that its time value is negligible and its price moves almost one-for-one with the underlying (delta near +1 for calls, -1 for puts). 'Deep' is an informal descriptor with no fixed regulatory threshold. A deep ITM option behaves almost like a leveraged surrogate for the stock itself, with most of its value being intrinsic.

A deep out-of-the-money option is an option whose strike is far from the current underlying price, so it has no intrinsic value, a very small delta, and a premium close to zero that consists only of time value. 'Deep' is informal; no fixed threshold defines it. A deep OTM option is a cheap tail-risk ticket: it almost always expires worthless but can multiply in value during extreme moves.

An option chain is a quotation display listing all available option series for a given underlying — typically every strike and expiration for both calls and puts — together with bids, asks, last prices, volume, open interest, and often implied volatility and Greeks. The option chain is the menu of every option available on a stock or index, laid out so you can compare strikes and expirations at a glance.

An option series is the set of option contracts of the same type (all calls or all puts) on the same underlying instrument that share the same expiration date and the same strike (exercise) price — i.e., a single line of an option chain, such as 'XYZ January 100 calls'. If the option chain is the menu, a series is one specific dish: one underlying, one expiry, one strike, one side (call or put).

An option class is the set of all option contracts of the same type (calls or puts, but not both) covering the same underlying instrument — for example, all listed calls on XYZ stock across every strike and expiration. A class is the whole family of calls (or puts) on one underlying; series are the individual family members.

a: option seller option grantor option maker
x: An option writer is the party that originates (sells to open) an option contract, receiving the premium and in return accepting the obligation to sell the underlying (call) or buy it (put) if the holder exercises. The CFTC glossary also lists 'option grantor' as a synonym. The writer is like an insurance company: it collects the premium up front and must pay out if the insured event (exercise) happens.

A covered call is a position long the underlying asset and short a call option on it; the long asset 'covers' the writer's obligation to deliver if the call is exercised. It converts some upside potential into immediate premium income. You already own the stock and rent out the upside above the strike: you keep the premium, but if the stock rallies past the strike your shares get called away.

A naked (uncovered) call is a short call option position where the writer does not hold the underlying asset or an offsetting position to cover the obligation; the CFTC defines a naked option as the sale of a call or put without holding an equal and opposite position in the underlying instrument. You have sold someone the right to buy stock from you at a fixed price without owning the stock — if it soars, you must buy it at the market price to deliver, and there is no ceiling on that price.

A cash-secured put is a short put option position backed by enough cash in the account to buy the underlying at the strike price if assigned. The writer collects the premium and accepts the obligation to purchase the shares at the strike. You get paid a premium to place a limit-buy order: if the stock drops to the strike you buy it (at an effective discount of the premium), and if it doesn't you keep the premium.

A protective put is a position long the underlying asset plus a long put option on it, which sets a floor on the position's value: losses below the put strike are offset by gains in the put. It is the options-market analogue of buying insurance on a holding. You keep all the upside of owning the stock but pay a premium so that, no matter how far it falls, you can always sell at the strike price.

A married put is a protective put in which the underlying shares and the put option are purchased simultaneously as a single package, rather than the put being added to a pre-existing stock holding. The put guarantees a minimum sale price for the shares until expiration. It is buying a stock and its insurance policy on the same ticket — you know your maximum possible loss on the combined position from day one.

A collar is a position long the underlying asset, long an out-of-the-money put (the floor), and short an out-of-the-money call (the cap) on the same underlying and expiration; the call premium finances part or all of the put. It brackets the position's value between the two strikes. You give up the big upside above the call strike to pay for protection against the big downside below the put strike — outcome is 'collared' into a band.

a: long call spread call vertical debit spread
x: A bull call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate rise in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry. You buy upside participation but sell away the part above the higher strike to reduce the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.

a: short call spread call vertical credit spread
x: A bear call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays below the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (the credit) and maximum loss. You sell a call to bet the stock won't rise past your strike, and buy a higher call as a stop-loss so a rally can't hurt you beyond a known amount.

a: short put spread put vertical credit spread
x: A bull put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short put at a higher strike and a long put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays above the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (credit) and maximum loss. You sell a put betting the stock stays up, and buy a cheaper lower put as insurance so a sell-off can't cost more than a known amount.

a: long put spread put vertical debit spread
x: A bear put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long put at a higher strike and a short put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate decline in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry. You buy downside protection/participation but sell away the extreme-crash part to make the bearish bet cheaper.

a: bull call spread long call spread call vertical debit spread
x: A call debit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net debit because the lower-strike call costs more than the higher-strike call. It is synonymous with the bull call spread: a moderately bullish position with maximum gain and maximum loss both fixed at entry. You buy upside participation up to the higher strike and sell away everything above it to cut the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.

a: bear call spread short call spread call vertical credit spread
x: A call credit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net credit. It is synonymous with the bear call spread: a moderately bearish-to-neutral position whose maximum gain is the credit received and whose maximum loss is the strike width minus the credit. You sell a call betting the stock stays below your strike, and buy a higher-strike call as a built-in stop so a rally cannot hurt you beyond a known amount.

a: bear put spread long put spread put vertical debit spread
x: A put debit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long put at a higher strike and a short put at a lower strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net debit. It is synonymous with the bear put spread: a moderately bearish position with maximum gain and maximum loss both fixed at entry. You buy downside participation but sell away the extreme-crash part below the lower strike to make the bearish bet cheaper.

a: bull put spread short put spread put vertical credit spread
x: A put credit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short put at a higher strike and a long put at a lower strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net credit. It is synonymous with the bull put spread: a moderately bullish-to-neutral position whose maximum gain is the credit and whose maximum loss is the strike width minus the credit. You sell a put betting the stock stays above your strike, and buy a cheaper lower-strike put as insurance so a sell-off cannot cost more than a known amount.

A long straddle is the simultaneous purchase of a call and a put on the same underlying, at the same strike price (typically at-the-money) and the same expiration date. The position profits if the underlying moves far enough in either direction to overcome the combined premium paid. You are buying a big move without picking a direction: if the stock swings hard either way one leg pays off, and if it goes nowhere both legs decay.

A short straddle is the simultaneous sale of a call and a put on the same underlying, at the same strike price and the same expiration date, collecting both premiums. It profits most if the underlying finishes exactly at the strike and exposes the seller to unlimited loss above the strike and large loss below it. You are selling a big move: you keep both premiums if the stock goes nowhere, but a large swing in either direction costs you point-for-point past the breakevens.

A long strangle is the simultaneous purchase of an out-of-the-money put (lower strike) and an out-of-the-money call (higher strike) on the same underlying with the same expiration date. It is cheaper than a long straddle but requires a larger move in either direction to profit. You buy a cheaper ticket on a big move: the strikes are further apart so you pay less, but the stock has to travel further before either leg has value.

A short strangle is the simultaneous sale of an out-of-the-money put (lower strike) and an out-of-the-money call (higher strike) on the same underlying with the same expiration date, collecting both premiums. It profits if the underlying stays between the strikes and carries unlimited loss above the call strike and large loss below the put strike. You sell insurance on both tails at once: you win small credits repeatedly as long as the stock stays in a range, but a breakout in either direction hurts.

An iron condor is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining an out-of-the-money bull put spread (long lower put, short higher put) and an out-of-the-money bear call spread (short lower call, long higher call), all at four different strikes. The standard ('short') iron condor is entered for a net credit and profits maximally when the underlying finishes between the two short strikes. It is a short strangle with the tails cut off: you sell options on both sides of the market but buy further-out options as wings, so your worst case is fixed.

A reverse iron condor (long iron condor) is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining a bear put spread (long higher put, short lower put) and a bull call spread (long lower call, short higher call) — the mirror image of the standard iron condor, entered for a net debit. It profits when the underlying moves beyond either of the long inner strikes, with both maximum gain and loss fixed. It is a long strangle with the far tails sold off: you pay a smaller debit for a big-move bet, accepting a capped payoff instead of unlimited upside.

An iron butterfly is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining a short straddle at the middle strike (short call and short put at the same strike) with a long out-of-the-money strangle as wings (long lower-strike put, long higher-strike call). Entered for a net credit, it reaches maximum profit when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike. It is a short straddle with wings: you sell the at-the-money call and put for a large credit, then buy cheap far-out options to cap the damage if the stock runs.

A long call butterfly is a three-strike, same-expiration spread built from calls only: long one call at a lower strike, short two calls at a middle strike, and long one call at a higher strike, with the middle strike equidistant from the wings. Entered for a small net debit, it reaches maximum value when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike. You are buying a target: a cheap bet that the stock will land near the middle strike at expiration, with the wings defining your worst case.

A long put butterfly is a three-strike, same-expiration spread built from puts only: long one put at a higher strike, short two puts at a middle strike, and long one put at a lower strike, with the middle strike equidistant from the wings. Entered for a small net debit, its expiration payoff matches the long call butterfly at the same strikes, peaking when the underlying finishes at the middle strike. The same target bet as the call butterfly, assembled from puts instead — by put-call parity the two structures are economically equivalent at identical strikes.

A broken-wing butterfly is a butterfly variant in which the distances between the middle strike and the two wing strikes are unequal — typically the far wing is placed further away (or a strike is skipped), skewing the payoff so that risk is reduced or eliminated on one side at the cost of added exposure on the other. It is a butterfly bent out of symmetry: you give up the balanced payoff to create a trade that can profit, or at least not lose, on the side you fear less.

A calendar spread is the simultaneous sale of an option at a given strike with a nearer expiration and purchase of the same type of option at the same strike with a later expiration, on the same underlying, entered for a net debit. The long calendar profits if the underlying is near the strike when the short leg expires, exploiting the faster time decay of the near-dated option. You sell the fast-decaying front month and buy the slow-decaying back month at the same strike, harvesting the difference in decay if the stock stays put.

A diagonal spread is a spread between two calls or two puts on the same underlying that differ in both strike price and expiration date — typically long a longer-dated option at one strike and short a shorter-dated option at a different strike. It combines the directional character of a vertical spread with the time-decay differential of a calendar spread. It is a calendar spread tilted with a directional view: the different strikes add a bullish or bearish lean to the front-month decay harvest.

A ratio spread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are sold than bought at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, long one call at a lower strike and short two calls at a higher strike. The extra short option(s) leave part of the position uncovered, giving the spread undefined or large risk beyond the short strikes. You finance a directional option purchase by selling two further-out options instead of one — cheap or free to enter, but the second short option is naked and can hurt badly in a big move.

A backspread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are bought than sold at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, short one call at a lower strike and long two calls at a higher strike. It is the converse of the ratio spread: the CFTC glossary describes it as a delta-neutral ratio spread in which more options are bought than sold, benefiting from an increase in volatility. You sell one near option to finance two further-out options, creating a position that loses a little in a quiet market but pays off disproportionately in a large directional move.

A jade lizard is a retail-coined, three-leg strategy with one expiration: short an out-of-the-money put and short an out-of-the-money call spread (short a call, long a further OTM call), structured so the total credit collected exceeds the width of the call spread. That sizing condition eliminates upside risk in theory, leaving the naked short put as the only source of loss. It is a short strangle with the upside tail capped: you collect premium on both sides, and if the call-spread credit is wide enough, even a runaway rally cannot lose money — only a sell-off can.

A big lizard is a retail-coined, three-leg strategy with one expiration: short an at-the-money straddle (short call and short put at the same strike) plus long a further out-of-the-money call as an upside wing, sized so the total credit exceeds the width between the straddle strike and the long call. It is the straddle-based analogue of the jade lizard, leaving the naked short put as the only source of loss. It is a short straddle with the upside tail capped: you collect a large ATM premium, and if the credit exceeds the call wing's width, a rally cannot lose in theory — only a sell-off can.
