Stocks that went up over roughly the past year (skipping the most recent month) have tended to keep outperforming recent losers for a while - the factor trades that continuation.

a: QMJ Quality Minus Junk profitability factor
x: A stock factor that is long high-quality stocks - companies that are profitable, growing, safe, and well managed - and short low-quality 'junk' stocks; Asness, Frazzini, and Pedersen formalize it as the Quality Minus Junk (QMJ) factor, with the Fama-French profitability factor RMW being a closely related construction. All else equal, the market underprices boring excellence: profitable, stable firms have historically delivered high risk-adjusted returns relative to their struggling counterparts.

a: low-beta anomaly betting against beta BAB low-risk anomaly
x: A factor built on the empirical finding that low-beta and low-volatility stocks have historically earned higher risk-adjusted returns than the CAPM predicts - the security market line is empirically too flat - formalized by Frazzini and Pedersen as the Betting Against Beta (BAB) factor, which goes long leveraged low-beta assets and short de-leveraged high-beta assets. Risky stocks don't pay as much per unit of risk as theory says they should, so tilting toward calm stocks has historically improved Sharpe ratios.

A cross-asset factor based on an asset's carry, defined by Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, and Vrugt as its expected return assuming that market conditions, including its price, stay the same; carry strategies go long high-carry and short low-carry securities across global equities, bonds, currencies, commodities, and other markets. Carry is what you earn if nothing changes: the coupon, the yield differential, the futures roll-down - the 'getting paid to wait' component of return.

a: TERM term premium factor maturity factor
x: One of the two bond-market factors in Fama and French (1993), capturing maturity risk: TERM is the difference between the return on long-term government bonds and the return on short-term risk-free instruments (the one-month Treasury bill rate), proxying the term premium for bearing interest-rate risk. Long bonds swing more when rates move, and investors historically demanded extra return for that - TERM measures that extra return month by month.

a: DEF default factor default premium factor credit premium
x: One of the two bond-market factors in Fama and French (1993), capturing default risk: DEF is the difference between the return on long-term corporate bonds and the return on long-term government bonds, proxying the compensation for bearing corporate default risk. Corporate bonds pay more than Treasuries because they can default; DEF measures, each period, how much that credit exposure actually earned or lost.

a: liquidity risk factor Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity factor traded liquidity factor
x: A factor capturing exposure to market-wide liquidity fluctuations: Pastor and Stambaugh (2003) show that stocks whose returns are more sensitive to innovations in aggregate liquidity earn higher expected returns, so liquidity risk is a priced state variable beyond market, size, value, and momentum exposures. Stocks that fall hardest when market liquidity dries up are unpleasant to hold, so investors demand a premium for owning them - that premium is the liquidity factor's return.

A model that relates an asset's return linearly to a limited number of common factors plus an asset-specific residual, used to decompose returns, estimate expected returns, and build covariance matrices with far fewer parameters than direct estimation. Instead of tracking how every pair of thousands of assets moves together, you describe each asset by how it responds to a handful of shared drivers - the rest is treated as idiosyncratic noise.

a: market model single-factor model Sharpe's diagonal model
x: The simplest factor model, in which each asset's return is related to a single common factor - typically the return on a market index - plus an asset-specific residual; introduced by Sharpe (1963) as a simplified model for portfolio analysis that drastically cuts the number of estimates needed for covariance-based optimization. Assume everything moves together only because everything moves with the market; then you only need each stock's beta to rebuild the whole covariance matrix.

An empirical asset-pricing model from Fama and French (1993, 'Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds') that explains stock returns with three factors: the market excess return (Rm-Rf), the size factor SMB, and the value factor HML. How a stock moves is largely explained by three dials: how the whole market did, how small caps did relative to big caps, and how cheap (high book-to-market) stocks did relative to expensive ones.

An extension of the Fama-French three-factor model (Fama and French 2015, 'A Five-Factor Asset Pricing Model') that adds a profitability factor, RMW (robust minus weak operating profitability), and an investment factor, CMA (conservative minus aggressive asset growth), to the market, size, and value factors. Beyond market, size, and value, two more dials matter: profitable firms tend to beat unprofitable ones, and firms that invest conservatively tend to beat firms that expand aggressively.

An extension of the Fama-French three-factor model introduced by Mark Carhart (1997, 'On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance') that adds a momentum factor - long stocks with high prior 2-12 month returns and short those with low prior returns - to the market, size, and value factors. To judge a fund fairly you must also control for whether it was simply riding recent winners, because momentum explains much of what looked like persistent skill.

a: risk parity equal risk contribution ERC
x: A portfolio construction approach that allocates risk rather than capital: each asset, asset class, or strategy is assigned a budget for its contribution to total portfolio risk, and weights are solved so realized risk contributions match those budgets; the special case of equal budgets for all assets is the risk-parity (equal risk contribution) portfolio. Instead of deciding '60% of my money in stocks', you decide 'stocks may consume at most 60% of my total risk' - because equal dollars in stocks and bonds produce wildly unequal risk.

a: volatility targeting vol targeting volatility management
x: A position-sizing technique that adjusts exposure inversely to recent volatility - leveraging up when volatility is low and scaling down when it is high - so the portfolio targets a roughly constant level of volatility rather than a constant notional exposure. Because vol clusters (calm follows calm, storm follows storm), you can keep risk steadier by trading smaller when markets are stormy and larger when they are calm.

a: correlations go to one correlation asymmetry crisis correlation
x: The empirically documented tendency for correlations between markets and assets to rise sharply in bear markets and crises - but not in bull markets - so that diversification benefits shrink precisely when they are most needed; Longin and Solnik (2001) established the asymmetry formally using extreme value theory. In a panic, everything sells off together: the low correlations that justified your diversification in calm times evaporate in the crash.

The ratio of the size of the position taken in a hedging instrument (e.g., futures contracts) to the size of the exposure being hedged; it determines how much of the price risk is offset by the hedge. It is the proportionality dial on a hedge: ratio 1.0 means you hedge dollar-for-dollar; 0.6 means you take a hedge position only 60% as large as your exposure.

The hedge ratio that minimizes the variance of the value of the hedged position, equal to the correlation between spot-price changes and futures-price changes times the ratio of their standard deviations; equivalently, the slope of the best-fit regression of spot-price changes on futures-price changes. It is the hedge size that makes your combined position wobble the least, given how tightly the hedge instrument actually tracks your exposure.

A hedge in which the asset giving rise to the hedger's exposure differs from the asset underlying the futures (or other derivative) contract used for hedging, employed when no suitable contract exists on the exposure itself. If you can't buy insurance on the exact thing you own, you insure something that tends to move with it - imperfectly.

An options-hedging technique that offsets a position's delta - the theoretical sensitivity of the option's premium to a $1 move in the underlying - by taking an opposing position in the underlying, so the total position is approximately insensitive to small price moves. If your option gains $0.50 when the stock rises $1, shorting half a share per option makes the combined position roughly flat for small moves.

An options-hedging technique that neutralizes a position's gamma - the rate at which delta changes per $1 move in the underlying - so that the delta hedge remains effective for larger price moves without constant rebalancing. Gamma is how fast your delta hedge goes stale; hedging gamma keeps the hedge from drifting out of alignment every time the underlying moves.

An options-hedging technique that neutralizes a position's vega - the change in option premium for a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility - so the book is insulated from shifts in the market's volatility expectations. Options get more expensive when expected volatility rises, even if prices don't move; a vega hedge makes your position indifferent to that repricing.

A fixed-income hedging technique that sizes an interest-rate futures (or bond) position so that the dollar sensitivity of the hedge to a small parallel yield change offsets the dollar duration of the portfolio being hedged. If your bond portfolio loses $X when yields rise 1 basis point, you short enough futures to gain $X on that same move - matching sensitivities rather than face values.

The general direction in which a security's price is traveling, inferred from the direction of successive peaks and troughs on a chart. Classical technical analysis, following Dow Theory, classifies trends as up, down, or sideways and by duration (primary, secondary, minor); it is an analytical framework for describing price behavior, not a proven predictive law. Prices rarely move in straight lines — they zigzag. The trend is simply the direction in which those zigzags lean.

A trend characterized by a series of ascending peaks and troughs — successively higher highs and higher lows. It is the classical chart-based description of sustained demand exceeding supply; an analytical construct, not evidence that prices must keep rising. Each rally carries price further than the last, and each dip stops at a higher floor — a staircase climbing upward.

A trend characterized by a series of descending peaks and troughs — successively lower highs and lower lows. It is the classical chart-based description of sustained supply exceeding demand; an analytical construct, not evidence that prices must keep falling. Each rally stalls lower than the last and each drop breaks to a new floor — a staircase descending.

a: ranging market horizontal trend flat market
x: A market state in which prices oscillate within a horizontal band with roughly equal peaks and troughs, reflecting a balance between supply and demand rather than directional movement. Also described as consolidation or a ranging market; a descriptive label for price behavior, not a forecast. Buyers and sellers are evenly matched, so price ping-pongs between an upper and a lower boundary.

A relatively tight horizontal price band, bounded by support below and resistance above, within which prices move while supply and demand are roughly balanced. In classical chart analysis a break of either boundary is taken as evidence that one side has gained control — a heuristic, not a law. A tug-of-war zone: neither bulls nor bears can push price out of the box, until suddenly one side wins.

A local price peak — a high flanked by lower highs on either side — marking the point where an advance stalled and turned down. Swing highs (peaks) and swing lows (troughs) are the basic building blocks from which trend direction is read in classical technical analysis. The top of one 'zig' before the market 'zags' back down.

A local price trough — a low flanked by higher lows on either side — marking the point where a decline stalled and turned up. Swing lows (troughs), together with swing highs, form the price structure from which trend direction is read. The bottom of one 'zag' before the market 'zigs' back up.

A swing high that exceeds the previous swing high. A sequence of higher highs combined with higher lows is the classical structural definition of an uptrend. Each upward push reaches new territory, showing buyers keep gaining ground.

A swing low that forms above the previous swing low. Together with higher highs, a sequence of higher lows constitutes the structural definition of an uptrend and shows declining selling pressure on pullbacks. Each dip finds buyers sooner than the last — the floor keeps rising.

A swing high that forms below the previous swing high. Together with lower lows, a sequence of lower highs constitutes the structural definition of a downtrend and shows weakening buying pressure on rallies. Each bounce runs out of energy sooner than the last — the ceiling keeps sinking.

A swing low that breaks below the previous swing low. Together with lower highs, a sequence of lower lows constitutes the structural definition of a downtrend. Each drop undercuts the last floor, showing sellers keep gaining ground.

A price level or zone at which demand is thought to be strong enough to prevent the price from declining further. It is a core hypothesis of technical analysis about where buying interest concentrates, not a guaranteed floor. As price gets cheaper, buyers become more willing to buy and sellers less willing to sell, so declines tend to pause there.

A price level or zone at which selling is thought to be strong enough to prevent the price from rising further. It is a core hypothesis of technical analysis about where supply concentrates, not a guaranteed ceiling. As price gets more expensive, sellers become more willing to sell and buyers less willing to buy, so rallies tend to stall there.

A price move above an established resistance level, range boundary, or chart-pattern upper boundary. In classical chart analysis a breakout is interpreted as evidence that demand has overcome supply at that level; it is an analytical reading, and a meaningful fraction of breakouts fail. Price finally escapes the ceiling that had been capping it, suggesting buyers are now willing to pay more than before.

A price move below an established support level, range boundary, or chart-pattern lower boundary. In classical chart analysis a breakdown is interpreted as evidence that supply has overcome demand at that level; an analytical reading, not a certainty of further declines. The floor that had been holding price up gives way, showing sellers are now willing to accept lower prices.

a: failed breakout bull trap bear trap fakeout
x: A breakout (or breakdown) that fails to hold: price moves beyond a watched level but cannot sustain itself there and closes back inside the prior range. It is the classical-TA label for a failed break; Smart Money Concepts frames the same event as a liquidity sweep. Price teases a move out of the box, luring in breakout traders, then snaps back inside — trapping them on the wrong side.

The return of price to a level it has just broken, testing whether the old barrier now acts as the opposite kind — broken resistance as new support, or broken support as new resistance (the polarity principle). A successful retest is treated as confirmation of the break; a failed one warns of a false breakout. After escaping the box, price comes back to check whether the old wall now works as a floor (or ceiling) from the other side.

A temporary counter-move against the prevailing trend — typically shallow and short-lived — after which the prior trend resumes. It is an interpretive label: whether a counter-move is a pullback or the start of a reversal is knowable only in hindsight. The trend takes a breather: some traders take profits, price slips a little, then the main move continues.

A period of sustained price increases over days to months. Rallies occur within both bull and bear markets; a rise within a dominant downtrend is a bear market rally — a counter-trend advance, not necessarily the start of a recovery. A stretch where buyers dominate and prices climb, whether as the main trend or as a pause inside a larger decline.

A counter-trend decline within a prevailing uptrend, conventionally defined at the index level as a fall of 10% or more from the recent peak (but less than the 20% associated with a bear market). It is a descriptive, magnitude-based label applied to price action, not a forecast of what follows. The market takes a meaningful step back inside a larger climb — deeper than a pullback, but short of a bear market.

A temporary reversal within a larger trend that gives back only part of the prior move before the trend resumes. The term is magnitude-focused — how much of the prior leg was retraced — and is usually measured in percentages (e.g., Fibonacci levels); it describes structure, not a prediction of resumption. The market gives back a slice of what it just gained, then carries on — the question is always how big the slice will be.

A durable change in the direction of the prevailing trend — an uptrend turning into a downtrend or vice versa — as opposed to a temporary counter-move. In chart analysis, reversals are confirmed through structure (broken swing sequences, broken trendlines, completed reversal patterns), and only after the fact with certainty. The tide actually turns: what was a staircase up becomes a staircase down.

The resumption of the prevailing trend after a pause, pullback, or consolidation. In classical chart analysis, continuation is the default expectation associated with congestion patterns and mid-trend gaps — a probabilistic heuristic, not a law. The trend catches its breath and then keeps going in the same direction.

A period during which price moves sideways within a relatively contained range after a prior move, reflecting a temporary balance between buyers and sellers. Consolidations are read as pauses that can resolve into either continuation or reversal; the label describes the pause, not its outcome. After running, the market rests — price churns in a band while both sides regroup.

A progressive narrowing of price swings and trading ranges, reflecting falling volatility as buyers and sellers reach a temporary equilibrium. In volatility-based frameworks (e.g., Bollinger Bands), compression is associated with the 'squeeze' state that often — but not reliably — precedes a directional expansion. Price action coils like a spring: swings get smaller and smaller until the stored energy releases in a sharp move.

a: range expansion volatility expansion (synonym in price-action usage)
x: A broadening of price swings and bar ranges, reflecting rising volatility as one side of the market gains decisive control. It is the counterpart of compression and typically accompanies breakouts, breakdowns, and trend acceleration. The coiled spring releases: small quiet bars give way to large directional ones.

a: volatility squeeze VCP (volatility contraction pattern, Minervini usage)
x: A measurable decline in price volatility — shrinking bar ranges, falling standard deviation, narrowing volatility bands — typically during consolidation. Frameworks such as Bollinger's squeeze treat contraction as a precondition that often precedes a volatility expansion, a statistical tendency rather than a law. The market goes quiet: each day's high-low span shrinks as price compresses into a tighter and tighter zone.

A measurable increase in price volatility — widening bar ranges, rising standard deviation, expanding volatility bands — typically accompanying breakouts and trend legs. It is the mirror of volatility contraction and marks regimes where price travels further per unit time. The quiet market wakes up: bars get longer and price starts covering ground fast.

A blank space on a price chart where no trading occurred between two consecutive bars — typically when the open of one session is entirely above the prior session's high (up gap) or below its low (down gap). Gaps are classified (common, breakaway, runaway, exhaustion) by location and context; the classifications are interpretive, not mechanical laws. Overnight news or sentiment shifts the supply-demand balance so much that the market has to reopen at a different price entirely, skipping the levels in between.

A gap in which a session's low is higher than the previous session's high, leaving an untraded void below the new session's range. Generally read as a sign of strong buying interest; its analytical meaning depends on where in the trend or pattern it occurs. Demand overwhelmed supply overnight, so the market had to reopen above yesterday's entire trading range.

A gap in which a session's high is lower than the previous session's low, leaving an untraded void above the new session's range. Generally read as a sign of strong selling pressure; its analytical meaning depends on where in the trend or pattern it occurs. Supply overwhelmed demand overnight, so the market had to reopen below yesterday's entire trading range.

A gap occurring near the end of an extended up or down move, typically on very high volume and a large price jump, interpreted as the final surge of euphoria or panic before the move ends. The label is only assignable with confidence in hindsight, since at the time it can be indistinguishable from a runaway gap. The last burst of FOMO buying (or panic selling) — the crowd all rushes in at once, and then there is nobody left to push further.

A gap that occurs as price breaks out of a trading range or congestion area, interpreted as marking the start of a new directional move. Breakaway gaps are conventionally expected NOT to be filled soon, distinguishing them from common gaps; the classification remains an interpretive heuristic. The market escapes its cage in one jump — enthusiasm is so strong that price skips the boundary levels entirely.

A gap occurring in the middle of an established trend, driven by a sudden surge of interest (or liquidation) in the trend's direction, and interpreted as evidence the trend is accelerating rather than ending. Also called a measuring gap, from the heuristic that it tends to appear roughly halfway through a move. Traders who waited for a pullback give up waiting and pile in all at once, gapping price further along the trend.

A small, uneventful gap occurring within a trading range or congestion area, typically on low volume (e.g., around ex-dividend dates), with no trend significance. Common gaps are usually filled quickly. A mundane hiccup in an already quiet market — price skips a few ticks and nobody much cares.

a: trend line up trendline / down trendline
x: A straight line drawn on a chart connecting two or more price points and extended forward, used to visualize a trend and to act as a dynamic reference for support (up trendline, connecting rising lows) or resistance (down trendline, connecting falling highs). It is a discretionary drawing tool, not an objective market feature. Connect the dots of the trend's pullbacks, and the resulting line sketches the trend's natural floor (or ceiling).

A chart structure formed by two parallel trendlines that enclose price action: a primary trendline along the trend's pullbacks and a parallel channel (return) line along the opposite swings. Channels frame trend direction plus likely reaction zones; they are descriptive constructs, not predictive guarantees. Price travels between two parallel rails — one rail supports it, the other caps it — until it jumps the track.

A channel whose two parallel boundary lines slope upward, enclosing an uptrend's higher highs and higher lows. The lower (support) line connects rising lows and the parallel upper (resistance) line caps the rallies; classically read as trend-consistent structure until broken. An uptrend with guardrails: each dip bounces off the lower rail, each push fades near the upper rail.

A channel whose two parallel boundary lines slope downward, enclosing a downtrend's lower highs and lower lows. The upper (resistance) line connects falling highs and the parallel lower (support) line floors the declines; classically read as trend-consistent structure until broken. A downtrend with guardrails: each bounce dies at the upper rail, each drop finds footing near the lower rail.

A channel whose two parallel boundary lines are roughly horizontal, enclosing a sideways market: resistance above and support below at approximately constant prices. It represents consolidation or indecision and is the channel equivalent of a trading range. Price bounces between a flat floor and a flat ceiling while the market makes up its mind.

A charting technique that marks horizontal levels at percentages of a prior price swing — conventionally 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, and 78.6% (ratios derived from the Fibonacci sequence, except 50%, a Dow Theory convention) — as candidate support/resistance zones for a counter-trend move. It is an analytical framework with no established predictive validity on its own. If trends tend to give back part of a move before resuming, these ratios are the conventional yardsticks for how much.

A charting technique that projects levels beyond the prior swing — conventionally 100%, 161.8%, and 261.8% of the measured move — as candidate profit-target or exhaustion zones once the trend resumes. Like retracements, it is an analytical convention, not a validated forecasting law. If the retracement yardstick measures how far price pulls back, the extension yardstick guesses how far the next leg might reach.

a: floor trader pivot standard pivot point PP
x: A calculated price level derived from the prior period's high, low, and close, used to frame the current period's directional bias and to derive support/resistance levels. Originating with floor traders, pivot points are deterministic calculations; their use as turning-point levels is a convention, not a validated edge. Yesterday's average price becomes today's line in the sand: above it leans bullish, below it leans bearish.

A pivot point computed from the previous trading day's high, low, and close, applied to the current day's trading — the original floor-trader usage. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 1- to 15-minute intraday charts use the prior day's data and remain fixed all day. Yesterday's H/L/C distill into today's map of where buyers and sellers are expected to contest control.

A pivot point computed from the previous calendar week's high, low, and close, applied to the current week. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 30- to 120-minute charts use the prior week's data and remain fixed for the entire week. Last week's price action condenses into this week's bias line and outer reference levels.

A pivot point computed from the previous month's high, low, and close, applied to the current month. On StockCharts' convention, pivots displayed on daily charts use the prior month's data and remain fixed for the whole month (weekly and monthly charts use the prior year's data). Last month's range and close set this month's reference grid for where longer-term buyers and sellers may engage.

In price-structure analysis, a break of the swing sequence defining the current trend: in an uptrend, a close below the most recent higher low (or, in continuation terms, a close above the prior swing high that extends the structure). SMC/ICT usage distinguishes a trend-continuing break of structure from a counter-trend structure shift; the terminology is a discretionary convention without a single canonical authority. The market's staircase pattern breaks a step — the rhythm of higher floors or lower ceilings is violated, so the structure may be changing.

In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the first structural break against the prevailing trend — e.g., in an uptrend, the first close below a higher low — read as an early signal that order flow may be shifting. It is the counter-trend counterpart of a trend-continuing break of structure; a discretionary convention with no canonical authority. The first crack in the trend's rhythm: the market does something it hasn't been doing, hinting the character of the move is changing.

a: stop hunt stop run grab purge raid
x: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a run through a level where resting orders cluster — stop-losses and breakout entries just beyond an obvious high or low — followed by failure to hold beyond it: price trades through, fills those orders, and closes back inside the prior range. The same chart event is called a false breakout in classical TA; 'sweep' adds an interpretation (order collection) that a chart cannot prove. Price pokes through an obvious level, triggers the crowd's stops, then snaps back — the level was the target of the move, not an obstacle in its way.

a: stop hunt running the stops stop raid
x: A move that pushes price through a level where stop-loss orders are known or presumed to cluster, triggering them, often followed by a quick reversal. In SMC vocabulary this is the liquidity sweep; in classical terms it overlaps with the false breakout. The deliberate-targeting framing is an inference, not an observable fact. Obvious levels have crowds of stops parked behind them; a push through sets off that cascade in one quick burst.

a: supply area drop-base-drop / rally-base-drop zone (formation names)
x: A price band marking the base from which a strong decline launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive drop. It is treated as potential resistance on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled sell interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical resistance. Price paused, then fell out of bed; the pause zone is where sellers were last in control, so the first return there may meet them again.

a: demand area rally-base-rally / drop-base-rally zone (formation names)
x: A price band marking the base from which a strong advance launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive rally. It is treated as potential support on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled buy interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical support. Price paused, then took off upward; the pause zone is where buyers were last in control, so the first return there may attract them again.

In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the last opposite-direction candle (or consecutive cluster of them) before an impulsive move — the final down candle before a rally (bullish) or the final up candle before a decline (bearish) — marked as a zone that may be defended on a return. It is read as the footprint of institutional position-building; that reading is an interpretation, since the candle alone shows only price, not orders. The last place price sat before the big move launched is treated as the move's origin — and origins are where defenders may remain.

In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a three-candle pattern in which the middle candle's range does not overlap with the wicks of its neighbors — the low of the third candle sits above the high of the first (bullish FVG), or the high of the third sits below the low of the first (bearish FVG) — leaving a span price crossed in a single fast pass. It is read as an inefficiency that price may later revisit; that expectation is a hypothesis, not an established regularity. The middle candle moved so fast that a slice of prices was skipped; the gap marks the skipped slice.

A chart region where price moved so quickly in one direction that little two-sided trading occurred — operationalized in SMC/ICT practice chiefly as the fair value gap, the three-candle non-overlap span. The zone is hypothesized to attract a later revisit ('rebalancing'); the hypothesis is discretionary and unproven. A one-sided stampede leaves thin ice on the chart — a stretch where almost no business was done.

In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the upper half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything above the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in premium as poor value and shorts in premium as acceptable value; it is a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure. Split the range in half; buying in the top half means paying up relative to where the market has just been.

In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the lower half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything below the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in discount as acceptable value and shorts in discount as poor value; a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure. Split the range in half; buying in the bottom half means paying less than the range's typical price.

a: equilibrium 50% level consequent encroachment (when applied to a gap) dealing range midpoint
x: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the 50% midpoint of a dealing range (a significant swing low to swing high), separating the premium half above from the discount half below. It serves as the reference for the methodology's value heuristic; outside SMC, a 50% midpoint is simply the midpoint of a range (also a Dow Theory retracement convention). The range's center of gravity: above it price is relatively expensive, below it relatively cheap, within that range.

The study of how emotions, cognitive biases, and mental processes affect trading decisions and performance, and the applied discipline of managing those factors. It is a core topic of behavioral finance, which documents systematic, predictable departures from the rational-agent model of traditional finance. Two traders with the same strategy get different results because fear, greed, and bias change what they actually do. Trading psychology is about understanding and managing that human layer.

The empirically documented tendency for losses to be psychologically weighted more heavily than equivalent gains relative to a reference point; in Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory the value function is steeper for losses than for gains. It is a component of prospect theory and is distinct from rational risk aversion. Losing $100 hurts roughly twice as much as winning $100 feels good, so people go to disproportionate lengths to avoid realizing losses.

A descriptive model of decision making under risk developed by Kahneman and Tversky (1979) as a critique of expected utility theory, in which people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point and weight probabilities by a subjective decision-weighting function. It predicts risk aversion over gains, risk seeking over losses (the reflection effect), and overweighting of small probabilities. People do not think in terms of final wealth; they think in wins and losses from where they stand now, and they treat 'almost certain' very differently from 'certain'.

The empirically documented tendency of investors to sell winning positions too early and hold losing positions too long, named by Shefrin and Statman (1985) and confirmed in brokerage-account data by Odean (1998). It is a descriptive behavioral pattern, explained in part by prospect theory, mental accounting, and regret avoidance. Traders cash in winners quickly to enjoy the win, but let losers run because selling would mean admitting a mistake.

A cognitive bias in which subjective confidence in one's judgments reliably exceeds their objective accuracy, appearing as overestimation of one's own performance, overplacement relative to others, or overprecision of beliefs. In markets it is linked empirically to excessive trading volume and to the underperformance of the most active individual traders. Traders systematically think their forecasts are better than they are - when they say 90% sure, they are right far less than 90% of the time.

The tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in ways that confirm one's preexisting beliefs or hypotheses while discounting disconfirming evidence. Documented experimentally since Wason's 1960s work, it operates through biased search, biased interpretation, and biased recall, and is strongest for emotionally charged or deeply held beliefs. Once a trader decides the market is going up, every headline starts looking bullish and bearish evidence gets explained away.

A cognitive bias that assigns disproportionate weight to recent events over older ones when forming judgments or forecasts, related to the recency effect in memory research. In markets it manifests as extrapolating the latest trend, returns, or volatility into the future at the expense of long-run base rates. After three green months it feels like the market only goes up; after a crash it feels like it will never recover.

The tendency for judgments and estimates to be biased toward an initially encountered reference value (the anchor), even when it is arbitrary or irrelevant, introduced as a heuristic by Tversky and Kahneman (1974). Adjustments away from the anchor are typically insufficient, so final estimates cluster near it. The first number you hear - a purchase price, a 52-week high, an analyst target - quietly drags every later estimate toward itself.

A mental shortcut, identified by Tversky and Kahneman (1973), in which the judged frequency or probability of an event depends on how easily instances come to mind rather than on actual base rates. Ease of recall - driven by recency, vividness, emotion, and media exposure - substitutes for statistical reasoning. If you can picture it quickly, you think it is common; after a week of crash headlines, a crash feels imminent.

The tendency, after an outcome is known, to perceive the event as having been more predictable than it actually was, first demonstrated experimentally by Fischhoff (1975). It distorts memory of prior beliefs, inflates confidence in one's forecasting ability, and degrades the quality of performance review. After the market sells off, everyone saw it coming - but almost nobody acted on it beforehand.

The error of evaluating the quality of a decision by its realized outcome rather than by the information and reasoning available when the decision was made, demonstrated by Baron and Hershey (1988). Identical decisions are rated better when they happen to end well and worse when they end badly, even when outcomes are driven by chance. A reckless trade that made money gets praised; a disciplined trade that lost gets criticized - same process, different luck.

a: Monte Carlo fallacy Fallacy of the maturity of chances
x: The mistaken belief that, for independent random events, a run of one outcome makes the opposite outcome more likely next - as if chance had a memory and streaks must even out. Tversky and Kahneman traced it to the representativeness heuristic and the erroneous 'law of small numbers'. After five reds at roulette, black feels due - but the wheel has no memory and the odds are unchanged.

The belief that a person or process enjoying a run of successes has an elevated probability of continued success - the 'hot hand'. Gilovich, Tversky and Vallone (1985) found basketball shooting streaks consistent with chance, but Miller and Sanjurjo later showed the original statistical test was itself biased, so the existence of genuine streaks remains contested. After three winning trades in a row a trader feels in the zone and sizes up - as if success itself were contagious.

The tendency to continue an endeavor because of previously invested, unrecoverable resources - money, time, or effort - even when prospective costs exceed prospective benefits. Rational choice requires ignoring sunk costs (the bygones principle); Arkes and Blumer (1985) documented the systematic violation. 'I have already lost so much on this trade that I cannot sell now' - but the money is gone regardless of what you do next.

The finding that people value a good more highly once they own it: the minimum they will accept to give it up substantially exceeds the maximum they would pay to acquire it. Named by Thaler (1980) and demonstrated experimentally by Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (1990), it is commonly explained by loss aversion around an ownership reference point. The moment a position is in your account, it feels worth more than the identical position you do not own.

A preference for maintaining the current state of affairs, such that an option is disproportionately favored when it is designated as the status quo or default. Documented by Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988), it is linked to loss aversion, regret avoidance, and the endowment effect, and is distinct from a rational preference for the current state. Whatever allocation or position you already have feels safer than any change, so portfolios drift and stale positions linger.

The tendency of individuals to suppress their own judgment and conform to the behavior of the group; in financial markets, the clustering of investors into the same trades, driven by conformity, information cascades, and reputational concerns. It is a documented behavioral pattern associated with bubbles, panics, and momentum, not a reliable signal in itself. When everyone is buying, not buying feels wrong; the crowd feels like information even when it is just a crowd.

The tendency to impose coherent stories on sequences of events and to treat a plausible narrative as explanation or evidence, even when outcomes were driven substantially by chance. Taleb calls this the narrative fallacy: we compress complex, random reality into memorable stories and then overtrust them. The market rallies and someone supplies a reason; the reason feels like knowledge, but the same story machine would have explained a sell-off just as smoothly.

The tendency to attribute successes to one's own skill and failures to external factors such as luck, market conditions, or other people. A self-serving attribution pattern studied since Miller and Ross (1975), it is listed among the behavioral patterns that distort investor decision-making in the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress review. Winning trades prove you are skilled; losing trades prove the market was rigged - so the mental scoreboard always flatters you.

The tendency to overestimate one's ability to control or influence outcomes that are partly or wholly determined by chance, named by Ellen Langer (1975). It is strengthened by 'skill cues' such as personal choice, competition, and familiarity - all abundant in trading environments. Clicking the buy button yourself, watching the screen, and having a system all feel like control over an outcome that is mostly random.

The apprehension that others are having rewarding experiences or opportunities one is absent from, coupled with a drive to stay continually connected; the term was popularized by Patrick McGinnis in 2004 and studied psychologically by Przybylski and colleagues (2013). In trading it manifests as chasing fast-moving assets to avoid the regret of missing gains, a dynamic exploited in pump-and-dump schemes. Watching an asset triple while strangers post profits online creates an itch to buy at any price - the pain of missing out outweighs the fear of loss.

A practitioner term for impulsive trading driven by anger or the urge to win back money immediately after a loss: re-entering the market without a valid setup, often with increased size, to get even. It is treated in the trading-psychology literature as an emotional-control failure that compounds losses rather than recovers them. After a stinging loss, the next trade is not analysis - it is retaliation against the market.

Trading more frequently or in greater aggregate volume than one's strategy, edge, or costs justify. Brokerage-account research by Barber and Odean shows individual investors' net returns decline with trading frequency, and the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress report lists active trading among the most damaging investor mistakes. Every trade pays the spread, fees, and slippage - if the edge per trade is thin or absent, more trades just means more cost and more noise.

Habitually failing to take valid trades that meet one's own criteria - hesitating, freezing, or skipping signals out of fear, recent losses, or excessive doubt. At the investor-population level its analogue is documented non-participation: the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress report describes widespread reluctance to invest at all despite suitable options. The plan says buy, the setup is there, but fear of another loss keeps the finger off the button - and the missed winners never appear in the P&L to be noticed.

A state of emotional confusion or frustration - the term originates in poker - in which a person abandons sound strategy for suboptimal, usually overly aggressive play. In trading it denotes the degraded decision-making state that follows losses, humiliating outcomes, or provocation, and it also has a 'winner's tilt' variant after unexpected success. Tilt is the moment the plan leaves the room: you are no longer trading your system, you are trading your anger.

Anxiety triggered by the requirement to perform under evaluation or pressure, activating the sympathetic fight-or-flight response (racing heart, tremor, dry mouth) and degrading execution. In trading it appears around real-money exposure, position sizing, drawdowns, or being observed, and is related to choking under pressure in skilled performance. The setup is the same one you nailed in simulation a hundred times, but with real money and people watching, your hands shake and you cannot pull the trigger.

The amount of risk an individual or organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. In the ISO 31000 risk vocabulary, willingness (appetite/tolerance in the willingness sense) is distinguished from capacity - what the entity is able to bear - and from the risk threshold, the point at which action to reduce risk is required. Risk tolerance is how much drawdown you can stomach without abandoning the plan - a psychological willingness number, not a financial one.

The maximum loss an individual or organization can financially absorb without jeopardizing essential goals or solvency - what one is able to risk, as opposed to risk tolerance, which is what one is willing to risk. In the ISO-derived framing, capability bounds willingness: the accepted level of risk should never exceed capacity. Tolerance is about nerves; capacity is about math - the rent money has no risk capacity no matter how brave you feel.

The consistent execution of a predefined trading process - entries, exits, sizing, and risk limits - regardless of emotional state or short-term outcomes. In the trading-psychology literature it is treated as a trainable skill of aligning behavior with plan, countering the documented biases that push traders off process. Discipline is doing the boring, correct thing - taking the stop, skipping the marginal setup - especially on the days you least want to.

An evaluative stance that judges trading performance by the quality of decisions and adherence to process rather than by individual trade outcomes. It is the deliberate correction for outcome bias, on the principle that in probabilistic domains good processes produce good results only on average, not on any single trial. You cannot control whether this trade wins; you can control whether it was a good trade - so grade the decision, not the dollar result.

A written document specifying in advance what will be traded, under which setups and conditions, with what entry, exit, sizing, and risk rules, and how performance will be reviewed. It converts trading from ad hoc reaction into an explicit, testable procedure and is a foundational tool of trading discipline. The plan is the contract you sign with yourself before emotions show up: it answers every 'what now?' question before the market asks it.

A short list of conditions verified immediately before entering a trade - setup validity, thesis, risk size, stop location, catalysts, and emotional state - designed to filter impulsive trades and enforce the trading plan at the moment of execution. Pilots do not take off on memory and gut feel; the checklist is the ten seconds that stops a FOMO click from becoming a trade.

The structured analysis of completed trades - thesis versus execution, rule adherence, and outcome in R-multiples - conducted after the trade to extract lessons and feed them back into the playbook. Sound review evaluates decisions by ex-ante quality, not merely by whether the trade made money. The trade is not over when you exit; it is over when you have written down what the market just taught you.

A systematic record of trades and the reasoning behind them - entries, exits, size, thesis, emotional state, and lessons - used to create an objective feedback loop for performance. Research on hindsight bias specifically recommends contemporaneous decision diaries because memory of past reasoning is unreliable. Your memory says you are a disciplined genius; the journal shows the trades you actually took.

A contemporaneous record of the reasoning, expectations, and estimated probabilities behind significant decisions, written before outcomes are known. Its purpose is to make judgment auditable: it counters hindsight bias, enables calibration of forecasts, and separates decision quality from luck. Write down what you expect and why before the market answers; later you get to grade your thinking instead of your self-image.

A concise, falsifiable statement of why a trade should work: the setup, the edge being exploited, the conditions required, the expected path, and what would prove the idea wrong. It is the pre-committed reasoning against which execution and outcome are later reviewed. If you cannot say in two sentences why the trade exists and what kills it, you do not have a trade - you have a hope.

The predefined price level, event, or condition at which the trade thesis is considered proven wrong and the position must be exited regardless of emotion. It is the logical core of a stop: the exit occurs because the reason for the trade is gone, not merely because pain is felt. Decide at entry what would prove you wrong; when it happens, the debate is over.

The explicit, predefined conditions that must all be present before a position is opened - the setup pattern, trigger, context filters, and confirmation requirements of the trading plan. Entry criteria turn good ideas into repeatable, testable decisions. The difference between a system and gambling is that the system can say 'not yet' in one sentence.

The predefined rules governing when and how a position is closed - profit targets, stop or invalidation exits, time stops, and trailing logic. Exit criteria are decided at entry so that exits respond to information and structure rather than to fear or greed in real time. Anyone can get into a trade; the exit is where the P&L is actually written, so it cannot be improvised mid-emotion.

A grade of how well a specific trade opportunity matches the trader's validated setups and current market conditions - in proprietary-trading practice expressed as tiers (A/B/C) that gate size and frequency. It operationalizes selectivity: capital concentrates on the highest-quality instances of proven patterns. Not every valid-looking pattern deserves the same money; an A-setup in the right market is a different bet from a marginal lookalike.

The degree to which actual trading behavior matches the written rules of the trading plan - entries, exits, sizing, and risk limits taken as specified, with deviations logged. It is the primary process metric of trading discipline. The system only works if the operator runs it; rule adherence measures whether you ran your system or your mood.

A mistake in implementing an intended trade - wrong order type or price, fat-fingered size, missed or late entry, early or late exit relative to plan - as distinct from a flawed idea. It is measured as the gap between intended and actual execution. The analysis was right and the plan was right; the fingers or the timing were wrong.

A flaw in the reasoning or information processing behind a trade - misread trend, wrong level, ignored evidence, miscalibrated probability - as distinct from an execution mistake or a risk-management breach. It is the error class that review and education, rather than checklists, must fix. You did exactly what you planned; the problem is the plan was built on a misread chart.

A breach of the rules that bound loss - oversizing, moving or removing stops, exceeding daily loss limits, adding to losers, or ignoring correlation between positions. It is the most dangerous error class because it converts bounded, survivable mistakes into account-threatening losses. You can be wrong a hundred times and survive if risk is controlled; one risk-management error at the wrong leverage can end the account.

A quantitative measure of how well the trading process was executed - rule-adherence rate, setup-selection grade distribution, slippage versus plan, review completion - independent of whether individual trades won or lost. Process metrics make discipline measurable and correct for outcome bias in self-evaluation. P&L tells you what the market did; process metrics tell you what you did.

A measure of trading results - net P&L, expectancy, win rate, average R-multiple, drawdown, risk-adjusted return - capturing what the strategy earned rather than how it was executed. Outcome metrics are the ultimate test of a process but are noisy and must not be read trade by trade. Outcomes are the scoreboard, but over any small number of games the scoreboard mostly measures luck.

In the setup-grading taxonomy used in proprietary trading (popularized by Mike Bellafiore's SMB framework), the highest grade of opportunity: a trade matching the trader's best playbook patterns under favorable conditions, warranting full planned position size. The grade is a sizing decision based on the pattern class's tracked expectancy, not a claim about certainty. An A-trade is the one you trained for - your best pattern, in the right market, at the right time; that is where size belongs.

In the A/B/C setup-grading taxonomy used in proprietary trading, a valid playbook setup taken under only partially favorable conditions - worth trading but at reduced size relative to an A-trade. It is the middle tier of the setup-quality hierarchy that links conviction to position size. The pattern is right but the context is average - you can play it, just not with A-trade money.

The lowest grade in the A/B/C setup taxonomy used in proprietary trading: a marginal or borderline opportunity that technically resembles a playbook setup but lacks confluence, so its historical expectancy does not cover costs. Standard practice is to skip C-trades or trade them only at minimal, exploratory size. A C-trade is a trade you take because you are bored or afraid of missing out - the grade exists so you recognize it and pass.

An end-of-day routine in which the day's trades are logged, graded against plan rules, and analyzed for errors and lessons before the next session. It is the shortest feedback loop in the trading process and the primary driver of incremental improvement. Ten honest minutes with the day's trades each evening is worth more than ten hours of new course material.

A weekly aggregation and analysis of the trading journal - process metrics, outcome statistics by setup, recurring errors, and psychological patterns - used to adjust the playbook and plan on a sample less noisy than daily results. It produces a small number of concrete, testable adjustments rather than wholesale rewrites. Days are noise; the week is the first window where your actual habits become visible as data.

A trader's curated, documented collection of proven setups - each with context conditions, entry, exit, sizing, and a worked example - built from personal trading results and reviewed regularly. Instead of trading everything the market shows you, you trade only the handful of patterns you have written down, tested, and own.

Growth is paid for out of accumulated profit rather than account percentage: the equity must prove it can carry one more unit before that unit is added.

a: volatility scaling vol targeting volatility management
x: A portfolio management rule that scales exposure inversely to an estimate of current volatility so that portfolio risk stays near a constant target level: taking less risk when volatility is high and more when it is low. If the market is twice as wild, hold half as much: keeping risk (not capital) constant smooths the return stream and prevents risk from ballooning exactly in crises.

a: risk premia parity equal risk contribution ERC
x: A portfolio construction approach that allocates so that each asset or asset class contributes equally to total portfolio volatility, rather than allocating equal capital. Its best-known form is the equally-weighted risk contributions portfolio; leveraged implementations (e.g. Bridgewater's 1996 All Weather fund) scale the balanced portfolio to a target return. A 60/40 stock-bond portfolio carries roughly 90% of its risk in stocks; risk parity rebalances so bonds, equities, and other assets each carry an equal share of the portfolio's ups and downs.

a: Kelly strategy Kelly bet growth-optimal fraction
x: A bet-sizing rule that maximizes the long-run expected logarithm of wealth — equivalently the expected geometric growth rate — by choosing the fraction of capital to risk on each favorable bet. Introduced by John L. Kelly Jr. of Bell Labs in 1956 and applied to gambling and markets by Edward Thorp. It answers 'how much of the bankroll should I bet?' by balancing edge against odds: bet too little and growth is slow; bet more than Kelly and volatility drag lowers long-run growth while ruin risk climbs.

Betting a fixed fraction (commonly one-half or one-quarter) of the full Kelly fraction rather than the full amount, trading some expected growth for a large reduction in volatility, drawdown depth, and sensitivity to estimation error. Because the growth-rate curve is nearly flat near its peak, half-Kelly sacrifices only about a quarter of the growth rate while roughly halving volatility — a bargain most practitioners gladly take.

The predetermined price at which an open position is closed to cap its loss, implemented as a stop (stop-loss) order that triggers a market — or, for stop-limit, a limit — order once the stop price trades. It defines the trade's initial risk (1R). It is the pre-commitment to admit being wrong at a specific price, converting an open-ended loss into a bounded, planned one.

a: profit target TP order target price
x: The predetermined price at which a position is closed to lock in a planned gain, implemented as a limit (take-profit) order resting at the target price. Together with the stop-loss it defines the trade's planned risk-reward ratio. It is the pre-commitment to get paid: exit automatically when the market hands you the planned profit instead of hoping for more.

A stop order whose trigger price follows the market at a fixed distance in points or percent, ratcheting in the direction of profit and never retreating, so it locks in progressively more of an unrealized gain while leaving room for the trade to run. It is a stop that only moves your way: each new favorable extreme drags the exit level behind it, converting paper profits into protected profits.

An exit rule that closes a position after a predetermined amount of time has elapsed, regardless of price, on the rationale that a setup whose expected move has not occurred within its typical window no longer justifies the capital at risk. Good trades usually work promptly; if nothing has happened by the time the edge should have played out, free the capital for a better opportunity.

A stop-loss placed at a multiple of a volatility measure — typically Average True Range — away from entry or from a reference extreme, so the exit distance adapts to current market conditions instead of being a fixed number of points or percent. A 2-point stop is noise in a wild market and a chasm in a quiet one; sizing the stop by ATR keeps the exit outside normal random fluctuation in any regime.

A pre-set quantitative bound on the risk a trader, desk, or account may carry — expressed as maximum position size, leverage, loss amount, VaR, or margin usage — enforced by the firm, broker, or exchange to keep exposures within tolerance. Risk limits are the guardrails: they decide in advance how much damage one trader or one book is permitted to do before the system cuts it off.

a: max daily loss daily drawdown limit
x: A risk control that stops or restricts trading for the rest of the day once cumulative losses — realized plus, in strict versions, floating P/L on open positions — reach a predetermined amount, typically a fixed sum or a percentage of equity. It is the circuit breaker for a bad day: cap the damage a single session can do and force the trader to step away before tilt and revenge trading compound the loss.

a: weekly drawdown limit max weekly loss
x: A risk control that suspends or down-sizes trading for the remainder of the week once cumulative weekly losses reach a preset threshold, layering a slower-timescale brake on top of daily loss limits. Bad weeks cluster when a system is out of sync with the regime; the weekly cap forces a pause and review before a rough patch becomes a ruined month.

A cap on the size of the net long or net short position a single person or account may hold or control in a given instrument, set by regulators or exchanges (speculative position limits) and by firms internally, to curb concentration and market-cornering risk. No single player should be big enough to break the market or break themselves; the limit predetermines how much is too much.

The total absolute value of a portfolio's long and short positions, conventionally expressed as a percentage of capital: long exposure plus short exposure, without netting. Values above 100% indicate the use of leverage. It measures how much exposure the fund is carrying in total — the gross weight on the scale, regardless of how the bets offset each other.

a: net market exposure net long/short exposure
x: The difference between a portfolio's long and short exposures, expressed as a percentage of capital: long exposure minus short exposure. It measures net directional sensitivity to broad market moves. It is the portfolio's lean: net long books gain when markets rise, net short books gain when they fall, and zero net is directionally market-neutral.

a: market direction exposure delta exposure (book level)
x: The portion of a portfolio's exposure that profits or loses with the direction of the underlying market — the signed, unhedged sensitivity to price moves, as distinct from offsetting relative-value exposure. It answers 'which way does this book need the market to go?': the residual bet left after hedges and offsets are accounted for.

The ratio of a portfolio's total position exposure to its equity — typically gross exposure divided by net asset value — expressing how many dollars of market exposure are controlled per dollar of capital. It is the real multiplier on your capital: effective leverage of 3x means a 10% adverse market move costs about 30% of equity, before hedging effects.

The daily (or intraday) cash settlement of gains and losses on a margined derivatives position: as positions are marked to market, losers pay winners through the clearing system so that gains and losses are realized incrementally rather than at expiry. Instead of letting P/L accumulate as an IOU until the end, the clearinghouse settles up every day: yesterday's loss is today's cash payment.

A demand by the broker or clearinghouse to deposit additional funds, or reduce positions, when account equity falls below the maintenance margin requirement, restoring the account to the initial margin level. It is the lender's alarm bell: your cushion is gone, so top it up now or positions start getting sold for you.

The mark price at which a leveraged position's margin balance falls to the maintenance margin requirement, triggering the venue's liquidation process. On crypto derivatives venues it is derived from entry price, leverage, and the tiered maintenance margin rate. It is the line in the sand: if the market prints there, the exchange takes over and closes the position because your collateral can no longer safely cover the loss.

The mandatory closing of a position by the broker, clearinghouse, or exchange without the holder's consent, triggered when account equity falls below the maintenance margin and margin calls are not — or cannot be — met. When you can't or won't post more collateral, the venue closes the trade for you, at whatever price the market gives, to stop the loss from eating other people's money.

The reduction of leverage — paying down debt or shrinking positions relative to equity — by a trader, firm, or, in aggregate, an economy; at the portfolio level it means cutting gross exposure to lower the amplification of gains and losses. Leverage multiplies both ways; deleveraging is deliberately shrinking the multiplier, usually after losses, in order to survive.

A last-resort loss-allocation mechanism on leveraged crypto derivatives venues: when a liquidated position cannot be closed above its bankruptcy price and the insurance fund cannot absorb the shortfall, the exchange forcibly reduces profitable opposing positions at the bankruptcy price to cover the deficit. If the loser is bankrupt and the insurance fund is empty, the winners' positions are trimmed to make the books balance: the system socializes the residual loss to stay solvent.

A reserve pool maintained by a crypto derivatives exchange, funded by venue contributions and by residual margin from liquidations closed better than the bankruptcy price, used to cover losses when a liquidated position's losses exceed its margin (bad debt) before auto-deleveraging is invoked. It is the venue's shock absorber between ordinary liquidations and socialized losses: small bankruptcies are absorbed from the pot so that winning counterparties are never touched.

The practice of valuing positions and accounts at current market prices (fair value) rather than historical cost, recognizing gains and losses as prices change; in futures markets it is performed daily or more often and drives variation margin flows. Your account reflects what positions are worth now, not what you paid: profits and losses become real every day, not just when you sell.

The risk arising from an uneven distribution of exposures — to a single counterparty or name (name concentration) or to a sector, region, or product (sectoral concentration) — such that one adverse event can produce losses large enough to threaten the portfolio or institution. Concentration is the opposite of diversification: the more eggs in one basket, the more one dropped basket costs.

The risk that the other side of a contract — a bond issuer, derivative counterparty, or insurer — fails to meet its obligations, including default before final settlement of the transaction's cash flows. For derivatives it is termed counterparty credit risk and is managed with collateral, netting, and central clearing. A contract is only as good as the entity standing behind it: if your counterparty fails, your winning trade becomes an unsecured claim in bankruptcy.

The risk that one party delivers its side of a transaction but does not receive the countervalue in return — most acutely principal risk in foreign exchange, where the two legs settle in different currencies and time zones. Also called Herstatt risk after the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure. You pay out your currency in the morning and the counterparty fails before paying theirs in the afternoon: the whole principal, not just the P/L, is gone.

The risk of being unable to fund increases in assets or meet obligations as they come due without incurring unacceptable losses (funding liquidity), or of being unable to exit positions at prevailing prices without moving the market (market/asset liquidity). BCBS principles treat its management as paramount because one institution's shortfall can have system-wide repercussions. Liquidity risk is the risk that you need cash or an exit right now and the market charges you ruinously — or does not trade at all.

The risk of losses in on- and off-balance-sheet positions arising from movements in market prices — interest rates, equities, foreign exchange, commodities, credit spreads, and volatilities. It is the risk class for which the Basel market-risk framework (FRTB) sets trading-book capital requirements. It is the risk that the market itself moves against you: the everyday exposure of any open position to prices, rates, and spreads.

The risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems or from external events — including fraud, execution errors, outages, and legal risk. It is the Basel definition used for bank capital purposes, and the risk is inherent in all products, activities, processes, and systems. It is the risk that something inside the machine — or an outside event hitting the machine — breaks: the rogue trade, the failed settlement, the system outage, the fat-finger order.

The potential for adverse consequences — financial loss, poor business decisions, reputational damage — from decisions based on model outputs that are incorrect or misused. Per Federal Reserve SR 11-7, model risk arises primarily when a model has fundamental errors or when it is used incorrectly or without regard for its limitations and assumptions. Every model is a simplified map of reality; model risk is what happens when you drive off the edge of the map while trusting it.

The risk that a hedge and the underlying exposure do not move in lockstep — that the basis (spot price of the hedged asset minus the futures or hedge price) changes unexpectedly — leaving residual profit or loss despite hedging. Your umbrella covers most of you but not exactly: basis risk is the part of the weather that still gets you wet.

The risk that a position's price jumps discontinuously from one trade to the next — typically between sessions, over weekends, or on sudden news — with no opportunity to transact at intermediate prices, so stops and risk limits execute far from their intended levels. Your stop at $48 doesn't help when the market closes at $50 and opens at $40: the loss is realized at the gap price, not the stop price.

The risk of extreme outcomes in the tails of the return distribution — conventionally moves beyond about three standard deviations — which occur far more often in financial returns than a normal distribution implies. Because losses matter more than gains, practice focuses on the left tail. The bell curve says the crash should almost never happen; market history says otherwise. Tail risk is the danger hiding in the 'impossible' part of the distribution.

The risk that a discrete, often unforecastable event — a takeover, reorganization, credit downgrade, product recall, regulatory action, natural disaster, or overnight headline — abruptly reprices a security or portfolio, independent of the prevailing market trend. You can be right about the market and still get wiped out by the press release: event risk is the discrete shock that doesn't care about your chart.

The risk that a trader or institution cannot obtain or roll over the funding — cash, credit, or margin — needed to carry its positions, forcing sales or default even when the positions are economically sound. It is distinct from market liquidity (the ease of trading the asset), with which it interacts in liquidity spirals. It's not that your position is wrong — it's that the money carrying it gets pulled: when the funding disappears, the position dies with it.

The risk that exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with that counterparty's credit quality — exposure grows precisely as the counterparty's probability of default rises. It is divided into specific wrong-way risk (a direct link through the nature of the transactions, e.g. collateral issued by the counterparty itself) and general wrong-way risk (correlation through broad market factors). The worst kind of counterparty risk: the bigger your claim on them, the less likely they are to be able to pay it.

A quantile-based measure of portfolio loss: for a given confidence level and horizon, the loss level that will not be exceeded with that probability under stated assumptions — a one-day 95% VaR of $1M means a 5% chance of losing more than $1M in a day. Formalized at J.P. Morgan in the early 1990s and embedded in bank capital regulation by the 1996 Basel market-risk amendment. It compresses the whole loss distribution into one sentence: on 19 days out of 20, we expect to lose no more than this.

a: CVaR conditional value at risk average value at risk tail VaR ES
x: The expected loss conditional on the loss exceeding a given VaR level — equivalently the average of VaR over all levels beyond the threshold. It is a coherent risk measure, more sensitive to tail shape than VaR, and it replaced VaR as the basis of Basel internal-models market-risk capital. Where VaR tells you where the bad region starts, expected shortfall tells you how bad the bad region is on average.

A risk management technique that evaluates the impact of severe but plausible adverse scenarios — historical replays or hypothetical shocks to prices, rates, spreads, and liquidity — on a portfolio or institution, reaching beyond what statistically calibrated models capture. BCBS principles make it both a core bank risk-management tool and a supervisory instrument. Models tell you about ordinary Tuesdays; stress tests ask what happens on the once-a-decade Wednesday that bankrupts the unprepared.

The evaluation of portfolio or firm outcomes under explicitly constructed states of the world — combinations of factor moves reflecting historical episodes, hypothetical narratives, or reverse-engineered loss targets — used to understand exposure to joint events rather than single-factor moves. It is structured what-if thinking: pick a coherent story (recession, rate shock, venue failure) and trace what it does to every position at once.

The measurement of how a portfolio's value or a model's output changes in response to a change in one input or risk factor at a time; the Greeks (delta, vega, rho), basis-point values, and one-at-a-time parameter perturbations are its standard forms. Rather than shocking the whole world, nudge one dial at a time and read the needle: how much does the book lose per basis point, per vol point, per day of decay?

The ratio of a fund's average differential (excess) return over a benchmark or risk-free rate to the standard deviation of that differential return — the reward-to-variability measure introduced by William Sharpe in 1966 and generalized in his 1994 exposition. It summarizes expected (ex ante) or realized (ex post) return per unit of total risk. It answers: for each unit of volatility endured, how much return above the risk-free alternative did the strategy deliver? Higher means more efficient conversion of risk into return.

A risk-adjusted performance measure that modifies the Sharpe ratio by penalizing only returns below a user-specified target (the minimum acceptable return): the excess of realized return over the target divided by the downside deviation (target semi-deviation). Upside volatility is profit, not danger; the Sortino ratio only charges the strategy for the harmful, below-target fluctuations.

A drawdown-based performance measure: the average annual (compound) rate of return over a trailing 36-month window divided by the maximum drawdown over the same window, computed monthly. Created by Terry W. Young in 1991 for evaluating commodity trading advisors. It prices performance in units of worst pain: how much annual return do you get for each unit of the deepest hole the strategy digs in three years?

A risk-adjusted return measure that divides the compound annual return by a function of average annual drawdown — originally, per Deane Sterling Jones (1981), the compound rate of return divided by the absolute value of (average annual drawdown minus 10%); modern variants use excess return over the average largest drawdown. Where Calmar charges only for the single worst drawdown, the Sterling ratio charges for the typical yearly drawdown: the routine pain, not just the record pain.

A performance measure defined by Keating and Shadwick (2002) as the probability-weighted ratio of gains to losses relative to a threshold return: the area of the return distribution above the threshold divided by the area below it. Because it uses the entire distribution, it captures all moments rather than only mean and variance. Split the whole return distribution at your 'good enough' line and weigh everything above against everything below — no moment is thrown away.

The ratio of active return (portfolio return minus benchmark return) to active risk (the tracking error, i.e. the standard deviation of the active return). It measures the consistency of a manager's value added per unit of benchmark-relative risk and is the natural analogue of the Sharpe ratio for benchmarked mandates. It grades the active bet itself: how much did deviating from the index earn, per unit of deviation risk taken?

A risk-adjusted performance measure relating a portfolio's excess return over the risk-free rate to its systematic risk (beta) rather than total volatility: the reward-to-volatility ratio introduced by Jack Treynor. It pays you only for market risk you can't diversify away: excess return per unit of beta, ignoring idiosyncratic swings a diversified investor needn't bear.

a: Jensen's measure ex-post alpha CAPM alpha
x: The intercept of the regression of a portfolio's excess returns on the market's excess returns — the abnormal return over what the CAPM predicts for the portfolio's beta. Introduced by Michael Jensen in 1968 to evaluate mutual fund managers; it generalizes to multi-factor models as the return unexplained by the included factors. It is the residual: after accounting for the market exposure you took (beta), how much return was left over that the market can't explain?

The standard deviation of a portfolio's active return relative to its benchmark — also called active risk — measuring how closely the portfolio follows its index. Measured historically it is ex post (realized) tracking error; model-predicted it is ex ante tracking error. It is the wobble between you and the index: an index fund hugs the benchmark (tracking error near zero) while an aggressive active manager wanders far from it.

The proportion of trades, forecasts, or periods that are 'hits' — profitable trades, correct directional calls, or outperforming intervals, depending on context. In trading-performance statistics it is synonymous with the win rate. The batting average of a strategy or forecaster: how often the call or the trade actually worked.
