a: cumulative PnL curve account equity curve
x: The time series of a trading account's or strategy's value — cumulative realized profit/loss plus open equity, net of deposits and withdrawals — plotted over time. It is the primary visual record of performance, from which drawdown, time under water, and related statistics are computed. It is the strategy's cardiogram: trend, smoothness, and depth of dips say more about robustness than any single return number.

The time series of percentage (or absolute) drawdown from the running equity peak, plotted as a persistently non-positive curve that touches zero only at new equity highs. It is the drawdown view of the equity curve, showing the depth and duration of every loss episode at a glance. Flip the equity curve's perspective: instead of how high you've climbed, the underwater curve shows how far below the surface you've spent your time.

A statistical measure of the strength and direction of association between two variables, expressed as a dimensionless coefficient bounded in [-1, +1]. The most common form is the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, which measures linear association; rank-based variants (Spearman, Kendall) measure monotonic association. It tells you whether two series tend to move together (+1), in opposite directions (-1), or without any linear pattern (0). In markets it describes how strongly two assets' returns co-move, which is the statistical basis of diversification.

The average of the squared deviations of a variable from its mean; the canonical measure of dispersion around the mean. Population variance divides by the population size N, while the unbiased sample variance divides by n - 1 (Bessel's correction). It measures how spread out values are around their average, in squared units. Squaring means points far from the mean contribute disproportionately, so variance is dominated by extremes.

The square root of the variance, restoring the measure of spread to the original units of the data. It is the most widely used single-number summary of variability and the standard proxy for volatility in finance. It is the typical distance of observations from their mean, expressed in the same units as the data. For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and 95% within two.

a: expectation mean of a random variable E[X]
x: The probability-weighted average of all possible values of a random variable; the long-run mean outcome if the experiment is repeated indefinitely. It is the first moment of a probability distribution. It is the average you would converge to after many repetitions, not necessarily a value that can actually occur. A bet has positive expected value if the probability-weighted payouts exceed the stake over the long run.

a: arithmetic return discrete return holding period return net return (single period)
x: The fractional change in value of an investment over a single period: the difference between final and initial value divided by the initial value, including any income such as dividends in the final value. It is the standard per-period return measure in empirical finance. It answers 'by what percentage did my money grow this period?' A 5% simple return means $100 became $105.

a: logarithmic return continuously compounded return force of interest
x: The natural logarithm of the gross return (price ratio) over a period, equivalent to the continuously compounded rate of return. Its key property is time-additivity: multi-period log returns are the sum of single-period log returns. Log returns convert compounding into addition. Gains and losses become symmetric: +10% and -10% log returns cancel exactly to zero, unlike simple returns.

Two usages coexist: (1) in asset-pricing mathematics, the gross return is the growth factor of an investment over a period, i.e., final value divided by initial value, equal to one plus the simple return; (2) in performance reporting, gross return is the return before deduction of fees, commissions, and taxes (gross of costs), as opposed to net return. In sense (1), it is 'what $1 becomes' - a multiplier like 1.07 for a 7% gain. In sense (2), it is what the investment earned before anyone took their cut.

a: total holding period return overall return
x: The total return of an investment over a multi-period horizon, obtained by compounding (geometrically linking) the single-period returns, assuming gains are reinvested. It measures the full change in value from the start to the end of the holding period. It is the answer to 'if I invested $1 at the start and reinvested everything, what fraction do I have now, minus one?' It compounds, so it is not the sum of the periodic returns.

a: annualized rate of return compound annual growth rate CAGR
x: The constant per-year rate of return that, compounded over the holding period, would produce the observed cumulative return. It converts returns measured over periods longer or shorter than a year to a comparable yearly basis. It answers 'what steady yearly growth rate would have gotten me to the same final value?' It lets you compare a 9-month return with a 5-year return on one scale.

The sum of a set of values divided by their count; the most common measure of central tendency (location). It is the value that minimizes the sum of squared deviations from the data. It is the 'fair share' value: if every observation were replaced by the mean, the total would stay the same. It balances the data like a center of gravity.

The nth root of the product of n positive numbers; the central-tendency measure appropriate when quantities combine multiplicatively rather than additively. In finance, the geometric mean of period growth factors gives the constant per-period growth rate that reproduces the compounded result. It is the average growth rate that actually compounds to the observed total. Where the arithmetic mean answers 'average change', the geometric mean answers 'average multiplier'.

The middle value of an ordered data set: the point with half the observations below it and half above. For an even number of observations it is conventionally the average of the two central values. It is the 'typical middle' value that ignores how extreme the tails are. Half the data lies on each side, by construction.

The value that occurs with the greatest frequency in a data set, or the location of the peak of a probability distribution. A distribution may have one mode (unimodal), several modes (multimodal), or no well-defined mode. It is the most common outcome - the value you would bet on if you had to guess exactly one number.

A measure of the joint variability of two random variables: the expected product of their deviations from their respective means. Its sign indicates the direction of the linear relationship (positive: variables tend to move together; negative: oppositely), and its magnitude depends on the units of the variables. It is the raw, unstandardized version of correlation: it tells you whether two variables move together and by how much in squared unit terms, but you cannot compare covariances across different unit scales.

a: Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient Pearson's r r
x: The standardized measure of linear association between two variables, equal to their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations, ranging from -1 (perfect negative linear) to +1 (perfect positive linear). Developed by Karl Pearson around the early 1900s. It measures how well a straight line describes the relationship: +1 or -1 means all points lie exactly on a line, 0 means no linear pattern at all.

a: Spearman's rho Spearman's rank correlation coefficient grade correlation
x: A nonparametric measure of monotonic association between two variables, defined as the Pearson correlation coefficient computed on the ranks of the observations rather than their raw values. It ranges from -1 to +1 and detects any consistent monotonic relationship, linear or not. It asks 'do bigger x values reliably come with bigger y values?' regardless of how big the steps are. Only the ordering matters, so outliers can do no more damage than their rank allows.

A nonparametric measure of ordinal association between two variables, computed from the difference between the number of concordant and discordant observation pairs, normalized by the total number of pairs. It ranges from -1 (perfectly reversed rankings) to +1 (identical rankings) and was introduced by Maurice Kendall in 1938. Pick any two observations; the pair is 'concordant' if both variables rank them in the same order. Tau is essentially the probability of concordance minus the probability of discordance.

A mathematical function that assigns probabilities to the possible outcomes of a random variable. For discrete variables it is a probability mass function giving P(X = x) with all masses non-negative and summing to 1; for continuous variables it is a probability density function whose integral over the whole line is 1, with probabilities defined over intervals. It is the complete map of what values a random quantity can take and how likely each is - the 'shape of uncertainty' for a variable such as tomorrow's return.

a: Gaussian distribution bell curve N(mu, sigma^2)
x: A continuous, symmetric, single-peaked probability distribution fully determined by its location parameter mu (mean = median = mode) and scale parameter sigma (standard deviation). It is the default modeling distribution in statistics, theoretically justified by the central limit theorem for sums and averages. It is the classic bell curve: most values cluster near the mean and extremes become rapidly rarer, with about 68% of probability within one sigma and 99.7% within three.

A continuous probability distribution of a positive random variable X whose natural logarithm is normally distributed. It is right-skewed with support on (0, infinity) and is the standard model for asset prices under geometric Brownian motion. If returns compound multiplicatively, prices end up lognormal: the product of many positive random growth factors has a log that is a sum, hence normal by the CLT. Prices cannot go below zero, which the lognormal respects.

A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution with heavier tails than the normal, parameterized by the degrees of freedom nu. It is the exact sampling distribution of the standardized sample mean when the population standard deviation is estimated from a small sample, and it converges to the normal distribution as nu grows. It is the 'cautious normal': when you estimate spread from limited data, the extra uncertainty fattens the tails, so extreme values are more likely than the bell curve suggests.

The probability distribution of a single trial with exactly two outcomes, conventionally 'success' (X = 1) with probability p and 'failure' (X = 0) with probability 1 - p. It is the building block of the binomial distribution, which counts successes across n independent Bernoulli trials. It models any one-shot yes/no event: will this trade close in profit, will this coin land heads? Only one number - p - fully describes it.

The discrete probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials, each with exactly two outcomes and the same success probability p. It is the sum of n independent Bernoulli variables and is probably the most commonly used discrete distribution. It answers: 'If each trade wins with probability p, what are the chances of exactly x wins in n trades?' The win count, not the order of wins, is what matters.

The discrete probability distribution of the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently at a constant average rate lambda. Both its mean and its variance equal lambda. It models rare, independent arrivals: 'If on average 2 news shocks hit per day, what is the chance of 5 tomorrow?' One rate parameter determines everything.

A continuous probability distribution on the non-negative reals modeling the waiting time between events that occur at a constant rate, with a constant hazard function. It is the unique continuous memoryless distribution: the probability of waiting t more time units is independent of time already waited. It answers 'how long until the next event?' when events strike at a steady average rate. Past waiting tells you nothing about remaining waiting - the process has no memory.

a: third standardized moment Fisher-Pearson coefficient of skewness
x: A measure of the asymmetry of a distribution about its mean, defined as the third standardized moment. Zero indicates symmetry, positive values indicate a longer right tail, and negative values a longer left tail. It tells you which side the surprises live on: negatively skewed returns have occasional large crashes amid small gains; positively skewed returns have occasional large wins amid small losses.

A measure of whether data are heavy-tailed or light-tailed relative to a normal distribution, defined as the fourth standardized moment. High kurtosis indicates heavy tails (frequent outliers); low kurtosis indicates light tails, and the normal distribution has kurtosis 3. It quantifies tail risk: two distributions with the same mean and variance can differ enormously in how often extreme moves occur, and kurtosis captures that.

The kurtosis of a distribution minus 3, the kurtosis of the standard normal distribution, so that the normal reference value becomes zero. Positive excess kurtosis indicates heavier-than-normal tails; negative values indicate lighter-than-normal tails. It is kurtosis re-zeroed at the bell curve: 0 means normal-like tails, positive means fatter tails than normal, negative means thinner.

Cut points that divide the range of a probability distribution (or an ordered sample) into intervals of equal probability. The p-quantile Q(p) is the value below which a proportion p of the probability mass falls, i.e., the inverse of the cumulative distribution function; special cases include quartiles, deciles, and percentiles. Quantiles answer 'what value marks the bottom 5%?' - the 0.05-quantile of a return distribution is the loss level that is exceeded only 5% of the time, the basis of Value-at-Risk.

The 100-quantiles of a distribution or ordered data set: the kth percentile is the value at or below which k percent of the observations fall. Percentiles express the relative standing of a value within a data set. Scoring in the 90th percentile means 90% of values are at or below yours and 10% above - a rank statement, not a statement about the score itself.

The difference between the third quartile (75th percentile) and the first quartile (25th percentile) of a data set; the spread of the middle 50% of the data. It is a robust measure of scale that ignores the tails entirely. It measures how wide the 'typical middle' of the data is, untouched by extreme values - the width of the box in a box plot.

A data point that is significantly different from the other observations in a sample - potentially an error, an abnormality, or a key to understanding the data. The standard box-plot rule flags points more than 1.5 times the interquartile range beyond the quartiles as potential outliers (and beyond 3*IQR as extreme outliers). It is an observation that does not fit the pattern of the rest - the one day in a quiet series when the market moved 10%.

The number of standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean of its distribution, obtained by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. Z-scores standardize values from different distributions onto a common scale. It converts any measurement into 'how many sigmas from average' - a -2 day means a move twice the typical size in the down direction, whatever the asset's units.

a: SE standard error of the mean
x: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic - most commonly the standard error of the mean, which measures how much a sample mean would vary from sample to sample. It shrinks with the square root of the sample size. The standard deviation describes spread of individual data points; the standard error describes the spread of your estimate. It answers 'how precisely does my sample pin down the average?'

An interval estimate for a population parameter constructed so that a stated proportion (the confidence level, e.g., 95%) of intervals built the same way from repeated samples would contain the true parameter value. For the mean with unknown variance it uses the t distribution with N - 1 degrees of freedom. Instead of one best-guess number, it gives a plausible range whose width communicates how uncertain the estimate is: narrow means precise, wide means noisy.

The default statement in a hypothesis test that there is no effect or no difference - the status quo that sample evidence must argue against. It always contains a statement of equality (e.g., mu = mu_0) and is the claim that is rejected or not rejected, never 'proven'. It is the skeptical position: 'this strategy has no edge, the apparent performance is luck.' Testing asks whether the data are surprising enough under that assumption to abandon it.

The claim about the population that contradicts the null hypothesis - typically what the researcher suspects or hopes to demonstrate - and the conclusion adopted when the null is rejected. It never contains an equality, taking forms mu != mu_0, mu > mu_0, or mu < mu_0. It is the contender: 'this strategy does have an edge.' You get to assert it only by showing the data are inconsistent with the null.

In null-hypothesis significance testing, the probability - computed assuming the null hypothesis is true - of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed. The smaller the p-value, the more incompatible the data are with the null model. It answers: 'If there were really no effect, how often would luck alone produce a result this strong?' A p-value of 0.01 means only 1% of no-effect worlds give data this extreme.

Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true - a false positive. Its probability is denoted alpha and is controlled by the chosen significance level of the test. It is declaring a lucky strategy to be skill: you concluded there is an edge when in truth there is none.

Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false - a false negative. Its probability is denoted beta, and 1 - beta is the power of the test. It is missing a real edge: the strategy genuinely works, but your sample was too small or noisy for the test to detect it.

The probability that a hypothesis test correctly rejects the null hypothesis when it is false, equal to 1 - beta where beta is the Type II error probability. It measures the test's ability to detect a real effect of a given size. It is the sensitivity of your detector: high power means that if a strategy truly has an edge, your test will almost surely notice; low power means real edges slip through as 'not significant'.

a: magnitude of effect Cohen's d (for mean differences)
x: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of a phenomenon, such as the correlation between two variables, a mean difference, or a risk difference, reported separately from its statistical significance. Standardized versions like Cohen's d express the effect in units of standard deviation so studies can be compared. The p-value asks 'is there anything there?'; the effect size asks 'how much is there?' A strategy can be statistically significant yet economically trivial - effect size is what reveals that.

The arithmetic average of the observations in a sample, denoted x-bar. It is the standard estimator of the population mean and is unbiased: its expected value equals the population mean. It is your best single-number guess of the true average when you can only see a slice of the data - the mean of the 250 daily returns you observed standing in for the mean of the return-generating process.

The mean of the entire population (or data-generating process), denoted mu; equivalently, the expected value of the underlying probability distribution. It is a fixed but typically unknown parameter that sample statistics estimate. It is the 'true average' you would get if you could observe every possible outcome - the quantity your sample mean is trying to approximate.

The average squared deviation of sample observations from the sample mean, computed with divisor n - 1 (Bessel's correction). The n - 1 divisor makes it an unbiased estimator of the population variance; the naive n-divisor version is biased downward. It is the variance you compute from the data you have, adjusted slightly upward because estimating the mean from the same data eats one degree of freedom.

a: bias of an estimator statistical bias
x: The difference between the expected value of an estimator and the true value of the parameter it estimates. An estimator with zero bias is called unbiased; bias is an objective, long-run property of the estimation rule, not of any single estimate. It measures systematic error: if you repeated your estimation procedure on many fresh samples, would the average of the estimates land on the truth (unbiased) or consistently above/below it (biased)?

A property of a sequence of estimators: as the sample size grows without bound, the estimates converge in probability to the true parameter value (weak consistency; almost-sure convergence gives strong consistency). The distribution of the estimates concentrates ever more tightly around the truth. A consistent estimator is one that is guaranteed to home in on the true value if you feed it enough data - the more you observe, the closer you get, with probability approaching certainty.

A measure of the quality of an estimator based on its variance: a more efficient estimator achieves the same precision with fewer observations. An unbiased estimator is called efficient if its variance attains the Cramer-Rao lower bound, the smallest variance any unbiased estimator can have. Given two honest ways to estimate the same thing, the efficient one wastes less data - its estimates bounce around the truth less, so you need a shorter track record to be sure.

The theorem that, as the number of independent trials grows, the sample average (or relative frequency of an event) converges to the expected value (or theoretical probability). The difference between the theoretical probability and the observed relative frequency approaches zero as trials increase. Luck averages out with repetition: a few trades can go anywhere, but over thousands of trades your win rate and mean return settle toward their true underlying values.

The theorem that the sampling distribution of the sample mean (or sum) of independent observations approaches a normal distribution as the sample size grows, regardless of the shape of the original distribution - provided its variance is finite. The limiting normal has the population mean mu and standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n). Averages of many small, independent influences look bell-shaped even when the individual influences are not - which is why so many statistics can be treated as approximately normal with enough data.

A sequence of observations on a variable recorded in time order, typically at equally spaced intervals, in which data points may have internal structure such as autocorrelation, trend, or seasonal variation that must be accounted for when modeling. In trading, prices, returns, volumes, and indicators are all time series. Unlike a random sample, the order of observations matters: yesterday's price is informative about today's, so time series methods model the dependence across time rather than treating points as independent draws.

The property of a stochastic process whose statistical behavior does not change over time. A strictly stationary process has all joint distributions invariant to time shifts; in practice stationarity usually means a flat-looking series with no trend, constant variance, a constant autocorrelation structure, and no periodic fluctuations. A stationary series behaves the same in 2020 as in 2010: it fluctuates around a stable level with stable variability, so its past behavior is a usable guide to its future behavior.

a: covariance stationarity second-order stationarity wide-sense stationarity
x: A form of stationarity in which only the first two moments of a process are required to be time-invariant: the mean and variance are constant and the autocovariance between two points depends only on the lag between them, not on their location in time. This is the assumption underlying ARMA modeling and most time-series inference. Weak stationarity demands only that the series' average level, spread, and lag-pattern of correlation stay the same over time - a much weaker requirement than the full probability distribution being unchanging.

a: unit root process integrated of order one I(1)
x: A property of a time series whose autoregressive representation has a root equal to one, making it difference-stationary rather than level-stationary: shocks have permanent effects and the series follows a stochastic trend. A unit-root process becomes stationary only after differencing. A series with a unit root has no tendency to return to any fixed level; every shock shifts it permanently, like a drunken walk that wanders without an anchor.

a: random walk hypothesis random walk process
x: A stochastic process in which each value equals the previous value plus an unpredictable increment (white noise), so the best forecast of tomorrow's value is today's. In finance, the random-walk hypothesis holds that price changes are unpredictable because new information is incorporated into prices immediately. Each step is a fresh coin flip added to where you stand now; knowing the whole history of steps tells you nothing about the next one.

The deterministic, systematic component of a stochastic process - the average rate at which the process is expected to move per unit of time, distinct from its random fluctuations. In a geometric Brownian motion or random walk with drift, it is the constant expected change per period. Drift is the steady current in a river; the waves are random, but the current carries you in one direction on average.

The correlation of a time series with itself at different time lags: a measure of how strongly an observation is linearly related to observations h periods earlier or later. Significant nonzero autocorrelation means the series is not random white noise. Autocorrelation asks: does a high value today tend to be followed by high values tomorrow (positive) or by low values (negative), or is there no relationship at all?

The correlation between a time series value and its value h periods earlier after removing the linear effect of all intervening lags (1 through h-1). It isolates the direct lag-h relationship that the ordinary autocorrelation confounds with indirect chains of correlation. If today's value correlates with last week's only because both depend on yesterday, the partial autocorrelation at lag 7 removes that indirect path and shows whether a genuine direct link remains.

The full set of autocorrelations of a time series viewed as a function of the lag h, usually plotted as a correlogram with confidence bands. The ACF's shape (exponential decay, cutoff, oscillation) characterizes the dependence structure and guides model identification. Instead of asking whether the series depends on its past at one specific lag, the ACF scans all lags at once, revealing the memory profile of the series.

The partial autocorrelations of a time series viewed as a function of lag h, plotted with confidence bands. Whereas the ACF measures total dependence at each lag, the PACF measures only the direct dependence net of intermediate lags, and its cutoff after lag p is the classic signature of an AR(p) process. The PACF is a lag-by-lag scan asking: after accounting for everything in between, does the value h steps back still tell me anything new about today?

A time series of uncorrelated random variables with zero mean and constant finite variance - a process with no linear dependence structure at any lag. White noise is the building block (shock sequence) of ARMA-type models and the benchmark against which randomness is tested. White noise is pure unpredictable static: every value is a fresh, unrelated draw, so no pattern in the past helps predict the future.

The unpredictable new information entering a time series at each period - the part of the current value that cannot be forecast from the series' own past. In ARMA and state-space models, innovations are the white-noise input sequence that drives the process. The innovation is the surprise in each new observation: the gap between what actually happened and the best prediction you could have made a period earlier.

A time-series model in which the current value is expressed as a linear combination of its own p previous values plus a white-noise innovation. It is a linear regression of the series on its own lags and is stationary when the roots of its characteristic polynomial lie outside the unit circle. An AR model says today is explained by momentum or mean-reversion from the recent past: how much of yesterday (and the days before) carries into today.

A time-series model in which the current value is a constant plus a linear combination of the current and q past white-noise innovations. Despite the name, it is not a smoothing average of the series but a regression on unobserved past shocks, and it is always stationary. An MA model says shocks linger for exactly q periods and then vanish: today's value reflects today's surprise plus fading echoes of the last q surprises.

A time-series model combining an autoregressive part of order p and a moving-average part of order q, expressing a stationary series as a function of its own lagged values and lagged innovations. Box and Jenkins popularized a systematic identification-estimation-validation methodology for ARMA models. ARMA captures both ways the past echoes into the present: through the series' own lagged levels and through lingering shocks.

An integrated autoregressive moving-average model, ARIMA(p,d,q), that extends the ARMA model to non-stationary series by differencing the data d times and then fitting autoregressive (order p) and moving-average (order q) terms to the differenced series. It is the core of the Box-Jenkins identification-estimation-validation methodology. Many real series wander with a trend or unit root, so you difference them until they look stationary, model the differences with an ARMA model, and sum forecasts back up to the original scale.

A multiplicative extension of the ARIMA model that adds seasonal autoregressive, seasonal differencing, and seasonal moving-average terms at the seasonal period s, written SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s, to model series with stable repeating periodic patterns. Monthly sales or quarterly earnings resemble not only the adjacent period but the same period a year ago, so the model regresses on lags spaced by the season length as well as on short lags.

A multivariate time-series model in which each variable of a system is regressed on its own lags and the lags of every other variable, treating all variables as jointly endogenous. Sims (1980) introduced it as an alternative to heavily restricted simultaneous-equation macro models. Instead of deciding in advance which variable drives which, let every variable potentially influence every other with lags and let the data reveal the dynamic interactions.

A property of two or more individually non-stationary (e.g., I(1)) series for which some linear combination of them is stationary, indicating a stable long-run equilibrium relationship even though each series wanders. Engle and Granger (1987) formalized the concept together with its representation, estimation, and testing. Two drunkards on a leash: each price wanders unpredictably, but the spread between them is tethered and keeps snapping back, so the spread is forecastable even though the levels are not.

A dynamic model for cointegrated series in which short-run changes respond to lagged changes plus an error-correction term measuring the deviation from the long-run equilibrium, so the system adjusts back toward equilibrium over time. Its validity follows from the Granger representation theorem of Engle and Granger (1987). The cointegrating spread acts like a rubber band: when last period's gap from equilibrium was wide, today's changes pull the series back toward it, at a speed set by the adjustment coefficient.

A statistical precedence concept: a series x Granger-causes y if past values of x improve the forecast of y beyond what past values of y alone provide, tested by F-tests on lagged coefficients in an autoregression or VAR. Introduced by Granger (1969). If knowing yesterday's thunder helps predict today's rain beyond what yesterday's rain tells you, thunder Granger-causes rain: it is incremental predictive content, not metaphysical cause.

A violation of the constant-error-variance assumption in regression in which the conditional variance of the disturbance varies across observations, typically as a function of the regressors or of time. OLS coefficients remain unbiased under heteroskedasticity but are no longer efficient, and conventional standard errors are biased. The size of the model's mistakes is not constant: errors may balloon for large values of a regressor or in turbulent periods, so treating every observation as equally precise is wrong.

Time-varying variance of a time series in which the variance of the innovation, conditional on past information, changes predictably over time, typically clustering so that large changes are followed by large changes. This is the defining feature modeled by the ARCH family introduced by Engle (1982). Volatility comes in waves: after a big market move, the near future is likely to be volatile too, so the risk forecast should update with recent shocks instead of being one fixed number.

Autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity: a model in which the conditional variance of the current innovation is a linear function of past squared innovations, so volatility is serially correlated and forecastable. Engle (1982) introduced it to model the time-varying variance of inflation. Treat variance like an autoregression on squared shocks: if yesterday's surprise was big, today's expected variance is big, which produces the volatility clustering seen in financial returns.

Generalized ARCH: a model in which the conditional variance depends on both past squared innovations and past conditional variances, parsimoniously capturing the slowly decaying volatility persistence of financial returns. Introduced by Bollerslev (1986). Variance today is a weighted average of a long-run level, yesterday's shock, and yesterday's variance estimate: a smoothing recursion that reacts to shocks but relaxes back to normal gradually.

Exponential GARCH: Nelson's (1991) model of the log conditional variance as a function of past standardized innovations with separate magnitude and sign terms, guaranteeing positive variance without parameter constraints and capturing the asymmetric (leverage) response of volatility to negative shocks. Because it models log variance, the variance can never go negative, and the sign term lets bad news lift volatility more than good news of the same size, matching the leverage effect in equity returns.

A threshold GARCH variant of Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993) in which squared innovations enter the variance equation with an extra coefficient when the previous innovation was negative, allowing bad news to raise volatility more than good news while remaining in the standard GARCH estimation framework. It is the GARCH recursion with a switch: yesterday's loss flips on an extra volatility boost that an equal-sized gain does not trigger.

A class of models in which volatility is itself a latent stochastic process evolving with its own innovations, rather than a deterministic function of past observed shocks as in GARCH. In continuous time, Heston (1993) models variance as a mean-reverting square-root process driven by its own Brownian motion, possibly correlated with the price shock. Volatility is an unobserved state variable that wanders randomly and mean-reverts; you see it only through the size of price moves, so inference filters the hidden volatility out of the return data.

A time-series model in which the parameters change according to a latent discrete state that itself follows a Markov chain, so the series alternates between distinct regimes such as low-volatility expansion and high-volatility contraction. Hamilton (1989) introduced the framework for business-cycle dynamics. The market behaves like two different machines, calm and stormy, and an invisible switch flips between them; at any moment you only have a probability of which machine is running.

A probabilistic model in which an unobserved finite-state Markov chain generates observable emissions whose distribution depends on the current hidden state, specified by initial-state, transition, and emission probabilities. Rabiner's (1989) tutorial standardized its three canonical problems: evaluation, decoding, and learning. You cannot see the weather directly, only whether people carry umbrellas; from the umbrella sequence you infer the hidden rainy-or-sunny sequence, given how states persist and how each state produces observations.

A recursive algorithm for optimal linear estimation of the hidden state of a linear Gaussian state-space system, alternating prediction and update steps that weight new observations by their information content. Kalman (1960) derived it as the solution to the linear filtering and prediction problem. Keep a running best guess of an unobservable quantity plus your uncertainty about it; each new noisy observation nudges the guess toward the data, by more when the data are precise relative to your uncertainty.

a: dynamic linear model structural time-series model
x: A general time-series framework that represents observed data as noisy measurements of an unobserved state vector evolving through a transition (system) equation, separating the dynamics of the hidden process from measurement error. It subsumes ARMA models, structural time-series models, and time-varying-parameter regressions, and is estimated via the Kalman filter and maximum likelihood. Split the world into what you cannot see (the true underlying state: trend, seasonal level, drifting coefficient) and what you measure (noisy data), then let filtering theory reconstruct the hidden part.

The estimation method that chooses regression coefficients to minimize the sum of squared residuals between observed and fitted values, yielding the closed-form estimator beta_hat = (X'X)^{-1} X'y for the linear model. Under the Gauss-Markov assumptions it is the best linear unbiased estimator. Draw the line (or hyperplane) that makes the total of the squared vertical gaps between data and fit as small as possible; squaring punishes big misses and keeps the algebra tractable.

A statistical model relating a response variable to one or more explanatory variables through a function linear in the unknown parameters, y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i + ... + epsilon_i, typically estimated by least squares. 'Linear' refers to linearity in the parameters, so transformed or polynomial terms in the variables are permitted. Summarize how y moves with x by a straight-line relationship plus noise: each coefficient reads as the expected change in y per unit change in its x, holding the others fixed.

Linear regression with two or more explanatory variables, y = X beta + epsilon, in which each coefficient measures the partial association between the response and one regressor holding the others constant. It is estimated by OLS as beta_hat = (X'X)^{-1} X'y. With several predictors at once, each coefficient answers: what does this variable add given everything else already in the model? That is why coefficients can change sign when a correlated variable is added.

A regression model for a binary outcome that models the log-odds of the event as a linear function of the predictors, so predicted probabilities stay bounded between 0 and 1. Developed in its modern form by Cox (1958) and estimated by maximum likelihood rather than least squares. Instead of predicting the 0/1 outcome directly, predict the odds of the event on a log scale, where a straight line makes sense, then squash the result back to a probability with the logistic curve.

A regularized least-squares estimator that shrinks coefficients toward zero by adding a penalty proportional to the sum of squared coefficients, trading a small bias for a large variance reduction when predictors are collinear. Introduced by Hoerl and Kennard (1970) for nonorthogonal problems. When predictors are highly correlated, OLS coefficients swing wildly between samples; ridge charges a price for large coefficients, keeping them small and stable at the cost of a slight pull toward zero.

Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator: a regularized regression that penalizes the sum of absolute coefficient values, which both shrinks coefficients and sets some exactly to zero, performing continuous variable selection. Introduced by Tibshirani (1996). The L1 penalty has corners at zero, so as the penalty tightens the least useful coefficients are pushed exactly to zero and drop out: shrinkage and feature selection in one step.

A regularized regression combining the L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) penalties, retaining the lasso's variable selection while adding a grouping effect that keeps strongly correlated predictors in or out of the model together. Introduced by Zou and Hastie (2005). Pure lasso tends to pick one variable out of a correlated cluster and drop the rest; mixing in ridge penalty makes the whole cluster share the coefficient, which is stabler when predictors travel in packs.

The difference between an observed response and the value fitted by a model, e_i = y_i - f(x_i; beta_hat). Residuals are the observable proxies for the unobservable error terms and the primary diagnostic for model adequacy. The leftover after the model has said its piece: if the model captured the structure, the leftovers should look like pure noise with nothing left to exploit.

The coefficient of determination: the proportion of the total sample variation in the response accounted for by the regression model, computed as one minus the ratio of the residual to the total sum of squares. For OLS with an intercept it equals the squared correlation between observed and fitted values. A 0-to-1 score of how much of the ups and downs in y the model reproduces: R^2 = 0.7 means 70% of the variance is captured by the regressors and 30% is left in the noise.

A degrees-of-freedom-corrected version of R^2 that penalizes model complexity, so it increases only when a new regressor improves fit more than would be expected by chance. The standard correction is due to Ezekiel. R^2 always rises when you add variables, even junk ones; adjusted R^2 charges a complexity tax per parameter so it only rises if the new variable genuinely earns its place.

A condition in regression in which two or more explanatory variables are highly linearly related, so the design matrix is nearly rank-deficient and individual coefficients cannot be estimated precisely, although the model as a whole may still predict well. If two predictors move together, the data cannot tell which one deserves the credit: many different coefficient splits fit almost equally well, so each estimate has a huge standard error and can flip sign between samples.

The failure of the exogeneity condition E[epsilon | X] = 0 in a regression, i.e., a regressor correlated with the error term, arising from omitted variables, simultaneity (reverse causation), or measurement error. It renders OLS estimates biased and inconsistent. The regressor and the leftover noise are tangled together, so the coefficient absorbs part of the noise's influence and no longer isolates the variable's own effect.

A variable used to identify a causal effect when the regressor of interest is endogenous: a valid instrument is correlated with the endogenous regressor (relevance) and affects the outcome only through that regressor (exclusion restriction), isolating an exogenous source of variation. Find a lever that shifts the troublesome variable for reasons unrelated to everything else in the error term, then measure how the outcome responds to those lever-induced shifts only.

A general estimation principle that chooses parameter values maximizing the likelihood, the probability (density) of the observed data viewed as a function of the parameters, so the fitted model makes the observed sample as probable as possible. Fisher (1922) founded the method and established its consistency, efficiency, and asymptotic normality. Treat the data as fixed and ask which parameter values would have made this exact dataset most likely to occur; those are the estimates.

A framework for statistical inference in which unknown parameters are treated as random variables with prior distributions that are updated to posterior distributions via Bayes's theorem as data arrive, so all conclusions are probability statements about parameters given the data. Start with a belief, weigh it against the evidence the data carry, and come out with an updated belief: inference is the continuous revision of probabilities.

The probability distribution of unknown parameters after conditioning on the observed data, obtained by Bayes's theorem as the normalized product of the likelihood and the prior. It is the central output of Bayesian inference. Your belief about the parameter after seeing the evidence, expressed as a full distribution rather than a single number, so it gives both a best guess and the remaining uncertainty.

The probability distribution assigned to unknown parameters before observing the data, encoding pre-existing knowledge or deliberately weak information; it combines with the likelihood through Bayes's theorem to form the posterior. What you believe before the experiment: it can be an informed guess from past data or a deliberately vague statement, but it must be written down so its influence on the answer is visible.

The joint probability (density) of the observed data expressed as a function of the model parameters with the data held fixed, L(theta) = f(y_1,...,y_n; theta). It measures the relative plausibility of parameter values and is the object maximized in maximum likelihood estimation, introduced by Fisher (1922). The same formula as the probability of the data, read backwards: instead of asking what data these parameters might produce, ask how probable this dataset is under each candidate parameter.

The use of repeated random sampling to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute analytically, such as expectations, distributions of estimators, option prices, or the sampling variability of a trading rule, by generating many pseudo-random realizations and averaging. Named and systematized by Metropolis and Ulam (1949). If you cannot solve the probability problem on paper, play it out thousands of times with a random number generator and use the empirical frequencies as the answer.

A resampling method that approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly resampling the observed data with replacement and recomputing the statistic, using the empirical distribution as a stand-in for the unknown population. Introduced by Efron (1979). Pretend your sample is the whole population: draw many new samples from it with replacement, watch how much the statistic wiggles across them, and read off standard errors and confidence intervals without distributional formulas.

A bootstrap variant for dependent data that resamples contiguous blocks of observations rather than individual points, preserving short-run serial dependence within each block while still generating artificial samples. Developed by Kunsch (1989) as the moving-blocks bootstrap. Resampling single returns would shuffle away the volatility clustering and momentum you need to preserve, so you resample whole chunks of consecutive days and let dependence live inside each chunk.

An exact, distribution-free significance test that computes the p-value by recomputing the test statistic over all (or many random) rearrangements of the data labels consistent with the null hypothesis, generating the null distribution from the data themselves. Systematized by Pitman (1937) following Fisher's randomization idea. If the treatment made no difference, the labels are meaningless: shuffle them thousands of times, recompute the statistic each time, and see how extreme the real statistic is among the shuffled ones.

The inflation of false-positive rates when many hypotheses are tested simultaneously: at a per-test level alpha, the probability of at least one false rejection across m tests grows toward 1 as m increases, so unadjusted testing reliably produces spurious discoveries. A 5% test cries wolf one time in twenty by design; test a hundred strategies and you should expect about five wolves even if every strategy is worthless.

The expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections in a multiple-testing procedure, FDR = E[V/R] (defined as 0 when R = 0), where V counts false positives among R rejections. Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) proposed controlling it as a less conservative alternative to familywise error rates. Instead of demanding zero chance of any false positive, accept that a small controlled fraction of your discoveries may be false, buying back the power to find real effects among many tests.

a: data mining bias specification search bias
x: The bias arising when the same data are used repeatedly to select and evaluate models or strategies, so the best-performing specification among those searched is optimistically biased in-sample even if none has genuine predictive ability. White's (2000) reality check formalized testing whether the best rule in a searched universe truly beats a benchmark. If you let the data pick your strategy and then judge it on the same data, you are grading an exam the student wrote for themselves: the winner's edge is partly luck harvested by the search.

A backtesting error in which a simulated decision uses information that would not have been available at the simulated decision time, such as future prices, revised fundamentals, or full-sample statistics, artificially inflating measured performance. It is trading with tomorrow's newspaper: any rule looks brilliant if at each historical date it quietly consults data that only became known later.

The distortion of sample statistics caused by conditioning on survival: analyzing only the funds, stocks, or strategies that persisted to the end of the sample while dropping those that failed or delisted, thereby overstating average performance and understating risk. Quantified for mutual funds by Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson and Ross (1992). Judging bomber safety by the holes in the planes that returned ignores the ones that never came back; the failures carry information the survivors cannot show.

Systematic error introduced when the data selected for analysis are not representative of the target population because selection is related to the variables under study, so associations measured in the selected sample differ from those in the population. You only observe the winners of some filtering process, whoever applied, survived, volunteered, or was listed, so what you measure reflects the filter as much as the phenomenon.

The distortion of the published research record caused by preferential publication of statistically significant or spectacular results over null or unremarkable ones, so the literature overstates effect sizes and the fraction of true effects. In finance it interacts with the 'factor zoo' documented by Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016). Journals and authors both prefer headline results, so the file drawer fills with failures and the literature shows only the winners, like reading only the strategies that survived.

The production of a model that corresponds too closely to the particular training data, fitting noise as if it were structure, so it performs well in-sample but fails to generalize to new data. It arises whenever the selection criterion (training performance) diverges from the evaluation criterion (out-of-sample performance). The model memorizes the textbook's answers instead of learning the subject: perfect on past questions, helpless on new ones.

The failure of a model to capture the systematic structure present in the data, because it is too simple, too constrained, or trained too little, resulting in high bias and poor fit on both training and new data. Drawing a straight line through a curve: the model is not wrong about the noise, it never even saw the signal.

An ultra-short-horizon trading style in which a trader opens and closes positions within seconds to minutes to capture very small price movements, often exploiting the bid-ask spread or momentary micro-imbalances in highly liquid instruments. It is the shortest-horizon form of day trading and relies on high trade frequency, tight risk limits, and low per-trade costs. Instead of trying to catch a big move, the scalper skims many tiny moves, accepting a few ticks of profit per trade and repeating this dozens or hundreds of times a day.

A speculative trading approach in which a trader buys and sells (or sells and buys) the same financial instrument within the same trading day, closing all positions before the session ends to avoid overnight gap risk. Under FINRA rules, a 'day trade' is the purchase and sale of the same security on the same day in a margin account, and customers executing four or more day trades in five business days are designated pattern day traders subject to special margin requirements. Day traders try to profit from intraday price swings, riding a stock's momentum for seconds to hours, and never hold positions overnight.

A speculative trading style in which positions are held for one or more days up to several weeks to profit from short- to medium-term price 'swings'. Holding periods sit between day trading (closed intraday) and position trading or buy-and-hold (months to years), and entries/exits are typically driven by technical analysis, sometimes combined with fundamentals. The swing trader tries to catch the middle chunk of a move that plays out over days, without needing to buy the exact bottom or sell the exact top.

A trading style in which positions are held for weeks to months (or longer) to capture major price trends, with decisions driven mainly by macro trends, fundamentals, or long-horizon technical analysis. The term is sometimes used interchangeably with buy and hold, though position traders may actively exit when the underlying thesis or long-term trend ends. Position traders ignore daily noise and try to own an asset for the big part of a long move, reviewing the thesis periodically rather than watching the tape.

a: trend trading managed futures trend following
x: A systematic trading approach that takes long positions in instruments whose own recent returns have been positive and short positions in those whose recent returns have been negative, on the hypothesis that price trends persist. It is an empirical strategy family, not a proven predictive law; academic work documents that a security's own past returns positively predict its near-term future returns across many futures markets, with partial reversal at longer horizons. Rather than predicting turning points, trend followers assume a market that has been going up will keep going up for a while, and they ride it until the trend reverses.

The hypothesis, and the family of strategies built on it, that asset prices or returns contain a transitory component that tends to revert toward a long-run mean, so that extreme moves are at least partially undone. Empirically, stock returns show positive serial correlation at short horizons and negative autocorrelation at long horizons, consistent with a slowly decaying transitory price component, though the effect is statistical and contested, not a law. What stretches too far from its usual level tends to snap back; mean-reversion traders buy what has fallen too far and sell what has risen too far.

A family of strategies that buy assets with strong recent performance and sell or short assets with weak recent performance, based on the empirically documented pattern that securities outperforming their peers over the past 3 to 12 months tend to keep outperforming over the following month. Momentum is a well-studied cross-sectional anomaly, not a guaranteed law, and is distinct from time-series momentum, which uses an asset's own past return rather than its rank versus peers. Winners tend to keep winning for a while, so the momentum trader buys what is already strong and avoids or shorts what is weak.

A technical-analysis trading style that enters a position when price passes through and holds beyond a defined support or resistance level, on the hypothesis that such breakouts mark the early stage of a new trend. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law; broken resistance is often treated as new support and vice versa. When price finally escapes the ceiling or floor where it has been stuck, breakout traders jump in, betting the escape is the start of a real move.

A trading style applied to non-trending markets in which price repeatedly rises off a support level and falls off a resistance level; the trader buys near support and sells or shorts near resistance, expecting the oscillation to persist. It is a technical-analysis heuristic whose validity ends when the range breaks. If a stock keeps bouncing between the same floor and ceiling, trade the bounce: buy low in the band, sell high in the band.

A market-neutral strategy that matches two securities whose prices historically move together, then goes long the underperformer and short the outperformer when their prices diverge, profiting if the spread between them reconverges. Gatev, Goetzmann, and Rouwenhorst (2006) formalized the canonical version: stocks are paired by minimum distance between normalized historical prices and traded with a simple divergence/convergence rule. If two similar companies' prices drift apart, bet they will come back together: buy the laggard, short the leader, and you profit on the gap closing regardless of market direction.

A family of quantitative, typically market-neutral strategies that exploit statistical mispricings among large portfolios of related securities, using short-horizon mean reversion and factor models rather than the strict riskless mispricing of classical arbitrage. Pairs trading is the canonical example; profits are expected values over many small trades, not risk-free arbitrage. Instead of one guaranteed mispricing, stat arb places hundreds of small, hedged bets that each have a slight statistical edge, so the law of large numbers does the work.

A market-neutral hedge-fund strategy involving the simultaneous purchase of a convertible security (usually a convertible bond) and the short sale of the same issuer's common stock, designed to exploit inefficient pricing of the convertible relative to the underlying equity. The short stock position is sized to the convertible's equity sensitivity (delta), and the position is dynamically re-hedged. Buy the convertible bond, short the stock against it: if the bond is cheap relative to the stock-plus-option it embeds, you harvest the difference while staying roughly immune to small stock moves.

A group of market-neutral strategies that exploit pricing differences between related fixed-income securities or contracts, such as swap-spread, yield-curve, mortgage, and cash-futures basis trades. Positions pair long and short exposures in economically similar instruments and bet on the convergence of small yield or price discrepancies, usually with substantial leverage. Two bonds or rates that should be priced almost identically sometimes are not; fixed-income arbs buy the cheap one, short the rich one, and wait for the tiny gap to close.

A class of option-based relative-value strategies that trade the difference between an option's implied volatility and a forecast of the underlying's future realized volatility, implemented through a delta-neutral portfolio of options and the underlying. The trader treats volatility, rather than price, as the unit of relative value: buying options delta-hedged is a bet that realized volatility will exceed implied, and selling them is the opposite bet. If the market is pricing options as if the stock will move 10% but you think it will move 20%, you can buy the options, hedge out the direction, and profit from the extra movement itself.

An options relative-value strategy that trades the spread between the implied volatility of an index and the implied volatilities of its constituent stocks. The classic construction is short index options (straddles or variance) against long options on the components - a position that profits when realized correlation comes in below the correlation embedded in index option prices. Index option implied volatility embeds an average pairwise correlation among components; if the stocks move less in lockstep than implied, the index's realized volatility undershoots the volatility of its parts, rewarding the short-index/long-components book.

A dynamic-hedging options strategy in which a trader holds a long-gamma options position (such as a straddle) and repeatedly rebalances an offsetting position in the underlying to keep the book delta-neutral, harvesting small gains from realized price oscillations. It monetizes the difference between realized volatility and the implied volatility paid for the options. Being long gamma means your delta grows when the underlying rises and shrinks when it falls, so re-hedging mechanically forces you to sell high and buy low; if the underlying wiggles more than the implied volatility you paid for, the scalps can outearn the theta decay.

A portfolio construction approach that offsets positive and negative deltas so the combined position has near-zero sensitivity to small moves in the underlying's price. Directional risk is neutralized so that other exposures - volatility, time decay, or carry - drive the P&L. If an option behaves like 40 shares, holding 40 offsetting shares cancels first-order price risk; what remains is the curvature (gamma), the clock (theta), and the volatility exposure (vega).

A liquidity-provision activity in which a firm continuously quotes two-sided bid and ask prices, earning the spread (and any rebates) on turnover while managing the inventory risk of positions accumulated from filling customer orders. In U.S. equities, registered and off-exchange market makers also internalize a large share of retail order flow under Regulation NMS execution and disclosure rules. The market maker is a dealer, not an investor: it tries to buy at the bid and sell at the offer thousands of times a day, and its enemy is holding inventory when prices move against it.

A systematic order-placement technique that lays a ladder of buy and sell orders at fixed price intervals above and below a reference price, harvesting oscillation or trend mechanically without forecasting direction. With-the-trend grids add exposure as price runs; against-the-trend (range) grids buy lower rungs and sell higher rungs to monetize mean reversion. Instead of predicting where price will go, the grid turns the price axis into a conveyor belt: each step down triggers a buy and each step back up triggers a sell at the next rung, locking the spacing in as gross profit per completed cycle.

An accumulation strategy that invests a fixed dollar amount into an asset at regular intervals regardless of price, so that more units are bought when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. It replaces market-timing decisions with a mechanical purchase schedule. A fixed $500 buys twice as many shares at $10 as at $20, so the average cost per share ends up below the average price over the period - the schedule does the buying-low work automatically.

An accumulation strategy, introduced by Michael Edleson in a 1988 AAII Journal article, in which the investor targets a fixed increase in the portfolio's total value each period (the value path) and invests or sells whatever amount is required to hit that target. Purchases are larger after declines and smaller - or negative - after rallies. Dollar-cost averaging fixes the dollars you invest; value averaging fixes the growth of your portfolio's value, so the market itself dictates each installment - more when it is cheap, less, or even a sale, when it is rich.

A position-building tactic that adds to a winning trade in predefined increments as price moves in the position's favor, so that full size is carried only after the trade has proven itself. In trend systems the adds are mechanical - the Turtle rule adds one unit every 0.5N (half the average true range) above the previous fill. Start small, let the market pay for confirmation, then press: each add is effectively financed by open profit, while stops trail so that the worst case on the full pyramid approximates the risk of the first unit.

a: buying the dip adding to a loser
x: Adding to an existing long position as its price falls, which lowers the average cost per share and reduces the rebound needed to break even. It is a position-sizing practice rather than a complete strategy, most defensible within a valuation framework and strict risk limits. Buying 100 shares at $50 and 100 more at $40 puts the cost basis at $45, so the position needs only a 12.5% recovery from $40 instead of a 25% one - but the investor now owns twice as much of a falling asset.

a: adding to strength leaning into winners
x: Buying additional shares of an existing position at successively higher prices, raising the average cost basis while increasing exposure to a rising asset. It is the mirror of averaging down and the discrete-time cousin of pyramiding into strength. Leaning into winners trades a worse average price for a bigger position in a confirmed trend - you pay up precisely because the market is validating the thesis.

Building a position in multiple tranches at different prices instead of committing full size at once - either into weakness (lowering average cost) or into strength (adding as the trade proves itself). It spreads execution and timing risk and lets the trader confirm the thesis before full deployment. Splitting a 1,000-share buy into four 250-share steps at descending prices turns one all-or-nothing decision into a graduated one, at the cost of sometimes never reaching full size.

Closing a position in partial tranches at successively more favorable prices rather than exiting all at once, banking profits progressively while leaving a residual position to capture further movement. Selling a third at each target converts an all-or-nothing exit into a ladder: some profit is locked in, and the remaining runner is effectively financed by realized gains.

A portfolio-construction framework that places the majority of assets in a low-cost, passively managed core tracking broad market indexes, surrounded by smaller actively managed satellite positions intended to add alpha or diversification. It blends passive efficiency with bounded active risk. Lock in the market return on most of the money and confine your bets to a satellite sleeve, where manager skill or concentrated themes can only help or hurt at the margin.

A passive investment strategy of purchasing securities - typically diversified equity funds - and holding them for years regardless of short-term price fluctuations, forgoing timing decisions in favor of long-run participation in asset growth. Positions are selected once and traded only for rebalancing, contributions, or withdrawals. If you cannot reliably predict next month's price, own productive assets and let compounding and time in the market do the work; every round trip avoided is costs and taxes not paid.

A strategy of funding in a low-interest-rate currency (or asset) and investing in a high-interest-rate one to earn the interest differential, in violation of the uncovered-interest-parity benchmark that predicts offsetting depreciation. Its return profile is short-volatility: steady differential income punctuated by crash risk on the investment currency. Borrow yen at 0.5%, buy Australian dollars at 4.5%, and pocket the four-point spread - as long as AUD does not slide; the trade earns until everyone unwinds at once, which is why it goes up by the stairs and down by the elevator.

A relative-value strategy that trades the basis - the spread between an asset's cash (spot) price and its futures price - by going long the cheap leg and short the rich leg, expecting convergence as the futures contract approaches delivery. The position is neutral to the asset's outright price and earns or loses the change in the spread. A futures contract and the deliverable asset are the same thing at expiry, so any gap between them today beyond financing and carry is a harvestable mispricing: buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and wait for them to meet.

The Treasury-market instantiation of the basis trade: arbitrageurs, chiefly hedge funds, buy cash Treasury notes and bonds and short Treasury futures when futures trade above their no-arbitrage price, financing the bond in the repo market so the position requires almost no net cash outlay. Profit comes from cash and futures prices converging by the delivery date. If the future is priced above what the deliverable bond plus financing costs, you can warehouse the bond, deliver into the future, and lock in the gap - as long as your repo funding survives until delivery.

A crypto-market cash-and-carry style strategy that pairs a position in a perpetual futures contract with the opposite position in spot to harvest the funding rate - the periodic payment exchanged between perp longs and shorts that tethers the contract to the index price. When funding is positive, the classic trade shorts the perp and holds spot, collecting funding from longs. Perpetual futures never expire, so exchanges tax the crowded side: when longs pay shorts 0.01% every eight hours, being short the perp and long the coin collects the toll while the two legs' price risk cancels.

a: exchange arbitrage kimchi premium trade (crypto context)
x: Buying an asset on the exchange where it is cheaper and simultaneously selling it where it is dearer to capture the price gap between venues. In cryptocurrency markets, Makarov and Schoar (2020) document that such deviations are recurrent and much larger across countries than within them, reflecting capital controls and limits to arbitrage. The same bitcoin should not be worth $30,000 in Seoul and $29,400 in New York for long - but moving dollars and coins across borders and exchanges is slow and costly, so the gap persists and pays whoever can bridge it.

A high-frequency strategy that exploits the mechanical arbitrage opportunities created when correlated securities' prices update at slightly different times across venues, racing to trade on a stale quote before its owner can update it. Budish, Cramton and Shim (2015) show this arms race is built into the continuous limit order book design itself. When the E-mini jumps in Chicago, the SPY quote in New York is wrong for a few milliseconds; being first to pick off that stale quote is worth millions a year, so firms spend hundreds of millions on being microseconds faster.

A strategy that exploits deviations between the price of an index futures contract (or ETF) and the theoretical fair value of the underlying constituent basket, buying the cheaper side and selling the richer. It is the engine of classic program trading and enforces the law of one price between index derivatives and their components. The S&P 500 future is just the 500 stocks in a wrapper; if the wrapper trades rich to the contents, sell the wrapper and buy the contents - computers do this in milliseconds, which is why the gap rarely exceeds transaction costs.

Trading the price relationship between futures (or options) on the same underlying with different expiration months - the intra-commodity calendar spread - by buying one expiry and selling another to capture changes in the term-structure gap rather than the outright price. Framed as arbitrage, it targets spreads that deviate from carry-implied or historical norms. March wheat and September wheat are the same wheat at different dates; the gap between them reflects storage, financing, and seasonal demand - trade the gap when it stretches beyond what carry justifies.

a: trading the news event-driven day trading
x: A short-horizon style that trades the price impact of scheduled announcements (earnings, central-bank decisions, economic data) and unscheduled events, entering just before or immediately after the release to capture the volatility burst. Most news traders operate intraday, since the exploitable reaction is typically short-lived. News is the one scheduled source of volatility: everyone knows when the payrolls print lands, nobody knows its content - the game is positioning for, reacting to, or fading the crowd's reaction better than the crowd.

a: earnings momentum trading trading earnings announcements
x: Trading equity positions around quarterly earnings announcements to exploit the announcement-day volatility and the post-announcement price drift documented in the accounting literature. Implementations range from intraday reaction trades to holding surprise winners and losers for the multi-week drift. Earnings are scheduled surprises: prices jump at the print and then, on average, keep crawling in the direction of the surprise for weeks, as if the market digests the news only gradually.

An intraday strategy that marks the high and low of the session's first minutes (commonly the first 15) and enters in the direction of a break beyond that range, treating the opening battle as the day's reference for momentum. It is a named day-trading system without a canonical academic source. The first 15 minutes concentrate overnight information and the day's heaviest volume; whichever side wins that skirmish often keeps control, so the range edges become the day's natural trigger levels.

A day-trading momentum strategy that buys (or shorts) a stock that gaps at the open on high volume and continues trending in the gap direction without a meaningful pullback, entering on continuation beyond the opening range. It is a named practitioner setup with no canonical source. A high-volume gap means overnight information repriced the stock and trapped the other side; if price never looks back, the trapped traders' exits and momentum chasers feed a one-way move you ride with tight invalidation.

A contrarian tactic that trades against the prevailing move - selling into strength or buying into weakness - on the premise that the late stages of a move are driven by slow-reacting traders and prone to reversal. Common applications include fading overextended intraday moves and fading the initial reaction to economic data releases. If everyone who wanted to buy has already bought, the marginal flow runs out and the move stalls; fading is selling the exhaustion of a crowded move rather than its beginning.

a: z-score pairs trading standardized spread stat-arb
x: A statistical-arbitrage rule that monitors the spread between two historically linked securities, standardizes it as a z-score against its own rolling mean and standard deviation, and enters a market-neutral long/short when the spread stretches beyond a threshold (commonly two standard deviations), exiting at reversion. It is the standardized-distance variant of the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst pairs rule. If two stocks usually move together, the times they do not are opportunities: when the gap is two standard deviations wide, history says it more often narrows than widens - so you short the leader and buy the laggard.

A trend-entry rule that buys when price exceeds the highest high (or sells when it breaks the lowest low) of a trailing N-period channel, on the premise that a break of an established range marks the start of a sustained move. It is the 'trading range break' rule tested by Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) and generalized in Donchian-style systems. A market coiled in a box stores energy; a break beyond the box means buyers or sellers finally overwhelmed the range boundary, and the absence of nearby reference points lets the move run.

a: MA crossover golden cross / death cross system variable-length moving average rule
x: A trend-following rule that goes long when a short moving average crosses above a longer one and exits or shorts on the reverse cross, using the smoothed momentum of two lookback windows as the signal. It is the canonical moving-average rule in Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron's (1992) tests of simple technical trading rules. The short average is the market's recent mood, the long average its season; when mood crosses season something has changed - you trade the crossing, accepting that you will be late at both turns.

a: Donchian channel breakout N-day channel breakout
x: A channel-breakout system built on Donchian channels - the trailing N-day high and low - entering long when price exceeds the channel top and short when it breaks the channel bottom, most famously as the 20-day (System 1) and 55-day (System 2) entries of the Turtle rules. Exits use a shorter opposite channel: 10-day for System 1 and 20-day for System 2. Richard Donchian's insight was that you need not predict trends, only agree to join every new N-day extreme; most breakouts fail, but the few that run pay for all of them.

The complete mechanical trend-following system Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt taught their 'Turtle' trainees in 1983-84: Donchian-channel breakout entries, volatility-normalized position sizing in units of 1% risk per N, 2N stops, adds every 0.5N, and portfolio-level unit limits. Published in full by original Turtle Curtis Faith as 'The Original Turtle Trading Rules' (2003). Dennis's bet was that trading could be taught as rules: trade many liquid futures markets, risk a fixed volatility fraction per unit, take every breakout, and let a few giant trends pay for dozens of stopped-out false starts.

A macro positioning framework that rotates between higher-risk assets (equities, cyclicals, commodities, credit) in optimistic risk-on regimes and safe havens (Treasuries, gold, cash, reserve currencies) in fearful risk-off regimes, driven by shifts in aggregate investor risk tolerance. The correlated cross-asset moves in these regimes are the phenomenon the framework trades. In RORO markets the global portfolio breathes as one organism: when fear rises, everything risky is sold together and everything safe is bought together, so the trade is the regime, not the asset.

A top-down strategy class that takes long and short positions across equity indexes, government bonds, currencies, and commodities based on macroeconomic and political analysis - interest-rate paths, growth differentials, policy shifts, and geopolitics. It is practiced by global macro hedge funds in discretionary, systematic, and CTA forms.
