Instead of asking which stock is cheap, ask which country's whole story is mispriced - then express the view with the most efficient instrument: its currency, its bonds, its equity index, or its commodities.

a: sector momentum rotation relative strength investing
x: A cross-sectional allocation strategy that periodically rotates capital into the assets, sectors, or industries with the strongest recent relative performance and out of the weakest, harvesting the momentum effect at the group level. It operationalizes industry momentum, which Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) showed accounts for much of individual-stock momentum. Leadership persists longer than contrarians expect: the sectors that led last quarter tend to keep leading next quarter, so you systematically climb aboard the leaders and abandon the laggards on a fixed schedule.

a: relative strength momentum winners-minus-losers J/K momentum
x: The anomaly and strategy class of buying securities with the highest recent returns relative to their peers and selling those with the lowest, over 3- to 12-month formation and holding periods. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented that such relative-strength portfolios generated significant abnormal returns not explained by systematic risk or delayed reaction to common factors. Winners keep winning and losers keep losing for a while: rank the whole market by recent performance, buy the top decile, short the bottom, and let the persistence work over the next quarter.

A strategy that takes long positions in assets whose own trailing return is positive and short positions where it is negative - each asset against its own history rather than against peers - typically with volatility-scaled sizing. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) document significant time-series momentum across 58 liquid futures in equity indexes, currencies, commodities, and bonds, persisting about a year and partially reversing thereafter. Do not ask whether gold beat stocks; ask whether gold beat gold - if its own past year is up, be long, if down, be short, and size each bet so every market contributes equal risk.

The documented tendency of stock prices to continue moving in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks after the announcement, and the strategy of trading that continuation. Bernard and Thomas (1989) showed cumulative abnormal returns drift with the sign of the surprise for roughly 60 days, concluding the pattern is consistent with a delayed price response rather than risk mismeasurement. The market under-reacts to earnings: the announcement-day jump is only part of the move, so buying after good news - late, after everyone saw the print - historically still captured the slow digestion that followed.

a: squeeze trading (short side) short-covering rally trade
x: Trading that exploits the feedback loop in heavily shorted stocks, where rising prices force short sellers to buy shares to cover, pushing prices higher still and forcing further covering. Squeeze traders position long in high-short-interest names ahead of or during such cascades - a volatility event trade, not a valuation strategy. Every short seller is a future guaranteed buyer; when the price rises enough that their losses force buying, the squeeze feeds on itself as the available float shrinks exactly when demand explodes.

Trading around the downside mirror of a short squeeze: sharp price declines that force leveraged or stop-protected long holders to sell, whose selling pressures more longs into selling and accelerates the drop. The trade either shorts into the cascade or buys the capitulation once forced selling exhausts. Crowded longs with stops at the same levels are dominoes: the first forced sales hit the next stops, and a normal dip becomes an air pocket - the squeeze trader profits from the mechanics of others' exits.

The core pairs-trading position: when the spread between two historically co-moving securities diverges beyond a threshold, short the outperformer and buy the underperformer in expectation that the spread converges back to its historical relation. Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) formalized the rule, matching pairs by minimum distance between normalized price series and trading divergences beyond two standard deviations. Two near-substitute stocks cannot stay mispriced relative to each other forever; the convergence trade sells whichever got too expensive and buys whichever got too cheap, hedging out the market's direction.

a: divergence entry (pairs) pairs spread opening trade
x: The entry logic of a pairs trade: positioning as the spread between two linked securities diverges to an extreme, on the expectation that the divergence has run its course and the spread will close. In the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst framework, divergence beyond two historical standard deviations is precisely the event that triggers the dollar-neutral position. Divergence is the signal, not the enemy: you wait for the rubber band between two stocks to stretch beyond historical tolerance, then take the position that profits as it snaps back.

a: volume study effort versus result analysis
x: The study of trading volume — the number of shares or contracts exchanged over a period — and of how that volume behaves relative to price movement, used to gauge the participation and conviction behind a move. In the Wyckoff tradition it is formalized as the effort-versus-result principle: volume is the effort, price change is the result. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law. Price tells you what happened; volume tells you how much conviction was behind it. The same price move means something different on heavy participation than on a thin, uninterested tape.

The joint behavior of price change and traded volume, read as the link between effort (volume) and result (price progress). Wyckoff-style analysis treats harmony between the two as trend-confirming and discord between them as a warning that the supply-demand balance is shifting. It is a qualitative framework, not a statistical law. Like a car climbing a hill, a trend needs fuel: rising prices on rising volume look powered, while rising prices on falling volume look like coasting.

The use of expanding volume to validate a price move: breakouts, trend legs, and reversals are considered more credible when accompanied by above-average participation. Within Wyckoff logic, confirmation is effort (volume) producing a result (price movement) commensurate with it. A price level that the crowd actually had to trade through to break carries more information than one that slipped away in a thin book.

A discrepancy in which price registers a new extreme while volume fails to confirm it — for example a higher high made on noticeably lower volume than the prior high — read in Wyckoff and volume-spread practice as diminishing effort behind the trend. It is a warning heuristic, not a stand-alone timing signal. If each new push in the trend direction attracts fewer participants, the move may be running out of fuel even while price still advances.

An extreme volume surge — typically the heaviest volume in many bars and several times the recent average — occurring after an extended directional move and accompanied by a wide price spread. In Wyckoff analysis it is the volume signature of a buying or selling climax: the terminal effort of a crowd capitulating or chasing. When everyone who was going to trade finally rushes in at once, the burst of activity can mark the end of a move rather than its acceleration.

A pronounced contraction of volume during a pullback or a test of a prior extreme, interpreted in Wyckoff methodology as a drying up of pressure from the side being tested: secondary tests and springs are expected to occur on markedly lower volume than the climax that preceded them. If price revisits a level and hardly anyone trades, the side that drove it there last time may have run out of ammunition.

In Wyckoff's distribution schematic, the buying climax (BC) is the terminal event of an advance: a marked expansion of volume and price spread as urgent public buying near the top is filled by professional interests distributing positions. It is a descriptive label for auction behavior, confirmed only when further upside progress fails. The most euphoric buying tends to appear exactly where large operators need that public demand to sell into without depressing the price themselves.

In Wyckoff's accumulation schematic, the selling climax (SC) is the terminal event of a decline: widening spread and climactic selling pressure as panicked public selling is absorbed by large interests near the lows, typically on the heaviest volume of the down-move. It is confirmed only after the automatic rally and a successful secondary test. Capitulation day: when the last fearful sellers dump their positions, stronger hands can finally buy in size without moving the price against themselves.

a: bid trade volume volume at bid
x: The total traded volume classified as having occurred at the bid price — trades initiated by aggressive sellers whose market or marketable sell orders matched resting buy limit orders. It is the sell-initiated component of bid/ask order-flow analysis. Bid volume measures how much selling was aggressive enough to cross the spread and hit the prices buyers had posted.

a: ask trade volume volume at ask offer volume
x: The total traded volume classified as having occurred at the ask (offer) price — trades initiated by aggressive buyers whose market or marketable buy orders lifted resting sell limit orders. It is the buy-initiated component of bid/ask order-flow analysis. Ask volume shows how urgently buyers were willing to pay the seller's posted price rather than wait for a fill at the bid.

The net difference between volume traded at the ask (aggressive market buys) and volume traded at the bid (aggressive market sells) over a price level, bar, or period. It measures which side initiated more traded volume, on the premise that market orders are what move prices. It is a descriptive order-flow statistic, not a predictive signal by itself. Delta answers 'who was more impatient — buyers or sellers?' Positive delta means buyers lifted more offers than sellers hit bids.

The running accumulation of per-bar or per-trade volume delta over a chosen period (typically a session or an entire contract), showing the evolving net balance of aggressive buying versus aggressive selling. It summarizes who has dominated market-order flow since the chosen starting point. If delta is the score of each play, cumulative delta is the scoreboard of the whole game — it shows whether buyers or sellers have been net aggressive all session long.

A mismatch between price direction and volume delta: for example, price printing a new high while bar delta or cumulative delta fails to make a corresponding new high, indicating that the aggressive order flow no longer supports the price move. Practitioners read it as a warning of weakening initiative or active absorption by the passive side. If price keeps climbing but buyers are swinging less hard each push, someone on the other side may be quietly absorbing their market orders.

A chart type that decomposes each price bar into its constituent price levels and displays, for every level, the volume traded there — typically split between bid-side and ask-side trades, or shown as delta. It makes the intra-bar auction visible instead of showing only open, high, low, and close. A candlestick tells you where price went; a footprint shows you the fight that happened at each price along the way.

a: Bid x Ask footprint bid/ask footprint
x: The most common footprint display mode: at every price level inside a bar, two numbers are shown side by side — the volume traded at the bid (seller-initiated) and the volume traded at the ask (buyer-initiated). It exposes where aggressive buying and selling actually occurred within each bar. It is the scoreboard of the intra-bar fight, level by level: how much sellers hit bids versus how much buyers lifted offers at each price.

A footprint display mode in which each price level inside a bar shows the volume delta at that level — ask-traded volume minus bid-traded volume — rather than the raw bid and ask numbers. It highlights where net aggressive buying or selling was concentrated within the bar. Instead of showing both sides' scores, it shows only who won each price level and by how much.

A footprint display mode in which each price level inside a bar shows the total volume traded at that level, regardless of side. It reveals the intra-bar volume distribution — which prices attracted business and which were skipped — rather than the buy/sell split. It answers 'where inside this bar did the market actually do business?', exposing high-volume shelves and low-volume gaps within a single candle.

A footprint analysis mode that flags price levels where one side's traded volume overwhelms the other by a set ratio — commonly 3:1 or more — typically comparing the ask volume at one level diagonally against the bid volume at the level below (and vice versa). It is used to locate levels where aggressive flow was strongly one-sided. An imbalance marks a price where the fight was lopsided: one side hit or lifted with at least several times the force of the other.

A cluster of bid/ask imbalances occurring at several adjacent price levels within the same bar — typically three or more consecutive levels exceeding the imbalance ratio on the same side. It indicates sustained one-sided aggression across a price zone rather than at a single level. One lopsided level can be chance; a whole staircase of lopsided levels shows a determined initiative push through a zone.

A market condition in which sustained aggressive market orders hit a price level but fail to move it, because resting limit orders repeatedly fill the incoming flow. Heavy traded volume with little or no price progress is the footprint signature of a large passive participant absorbing the aggressive side. It is like waves breaking against a seawall: the market orders keep arriving, but a wall of limit orders soaks them up and price refuses to budge.

a: order-flow exhaustion buyer exhaustion seller exhaustion
x: The fading of aggressive order flow near the end of a move: successive pushes in the trend direction are made on shrinking market-order volume, showing that the initiating side is running out of participants willing to chase the price. On a footprint it appears as very small traded volume at the bar extreme compared with earlier bars in the move. The auction runs out of bidders: price may still tick to a new extreme, but almost nobody is left willing to trade there.

a: iceberg order detection hidden liquidity detection
x: The inference of iceberg orders — limit orders whose exchange-visible displayed size is only a small tip of a much larger hidden total — from market data. Because exchanges do not report the hidden size, detection algorithms watch for a displayed quote that keeps replenishing after executions, or trade volume at a price exceeding the displayed size. If the same 50-lot offer keeps reappearing after being hit and thousands of contracts trade through it, something much bigger is sitting below the waterline.

a: big trade large print block-size print
x: A single executed trade (or an exchange-fragmented series of prints from one large order) whose size is far above the typical trade size for that instrument, taken in order-flow practice as a sign of institutional participation. Platforms surface them with filters that flag prints above absolute or adaptive size thresholds. Retail trades in ones and tens; when a 2,000-lot print hits the tape, someone with serious size is doing business.

A privately negotiated futures, options, or combination transaction that is permitted to be executed apart from the public auction market (the central limit order book) and is then submitted to the exchange for clearing. On CME Group venues, participation is restricted to Eligible Contract Participants as defined in the Commodity Exchange Act, and each product has a minimum quantity threshold (CME Rule 526 regime). Two institutions agree a big price privately, then hand the trade to the exchange to clear — letting size change hands without tipping off or sweeping the public order book.

A real-time, trade-by-trade record of executions in an instrument, showing for each trade its time, price, and volume (and typically direction relative to the bid/ask). It is the modern digital descendant of the ticker tape and the raw feed from which footprint and delta statistics are built. Time and sales is the market's transaction ledger: every fill, in sequence, with its size and price.

The practice of inferring short-term buying and selling pressure by watching the stream of executed trades — originally the ticker tape, today the time-and-sales window — focusing on trade size, speed, and whether prints occur at the bid or the ask. It is one of the oldest forms of order-flow analysis, descending from the era of Wyckoff and Livermore. Instead of studying charts after the fact, the tape reader watches each transaction as it happens, sensing urgency from the rhythm and size of the prints.

a: Market Profile TPO chart TPO profile
x: A charting method developed by J. Peter Steidlmayer at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s that organizes a session's trading as a distribution: each price traded during each time bracket (conventionally 30 minutes, labeled A, B, C…) receives that bracket's letter, building a horizontal histogram of time-at-price. It is a way of organizing market-generated data for auction-market analysis — a chart format, not an indicator or a predictive system. Instead of plotting price against time, the profile plots time spent at each price, revealing where the market accepted value (fat middle) and where it rejected prices (thin tails).

The atomic unit of a Market Profile chart: one TPO records that the market had the opportunity to trade at a given price during a given time bracket (conventionally 30 minutes). Each bracket is assigned a letter, and that letter is stamped at every price the market touched during the bracket. A TPO is one half-hour 'vote' for a price — the more brackets that traded at a level, the more time the market accepted it.

In Market Profile, the price range in which approximately 70% of the session's TPOs (or, in volume-based variants, of traded volume) fall, bounded by the value area high (VAH) and value area low (VAL). The 70% convention approximates one standard deviation of a normal distribution and is read as the range where the market accepted price as fair value. The value area is where the auction actually did business — the prices both buyers and sellers kept agreeing on all day.

The price level with the greatest number of TPOs in a Market Profile — the longest row of the distribution, conventionally taken closest to the center of the range. It is interpreted as the session's fairest price: the level where the market spent the most time and, in Dalton's phrase, the fairest price at which to trade. The POC is the price the market kept coming back to — the session's center of gravity.

a: single prints single TPO prints singles
x: A price row in a Market Profile occupied by letters from only one time bracket, showing the market passed through that price so quickly it traded there in just one period. Single prints at session extremes form buying or selling tails; single-print columns inside a profile separate distributions and mark levels the market did not accept. Single prints are the skid marks of a fast auction — prices the market touched once and fled, leaving a gap in the distribution.

A Market Profile structure in which the session's high lacks excess: the extreme is formed by two or more brackets printing the same (or nearly the same) high rather than a single-print tail, suggesting the upward auction ended from inventory exhaustion among short-term traders rather than genuine rejection. It is read as an 'unfinished' auction that price has a tendency to revisit. A proper top is a spike the market rejected; a poor high is a blunt top the market simply stopped at — leaving business that looks unfinished.

A Market Profile structure in which the session's low lacks excess: the extreme is formed by two or more brackets printing the same (or nearly the same) low instead of a single-print buying tail, suggesting the downward auction stopped from short-term inventory exhaustion rather than demonstrated rejection. It is read as an unfinished auction with a tendency to be revisited. A poor low is a blunt bottom: the market stopped falling at a price but never proved it rejected that price, so the level remains suspect.

a: buying tail selling tail auction excess
x: In Market Profile, excess is the single-print tail at an auction extreme: a run of prices printed by only one bracket at the top (selling tail) or bottom (buying tail) of the distribution, marking where the market moved quickly away and demonstrating rejection. Excess is the structural signature that an auction in that direction has completed. Excess is the market slamming a door: prices were tried, found unacceptable, and left behind so fast that only one period ever traded there.

a: balance area D-shaped profile rotational profile
x: A Market Profile structure in which the session's TPOs cluster in an overlapping, roughly bell-shaped distribution around a central value: buyers and sellers found relative agreement, and price rotated back and forth within a range. Consecutive days with overlapping ranges and value areas define a multi-day balance or bracket. A balanced profile is a market at rest: neither side had the conviction to reprice, so trade piled up around a fair central price.

A Market Profile day type dominated from the open by longer-timeframe participants on one side: the initial balance is narrow, price extends the range repeatedly in one direction (one-time-framing, with successive brackets making higher highs or lower lows), and the profile is elongated and thin rather than bell-shaped. It is a structural description of strong directional conviction. On a trend day the market picks a direction early and never looks back — every rotation is shallow, and the close comes near the day's extreme.

A Market Profile day type in which the initial balance (first-hour range) is average to wide and holds for most of the session: the market rotates within or just beyond that early range, building a balanced, bell-shaped distribution with the point of control near the center. It is the most common day type, reflecting two-sided trade dominated by short-term participants. A normal day is the market's default setting: an early range is established, longer-term players see no reason to reprice, and the day rotates around fair value.

a: normal variation of a normal day
x: A Market Profile day type between a normal day and a trend day: the initial balance is somewhat narrower than on a normal day, and after the early range forms, longer-timeframe participants drive a one-sided range extension — commonly to roughly twice the initial range — before the market builds value around the extended area. The day starts quietly like a normal day, but partway through, bigger players step in on one side and push the auction to new ground.

a: neutral day (profile) neutral center day neutral extreme day
x: A Market Profile day type in which the initial balance is extended on both sides during the session: longer-timeframe buyers and sellers are both active but roughly matched, so the auction probes above and below the early range without either side taking control. Variants close near the day's center (neutral center) or near an extreme (neutral extreme). A neutral day is a tug-of-war: both sides show up, both push, and by the close neither has won.

a: double distribution day DD day trend multi-distribution day
x: A Market Profile day type in which the session forms two distinct value distributions separated by a column of single prints: after an initial balance and first rotation, longer-timeframe participants reprice the market to a new region, where a second balance forms and typically holds into the close. It is a structured form of trend day in which the market repriced mid-session. The market built one fair-value zone, decisively abandoned it, sprinted through a no-man's land of single prints, and built a second fair-value zone higher (or lower).

A charting study that displays, for a specified period, a horizontal histogram of total traded volume at each price level. Unlike the TPO-based Market Profile, which counts time brackets at price, the volume profile counts contracts or shares actually traded at price, revealing where business concentrated and where it was absent. It rotates the volume histogram 90 degrees: instead of volume per time bar, you see volume per price — the market's actual footprint of where trading happened.

The price level within a volume profile at which the greatest volume traded during the measured period — the highest-volume row of the histogram. It is the volume-based counterpart of the TPO point of control and is read as the price of maximum two-sided agreement by traded quantity. The VPOC is where the most contracts actually changed hands — the market's busiest price over the period.

A peak in the volume profile — a price zone where traded volume was significantly higher than in neighboring zones. HVNs mark areas of accepted value where buyers and sellers did heavy two-sided business, and price commonly slows or consolidates when it re-enters them. An HVN is a crowded marketplace: lots of transactions happened there because both sides found the price acceptable.

A valley in the volume profile — a price zone where traded volume was significantly lower than in neighboring zones, typically because price moved through it quickly during a breakout or breakdown. LVNs mark prices the market did not accept, and price tends either to traverse them quickly again or to bounce off their edges. An LVN is a stretch of road the market drove through without stopping — few transactions ever cleared there.

The value area computed from a volume profile rather than from TPO counts: the contiguous price band around the volume point of control that contains a chosen percentage — conventionally 70% — of the period's total traded volume, bounded by the volume-based VAH and VAL. It is the price range where 70% of the actual contracts changed hands, as opposed to the TPO value area's 70% of time.

A Market Profile or volume profile built by merging multiple sessions into one distribution, so that the combined structure of a multi-day balance, bracket, or swing becomes visible. Its composite point of control and value area aggregate activity across all included sessions and are treated as higher-weight references than single-session levels. One day's profile shows one battle; the composite shows the whole campaign — where the market has collectively done its business over weeks.

a: session volume profile SVP daily profile
x: A volume profile (or Market Profile) computed separately for each trading session, so that every day gets its own volume-at-price histogram with its own POC and value area. It is the standard per-day unit of profile analysis, with prior-session levels carried forward as references. Each session gets its own fingerprint of where business was done, and yesterday's fingerprint becomes today's map.

A volume profile computed over a user-selected, fixed span of the chart — the analyst manually anchors the start and end points, and the histogram shows how volume distributed across price levels within exactly that range. It isolates the volume structure of a chosen move, range, or event window. Instead of accepting session boundaries, you draw a box around the exact move you care about and ask: where inside this move did volume actually concentrate?

A volume profile computed over whatever bars are currently visible on the screen: the histogram and its POC, value area, and nodes automatically rebuild every time the user scrolls or zooms. It provides an always-current volume-at-price read of the displayed range without manual anchoring. The profile follows your eyes — zoom into a week and it profiles the week; zoom out to a year and it profiles the year.

A framework for understanding markets as continuous two-way auctions whose purpose is to facilitate trade: price advertises opportunities, and the market auctions up to attract sellers and down to attract buyers until trade occurs. Its central tenet is that price and value are distinct — value is where the market spends time and does volume, and markets alternate between balance (agreement) and imbalance (repricing). It is an interpretive philosophy, not a predictive model. A market behaves like an auction house: it keeps moving the price until buyers and sellers both show up, then does most of its business there until something changes.

In auction market theory, acceptance is the market demonstrating agreement with a price zone by spending time and doing volume there: repeated TPO prints and two-sided trade at a level show that both buyers and sellers are willing to transact at those prices. Acceptance inside a prior value area confirms balance; acceptance beyond it establishes value at new prices. Acceptance is the market lingering: if price arrives at a level and trade keeps happening there, the level is being treated as fair.

In auction market theory, rejection is the market demonstrating disagreement with a price zone by refusing to spend time there: price probes a level, finds no two-sided trade, and moves away quickly, leaving thin TPO rows, single prints, or a tail. Rejection of prices beyond value is the structural basis of tails, excess, and failed breakouts. Rejection is the market taking one look at a price and leaving — the auction tried the level and found no takers.

In Market Profile/auction terminology, initiative buying is aggressive buying occurring at or above the established value area — activity that is 'unexpected' at those prices because buyers are paying up through accepted value to push the auction toward new, higher value. It is the buying side of other-timeframe participation that breaks balance and drives range extension. Responsive buyers wait for cheap prices; initiative buyers chase — they buy where value already is, or above it, because they want prices to go higher.

In Market Profile/auction terminology, initiative selling is aggressive selling occurring at or below the established value area — 'unexpected' activity in which sellers hit bids through accepted value to force the auction toward new, lower value. It is the selling side of other-timeframe participation that breaks balance downward. Initiative sellers do not wait for a better price — they sell into and below value because they believe lower prices are coming.

In Market Profile/auction terminology, responsive buying is buying that appears below the established value area — the 'expected' behavior of buyers responding to prices that are cheap relative to accepted value. Responsive buying is what defends value area lows and rotates a balanced market back toward the point of control. Responsive buyers are bargain hunters: they step in when price gets cheap relative to where the market agreed value lies.

In Market Profile/auction terminology, responsive selling is selling that appears above the established value area — the 'expected' behavior of sellers responding to prices that are expensive relative to accepted value. Responsive selling caps rallies at value area highs and rotates balanced markets back toward the point of control. Responsive sellers are profit-takers at rich prices: when the market trades above agreed value, they sell into the strength.

a: Wyckoff analysis Wyckoff price cycle Wyckoff trading method
x: A discretionary technical-analysis framework developed by Richard D. Wyckoff in the early twentieth century that interprets price action, volume, and time to judge the supply/demand balance and hypothesized campaigns of large institutional operators. It organizes market movement into accumulation, markup, distribution, and markdown phases and is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law. Big players move markets by quietly building and unwinding large positions; if you can read their footprints in price and volume, you can trade in their direction instead of being trapped by them.

Wyckoff's heuristic device of treating all market fluctuations as if they were produced by one fictional large operator, the Composite Man, who plans, executes, and concludes campaigns of accumulation and distribution. It is a mental model for interpreting chart behavior, not the claim that a single entity actually controls prices. Pretend the whole market is one clever dealer running a shop: it builds inventory quietly, advertises to attract buyers at high prices, then sells out before prices fall.

The phase of the Wyckoff price cycle in which large interests buy a sizeable position inside a trading range after a downtrend, halting the decline and building the 'cause' for a later markup. It is a hypothesized pattern recognized through characteristic events and phases, not a guaranteed bottom formation. Smart money fills its shopping cart quietly while everyone else is still bearish; the price stops falling because every selloff gets absorbed.

The phase of the Wyckoff price cycle in which large interests sell (or short) a sizeable position inside a trading range after an uptrend, exhausting demand and building the 'cause' for a later markdown. It is a hypothesized topping structure, not a proven signal that prices must fall. The insiders quietly unload their holdings onto enthusiastic late buyers; the price stops rising because every rally meets a wall of supply.

A consolidation within an ongoing uptrend in which large operators take profits and acquire additional shares before the markup resumes. Wyckoff described these flat ranges as 'stepping stones' on the way to higher price targets. Halfway up the hill, the big players pause to catch their breath and reload, shaking out nervous holders before the next leg higher.

A consolidation within an ongoing downtrend in which remaining longs sell and large operators build or add to short positions before the markdown resumes. It mirrors reaccumulation on the downside and is identified only by the range's eventual downward resolution. During a bear market pause, hopeful buyers step in and the big players sell into that demand, restocking supply for the next leg down.

The Wyckoff event (PS) in which substantial buying first provides pronounced support after a prolonged decline, marked by widening price spread and increased volume that signal the downtrend may be approaching its end. It is an early warning, not a confirmed bottom. The first time in a long slide that buyers show up in force and noticeably slow the fall.

The Wyckoff event (AR) in which price rebounds sharply after a selling climax because intense selling pressure has been exhausted, fueled by institutional demand and short covering. Its high helps define the upper boundary of the accumulation trading range. Once the panic sellers are done, even modest buying pops the price back up, like a beach ball released underwater.

The Wyckoff event (ST) in which price revisits the area of a climax to test the supply/demand balance there. In accumulation, a successful secondary test shows significantly diminished volume and spread as price approaches the selling-climax low, confirming that supply is drying up. The market dips back toward the panic low to see if any frightened sellers are left; if hardly anyone sells this time, the bottom is more likely real.

The Wyckoff event in which price briefly breaks below the support of an accumulation trading range, then quickly reverses back into the range, trapping late sellers while large interests acquire remaining shares at bargain prices. It is a hypothesized bear-trap event whose bullish interpretation must be confirmed by subsequent strength; it is not a reliable standalone buy signal. A fake breakdown: price dips under support just far enough to scare out weak hands and trigger stops, then snaps right back.

A large, decisive version of a spring occurring at the end of an accumulation trading range, in which price breaks sharply below support and rapidly recovers, forcing the final transfer of shares from weak holders to large operators. The tutorial describes it as 'a spring on steroids'. The last violent flush that scares out everyone still holding, right before the real move up begins.

The Wyckoff event in which price revisits the low of a spring or shakeout to verify that supply is exhausted. A successful test makes a higher low (or holds near the spring low) on clearly lower volume, indicating the stock is ready for markup. After the fake breakdown, the market dips once more to double-check that no sellers remain; a quiet, low-volume dip passes the check.

The Wyckoff event (SOS) in which price advances on widening spread and relatively higher volume, showing demand in control; after accumulation, it often validates the preceding spring or test and typically carries price to or through the top of the trading range. The first rally with real conviction behind it, proving buyers have taken the wheel.

The Wyckoff event (LPS) marking the low of a reaction or pullback after a sign of strength, typically a retreat to former resistance-turned-support on diminished spread and volume. It is regarded as a low-risk area to initiate or add to long positions before markup. After the breakout rally, the market takes one last quiet step back to the old ceiling, now a floor — the final boarding call for longs.

n: Backup to the edge of the creek
a: back-up BU back up to the creek BUEC
x: The Wyckoff event (BU) in which price pulls back toward the resistance it just crossed with a sign of strength, combining profit-taking with a test for remaining supply around the old resistance area. The term comes from Robert Evans's creek metaphor and precedes a more substantial markup. After leaping over the creek of resistance, the market walks back to the water's edge to make sure the far bank is solid before marching on.

The Wyckoff event (PSY) in which large interests begin unloading shares in quantity after a pronounced advance, marked by expanding volume and widening price spread that signal a change of trend may be approaching. It mirrors preliminary support at market tops. The first time in a long climb that heavy selling shows up and noticeably slows the rise.

The Wyckoff event (AR) in distribution in which price falls sharply after a buying climax because intense buying has been exhausted while heavy supply continues. Its low helps define the lower boundary of the distribution trading range. Once the euphoric buyers are spent, the price drops on its own weight — no extra selling pressure needed.

The Wyckoff event (UT) in which price moves above the resistance of a trading range and then quickly reverses to close back inside the range, acting as a test of remaining demand and a trap for uninformed breakout buyers. It is the mirror image of a spring. A fake breakout: price pops above resistance just long enough to hook breakout traders, then falls back into the range.

The Wyckoff event (UTAD) occurring in the latter stages of a distribution trading range, in which price breaks above range resistance and then fails, providing a definitive test of new demand before markdown. It is the distributional counterpart of the spring and terminal shakeout in accumulation. One last fake breakout at the top of a topping range, engineered to squeeze shorts and unload remaining stock onto breakout buyers before the decline.

The Wyckoff event (SOW) in which price declines to or slightly below the lower boundary of a trading range on increased spread and volume, showing supply in control. Together with the automatic reaction, initial SOWs mark the change of character that precedes markdown. The first selloff with real conviction, proving sellers have taken control.

The Wyckoff event (LPSY) in which a feeble rally on narrow spread follows a sign of weakness, showing the market's inability to advance because of weak demand, substantial supply, or both. LPSYs represent the final waves of large operators' distribution and preferred areas for short entries before markdown. After support breaks, the market stages one last tired bounce — the final chance to get out or get short before the drop.

The first phase of a Wyckoff trading range, marking the stopping of the prior trend. In accumulation it contains preliminary support, the selling climax, the automatic rally, and secondary tests; in distribution it contains preliminary supply, the buying climax, the automatic reaction, and secondary tests. The moment the old trend finally runs out of gas — panic at bottoms, euphoria at tops — and the sideways battle begins.

The second phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which institutions build a 'cause' for the next trend by accumulating (or distributing) inventory over an extended period, sometimes a year or more. Its characteristic back-and-forth price action reflects large operators buying low and checking rallies (or the reverse in distribution). The long, boring middle of the range where the big players quietly load or unload the truck, one oscillation at a time.

The third phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which price undergoes a decisive test of remaining supply (accumulation) or demand (distribution), allowing large operators to judge whether the market is ready to leave the range. Springs, shakeouts, upthrusts, and UTADs are the characteristic Phase C events. The final exam: one engineered fake move probes whether any sellers (at bottoms) or buyers (at tops) are still out there.

The fourth phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which demand (accumulation) or supply (distribution) becomes consistently dominant: advances widen in spread and volume while reactions shrink, carrying price at least to the range boundary. LPSs and LPSYs in this phase are the framework's preferred position-entry areas. The tug-of-war ends and one side visibly wins — rallies get stronger and pullbacks weaker (or vice versa) as price presses toward the range edge.

The final phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which price departs the range and the new trend (markup or markdown) unfolds in the open, with demand or supply in full control. Setbacks are typically short-lived, and new higher- or lower-level ranges (reaccumulation or redistribution 'stepping stones') may form along the way. The range is over and the real move begins — the trend is now obvious to everyone.

Wyckoff's first law: when demand exceeds supply, prices rise; when supply exceeds demand, prices fall; and the balance is judged by comparing price and volume bars on a chart. It is the foundational heuristic of the method, a framework for reading charts rather than a measurable law of nature. More buyers than sellers pushes price up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down — and the tape tells you which side is winning.

Wyckoff's second law: the horizontal extent of accumulation or distribution within a trading range (the 'cause') is related to the distance of the subsequent trend out of that range (the 'effect'), allowing price objectives to be projected from point-and-figure counts. It is a heuristic projection technique, not a deterministic relationship. The longer and harder you compress the spring inside a range, the further price travels when it's released.

a: Wyckoff's third law effort vs. result volume-price divergence
x: Wyckoff's third law: divergences between volume (effort) and price movement (result) provide early warning of a possible change of trend. Harmony between effort and result suggests trend continuation; large effort with little result suggests absorption by large interests and a potential turn. If the market is pushing hard but going nowhere, someone big is standing in the way — and the direction of travel is about to change.

a: P&F count horizontal count Wyckoff count guide
x: Wyckoff's method of projecting price targets by counting the horizontal width of a trading range on a point-and-figure chart, embodying the law of cause and effect. The count measures the 'cause' built in the range and converts it into a projected 'effect' — a target zone rather than an exact destination. Measure how wide the base is, and that width tells you roughly how far the breakout should travel.

A Wyckoff metaphor, coined by teacher Robert Evans, for the zone of resistance at the upper boundary of an accumulation trading range — the 'creek' that price must jump across to begin markup. It is informal terminology for resistance, not a distinct technical pattern. Resistance is pictured as a stream of sellers; the market has to gather enough strength to leap over it.

A Wyckoff metaphor for the zone of support at the lower boundary of a distribution trading range, defined by the lows of the reactions within the range. Price that breaks decisively through it has 'fallen through the ice', marking the transition to markdown. Support is pictured as a frozen surface holding the market up; once it cracks, price plunges into the water below.

The Wyckoff metaphor for a sign of strength that decisively carries price above the resistance ('creek') of an accumulation trading range, signaling that demand has overcome the range's supply. It marks the transition from Phase D toward Phase E markup. The market finally leaps over the stream of sellers that capped every rally in the base.

The Wyckoff metaphor for a decisive downside break through the support ('ice') of a distribution trading range on wide price spreads and high or increasing volume, constituting a major sign of weakness and the first step of the markdown phase. The frozen floor under the market cracks and price plunges through — the downtrend has begun in earnest.

A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of buyers: typically an up-bar on narrow spread closing mid-range or lower on volume below that of the previous two bars. It signals that professional money is not interested in higher prices at that moment and warns of possible weakness ahead. The price ticks up but almost nobody is buying — a rally running on fumes.

a: test of supply NS no supply bar
x: A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of sellers: typically a down-bar on narrow spread closing off its low on volume below that of the previous two bars. It indicates that selling pressure has dried up and, in the right context, that higher prices are likely; Williams also called it a 'test of supply' and favored it for long entries. The price dips but almost nobody is selling — the path of least resistance is back up.
